(p-250) Surat Yusuf (upon him be peace) is Meccan, except verses 1, 2, 3 and 7, which are Medinan. Its verses number 111.

﴿Alif-Lam-Ra.﴾ The discussion of it, of its position, and of what is meant by the allusion (al-ishara), the verses (al-ayat) and the Book (al-kitab) in His saying ﴿These are the verses of the Book﴾ is exactly what preceded at the opening of Surat Yunus. ﴿Clear (al-mubin)﴾ is from abana, in the sense of baana (to be manifest), meaning: whose matter is manifest in that it is from God Most High, and in its inimitability (i'jaz) in both its kinds, especially its reports of the unseen (al-ghayb). Or it means: clear in its meanings to the Arabs, such that its realities are not confused for them and its subtleties are not obscure to them, because it was revealed in their language. Or it means in the sense of bayyin (evident), that is, it makes clear what it contains of rulings and laws (ahkam wa shara'i'), the hidden aspects of dominion and the realm of the unseen (al-mulk wa al-malakut), the secrets of the two states of existence (al-nash'atayn) in the two abodes, and other wisdoms, knowledge and narratives. And on the assumption that the Book refers to the surah, its making clear (ibana) is its informing about the story of Yusuf (upon him be peace). It has been narrated that the rabbis of the Jews said to the leaders of the polytheists: "Ask Muhammad (ﷺ) why the family of Ya'qub moved from Syria to Egypt, and about the story of Yusuf (upon him be peace)." They did so. Thus the description of the Book as clear is from the category of the excellence of the opening (bara'at al-istihlal) for what is to come. And when the Book was described with what indicates its intrinsic nobility, this was followed by what indicates its relative nobility, and so it was said:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 2:

﴿Indeed, We have sent it down﴾. That is: the Book described by the sublime attributes that have been mentioned. If it refers to the whole (and this is the more evident and more fitting, given His words, exalted is He, ﴿an Arabic Qur'an﴾, since it is the one well known by this name and familiar by this attribute, which comes immediately to mind when these two terms are used absolutely), then the matter is clear. If it is taken to refer to the surah, then its being called "Qur'an" is by virtue of what you have come to know previously. The secret behind this is that it is originally a noun of genus (ism jins) that applies to both the whole and the part, like "al-Kitab" (the Book). Or, it is a verbal noun (masdar) used in the sense of the passive participle (maf'ul), meaning: We have sent it down in a state where it is recited in your language ﴿so that you may understand﴾. That is: so that you may comprehend its meanings entirely, fully grasp the marvels within it, and come to know that it is beyond the capacity of humans, sent down from the Creator of powers and decree.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 3:

﴿We narrate to you﴾ means: We inform you and relate to you. Its derivation is from qassa athrahu, meaning he followed his trace, because one who relates a narrative follows what has been preserved of it bit by bit, just as it is said: talā al-Qur'an (he recited the Qur'an), because he follows what he has memorized of it verse after verse. ﴿the best of narratives﴾ means: the best of relating (iqtiṣāṣ). Its accusative is as a verbal noun (maṣdar) in two respects. Along with stating the reality, there is in it an implication (īhām) of the ugliness and defect found in the narrations of the People of the Book. The object is omitted either because it is understood from His words, Mighty and Majestic is He, ﴿by what We have revealed﴾, meaning: by Our revelation ﴿to you this Qur'an﴾, meaning: this surah. For its being revealed indicates that what is contained within it is narrated. The mention of its title as Qur'an is to establish that the relating is not by way of inspiration (ilhām) or non-recited revelation (waḥy ghayr al-matlū). Or it is because it is evident from the question of the polytheists, prompted by the scholars of the Jews. And its being the best is because it has been related in the most wondrous, splendid and refined methods, and the most amazing, surpassing and fitting styles, as is hardly hidden from anyone who has studied the story in the books of the earlier and later generations, even if he cannot distinguish the worthless from the valuable nor tell the left from the right. In the word "this" (hādhā) there is an indication of the difference between this Qur'an and what is in His words, Exalted is He, ﴿an Arabic Qur'an﴾, in that the intended meaning of that is the whole collection. So reflect.

Or: We narrate to you the best of what We narrate of the reports, which is the story of the family of Ya'qub, peace be upon him. On the basis that qaṣaṣ is a verb (fa'al) in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ūl), like nabaʾ and khabar, or a verbal noun by which the object is named, like khalq and ṣayd. (Aḥsan) is in the accusative as an object, and its being the best is because it includes wisdoms and lessons whose perfect excellence is not hidden.

﴿And indeed you were﴾: "in" (in) is a lightened form of the heavy one, the pronoun of the matter that is its subject is omitted, the lām is a distinguishing particle, and the clause is the predicate. The meaning: and indeed the matter is that you were ﴿before it﴾, before Our revelation to you of this surah, ﴿among the unaware﴾ of this story, it had not occurred to your mind, and it had never struck your hearing at all. This is an explanation for his being revealed to. The expression of lack of knowledge as heedlessness is to honour the status of the Prophet ﷺ, even though some of the heedless were unaware of him.

﴿When Joseph said﴾ is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb, "remember" (udhkur). It marks the beginning of the narrative, in fulfilment of the promise to relate the best of stories in the best manner. Alternatively, it is a substitute (badal) for "the best of stories" if that phrase is taken as the object, being a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal). The relating of the time that contains the event is, insofar as it contains it, a relating of the event itself.

"Yusuf" (Joseph) is a Hebrew name, not an Arabic one, since it has no other reason for indeclinability besides being a proper noun. The vowelling of the sin with fatha and with kasra in some readings is based on treating the name as a word subject to variation, not on its being a present-tense verb in the passive or active from asafa. This is because of the well-known evidence that it is a foreign name.

﴿to his father﴾, Ya'qub (Jacob), son of Ishaq (Isaac), son of Ibrahim (Abraham), peace be upon them all. It has been related from him (ﷺ): "Indeed the noble, son of the noble, son of the noble, son of the noble, is Yusuf, son of Ya'qub, son of Ishaq, son of Ibrahim."

﴿O my father﴾: the original form is "ya abi," and the feminine ending (ta' marbuta, taʾ al-taʾnith) was put in place of the yāʾ, because the two are alike in being added. Hence it is pronounced as a hāʾ when stopping, according to the reading of Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub. Its kasra is because it is a substitute for a letter that suits it. Ibn 'Amir read it with a fatha throughout the Qur'an, because it is the vowel of its original form; or because the original was "ya abata," so the alif was dropped and the fatha remained. The form "ya abati" is not permitted because it combines the substitute and what it substitutes. It was also read with a damma, treating it like feminine nouns ending in taʾ without considering the substitution. It is not left with sukun as its original form would be, because it is a sound consonant treated as a noun, so it must be vowelled, like the kaf of address.

﴿Indeed I saw﴾: this is from ru'ya (dream), not from ru'yah (sight), because of His words: ﴿Do not relate your dream﴾ and ﴿This is the interpretation of my dream﴾. Also, the apparent sense is that such wondrous events occurring in the world of witness are not limited to the seeing of one person over another, so it would be a great sign that is not hidden from anyone among people.

﴿eleven (p-252) stars, and the sun and the moon﴾. It is related from Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him, that "a Jew came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'Tell me, O Muhammad, about the stars that Joseph (peace be upon him) saw.' The Prophet (ﷺ) remained silent, so Jibril (peace be upon him) descended and informed him of that. He (ﷺ) said: 'If I tell you, will you become Muslim?' He said: 'Yes.' He (ﷺ) said: 'Jaryan, al-Tiraq, al-Dhayyal, Qabis, 'Amudan, al-Fulayq, al-Musbih, al-Daruh, al-Far', Wathab, and Dhu al-Kaftayn, which Joseph (peace be upon him) saw, and the sun and the moon descended from the sky and prostrated to him.' The Jew said: 'By Allah, these are indeed their names.'"

It has also been said that the sun and the moon are his parents, and it has been said that they are his father and his maternal aunt, and the stars are his brothers. The sun and the moon are mentioned after the stars to show their distinction and nobility above all the other risings, by conjoining them with the stars, as in the conjunction of Jibril and Mika'il with the angels (peace be upon them). It has been permitted that the waw be in the sense of "with," meaning: "I saw the stars with the sun and the moon." It is not far-fetched that this indicates the delay of his meeting them (the sun and the moon) compared with his meeting his brothers.

It is related from Wahb that Joseph (peace be upon him), when he was seven years old, saw that eleven long staves were fixed in the ground in the shape of a circle, and suddenly a small staff leapt upon them until it uprooted them and overcame them. He described that to his father, who said: "Beware of mentioning this to your brothers." Then, when he was twelve years old, he saw the sun, the moon and the stars prostrating to him, and related it to his father, who said: "Do not relate it to them, lest they plot evil against you." It has been said that between Joseph's dream and the coming of his brothers to him there were forty years, and it has been said eighty.

﴿I saw them prostrating to me﴾: this is a resumed sentence (isti'naf) explaining their state in which he saw them, as if a questioner asked: "How did you see them?" and he answered with that. The pronoun is treated as for rational beings because they are described with a description of rational beings, namely prostration. The placing of the prepositional phrase first is to show care and concern for what is more important, along with what it entails regarding the preservation of the rhyme (fasila).

Abu al-Su'ud, Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, on surah 12, verse 5:

﴿He said: "O my little son!"﴾ He diminished him (into the diminutive "bunayya") out of affection, or on account of her (the affection) and his young age. This is also a resumed sentence (isti'naf), answering the question of one who asks: "What did Ya'qub say after hearing this wondrous vision?" When Ya'qub, peace be upon him, recognized from this vision that Yusuf would be brought by Allah the Exalted to a sublime degree of wisdom, would be chosen by Him for prophethood, and would be blessed with the honour of both abodes, as He had done with his noble forefathers, he feared for him the envy and insolence of the brothers. So he said, to protect them from that and to spare him the hardships of toil and the suffering of sorrows, even though he was certain that Allah the Exalted would certainly bring that about, and hoping that it would be attained without hardship: ﴿Do not relate your vision﴾. The ru'ya (vision) is what is in sleep, just as the ru'ya (sight) is what is in wakefulness; they are distinguished by the two feminine endings, as in al-qurba (kinship) and al-qurba (nearness). Its reality is the imprinting of a form descending from the horizon of the imaginal faculty (al-mutakhayyila) onto the common sense (al-hiss al-mushtarak). The true one among them occurs only through the connection of the soul with the malakut (the realm of sovereignty), due to the affinity between them, when the soul is at its least occupied with managing the body; so it is imagined with what is in it of meanings befitting that realm, and then the imaginal faculty represents it in a form suited to it and sends it to the common sense, where it becomes something witnessed. Then, if it is highly proportionate to that meaning, such that the difference is only in generality and particularity, the vision dispenses with interpretation; otherwise it requires it.

﴿against your brothers, so that they will plot﴾ is in the accusative by the implied "an" (that), i.e., "so that they will do" (p-253) ﴿against you﴾, i.e., for your sake and for your destruction, ﴿a plot﴾, firm and established, from which you cannot escape, or hidden from your understanding, so that you do not confront its repelling. This suits the context of warning better, although Ya'qub, peace be upon him, knew that they were not capable of altering what the vision indicated would occur. This phrasing is more emphatic than saying "so that they will plot against you a plot," since it does not indicate that the act itself is intended to be carried out. It has been said: the lam was used to imply the meaning of "scheming," which takes the lam, so as to convey the meanings of both the implied and the implying for emphasis, i.e., "so that they will scheme for you and for your destruction a stratagem and a plot." The brothers here meant by "brothers" are those whose treachery and schemes he feared: the eleven half-brothers, namely Yahudha, Rubil, Shim'un, Lawi, Rabalun, Yashjur, and Dayna, sons of Ya'qub by Layya, daughter of his maternal aunt; and Dan, Naftali, Jad, and Asher, his sons by two concubines, Zulfa and Bulha. These are the ones referred to by the eleven stars.

As for Binyamin, who is the full brother of Yusuf, peace be upon him, and their mother is Rahil, whom Ya'qub married after the death of her sister Layya, or during her lifetime, since joining two sisters was not forbidden at that time, he is not included under this prohibition, since no harm from him is to be feared and no disgrace is to be dreaded; and he was not counted among them in the vision, since he was not with them in prostrating to Yusuf. The intent of the prohibition is to forbid him from relating the vision to them, all of them or some of them.

﴿Indeed, Satan is to man a clear enemy﴾: manifest in enmity, so he spares no effort in misleading your brothers, leading them astray, and driving them to what holds no good. This is a resumed sentence, as if Yusuf, peace be upon him, had said: "How could that come from my brothers, who were raised in the house of prophethood?" So it was said: Satan drives them to that. When he (Ya'qub), peace be upon both of them, alerted him that his vision had a great matter which would entail benefits, and warned him against spreading it, which would lead his brothers to come between it and the appearance of its effects and its realization, or to make the path to its attainment difficult, he began to interpret it and explain it in a general manner, saying:

**[Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud, *Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim*, on Surah 12, verse 6]**

﴿وَكَذَلِكَ﴾ *wa-kadhālika* (And thus): that is, like that wondrous *ijtibā'* (choosing), whose effects you witnessed in the world of images (*ʿālam al-mithāl*, the realm of imaginal forms) in the prostration of those luminous celestial bodies to you, and in accordance with it and in conformity with it. ﴿يَجْتَبِيكَ رَبُّكَ﴾ *yajtabīka rabbuka* (Your Lord will choose you): He will select you for the presence of His majesty and will make you a prophet (*yastanbiʾuka*). *Ijtibā'* is an *iftiʿāl* form from *jabāhu*, meaning he gathered it. ﴿وَيُصْطَفِيكَ﴾ *wa-yaṣṭafīka* (and will choose you): He will prefer you above the noblest of creation and the chiefs of all people. ﴿وَيُعَلِّمُكَ﴾ ... 

Hold on, let me restate the translation in order, without skipping anything.

﴿وَكَذَلِكَ﴾ (And thus): that is, like that wondrous *ijtibāʾ* (choosing) whose traces you witnessed in the world of images (*ʿālam al-mithāl*, the realm of imaginal forms), namely the prostration to you of those luminous celestial bodies, and in accordance with it and in conformity with it. ﴿يَجْتَبِيكَ رَبُّكَ﴾ (Your Lord will choose you): He will select you for the court of His majesty and will make you a prophet (*yastanbiʾuka*). *Ijtibāʾ* is an *iftiʿāl* form from *jabāhu*, meaning he gathered it. ﴿وَيُصْطَفِيكَ﴾ (and will choose you): He will prefer you over the noblest of creatures and the chiefs of people, all of them. ﴿وَيُبْرِزُ مِصْداقَ تِلْكَ الرُّؤْيا﴾ (and will bring forth the fulfilment of that vision): He will manifest the realisation of that dream in the world of witnessing (*ʿālam al-shahāda*, the visible world), exactly as you saw it, without any shortfall. The purpose of the comparison is to show the correspondence that exists between the forms seen in the world of images and what those forms became, as visible beings in the world of witnessing, according to their likeness. That is: just as those great celestial bodies were subjected to you, so He will subject to you the faces and foreheads of people, who will submit to your obedience, humbly subjected to you in a state of abasement. What is meant is an indication of the obedience of his parents and brothers to him, but he did not state it explicitly, out of fear of its being made public.

﴿وَيُعَلِّمُكَ﴾ (And He will teach you) is a new, independent sentence, not included under the comparison. By it, peace be upon him, he intended to confirm and establish his statement, and to reassure Yusuf, peace be upon him, regarding what he was told, in the manner of interpreting and explaining, as if he had said: "and He is teaching you..."

﴿مِن تَأْوِيلِ الأحادِيثِ﴾ (of the interpretation of narratives): that is, that kind of knowledge, or a suitable portion of it, so that you may perceive the truth of what I say. There is no concealing what this contains of confirming what came before, and of urging the acceptance of what is to come. The "interpretation of narratives" means the interpretation of dreams, since they are the "narratives" of the king if they are true, or the narratives of the self or of Satan if they are not. *Aḥādīth* is a collective noun (*ism jamʿ*) for *ḥadīth*, just as *abāṭīl* is a collective noun for *bāṭil*, and not the plural of *uḥdūthah*. It has been said that they formed *aḥdithah* as a plural of *ḥadīth*, then made the plural of that plural *aḥādīth*, like *qaṭīʿ* / *aqṭiʿah* / *aqāṭīʿ*. It has also been said that it means the interpretation of the obscure parts of God's books and the practices (*sunan*) of the prophets, peace be upon them. The first view is the more apparent. The naming of dream interpretation as *taʾwīl* is because the seen thing is made to return (*āʾil*) to what the interpreter mentions in the course of interpreting, and to revert to it. So he, upon whom be blessings and peace, by this indicated what would happen to Yusuf, peace be upon him, in his interpreting the dreams of the two companions of the prison and the dream of the king, and that this would be a means to what God would grant him of supreme rule, which was expressed by "completing the blessing." Ya'qub, peace be upon him, knew this about him through revelation. Or he meant that this quality would be a cause of the manifestation of his affair, peace be upon him, in general. In that case it is permissible that his knowledge, peace be upon him, of this came by way of physiognomy (*firāsa*) and inference from evidences, indications, signs, and tokens: that whoever God has enabled to have such a dream must be enabled to interpret it and interpret its like, and to distinguish what in it is external (*āfāqī*) from what is internal (*anfusī*). How could it not be so, when it indicates the perfection of his soul's establishment in the world of images and the strength of its dealings there? So he would be most receptive to the overflow of knowledge connected with that world and with what it represents of events occurring in correspondence with it in the world of witnessing, and more firmly aware of the relations existing between the forms seen in one of those two worlds and the beings manifest in accordance with them in the other world. This wondrous state must necessarily be a model for the manifestation of the affair of whoever possesses it, and a basis for the operation of his rulings. For every prophet, peace be upon them, has a miracle through which his effects appear and his rulings take effect.

﴿وَيُتِمُّ نِعْمَتَهُ عَلَيْكَ﴾ (and will complete His blessing upon you): by joining to the prophethood derived from the *ijtibāʾ* the kingship, and making it its completion. The mention of teaching placed between them is because it is one of the necessities of prophethood and *ijtibāʾ*, and in observance of the order of external existence, and for what we pointed to, that its effect is a means to the completion of the blessing. It is also permissible to count the vision itself among the blessings of God upon him, so that all the blessings reaching him according to it are its fulfilment, a complete completion of that blessing.

﴿وَعَلى آلِ يَعْقُوبَ﴾ (and upon the family of Ya'qub): they are his household, including his sons and others. Yusuf's seeing his brothers as stars by whose lights they are guided is among the blessings of God upon them, since it indicates that their affair will end in prophethood. Thus everything among their perfections that passes from potential to actual will, according to that, be a completion of that blessing without doubt. As for if the completion of that blessing is meant to be kingship, then it is so in relation to them in the sense that they will benefit from its effects in honour, status, and wealth.

﴿كَما أتَمَّها عَلى أبَوَيْكَ﴾ (just as He completed it upon your two forefathers): an accusative in the sense of a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), meaning: and He will complete His blessing upon you with a completion like His completion of His blessing upon your two forefathers, which is the blessing of messengership and prophethood.

Its completion upon Ibrahim, peace be upon him, was by taking him as a *khalīl* (intimate friend), delivering him from the fire, and from slaughtering his son. Upon Ishaq, by delivering him from being slaughtered, and ransoming him with a great sacrifice, and by bringing forth Ya'qub and the tribes from his loins. All of these are magnificent blessings that came to complete the blessing of prophethood. It is not required, in establishing the comparison, that what occurred on the side of the comparandum (*mushabbah bihi*) be exactly like what occurred on the side of the compared (*mushabbah*) in every respect.

﴿مِن قَبْلُ﴾ (before): that is, before this time, or before you. ﴿إبْراهِيمَ وإسْحاقَ﴾ (Ibrahim and Ishaq): an appositive (*ʿaṭf bayān*) to "your two forefathers." The expression of them as "fathers" although they were his grandfather and great-grandfather is to indicate the perfection of his connection to the noble prophets, peace be upon them, and to recall the saying (*"al-walad sirr abīhi"*, "the child is the secret of his father"), so that his heart might be reassured by what he was told within the general interpretation of his dream. The restriction, in the comparandum, to mentioning the completion of the blessing without alluding to the *ijtibāʾ* is for economy, since the completion of the blessing necessarily presupposes a prior blessing that calls for the *ijtibāʾ*.

﴿إنَّ رَبَّكَ﴾ (Indeed your Lord): a resumptive sentence confirming the content of the sentences mentioned, that is: He does what has been mentioned, because He is ﴿عَلِيمٌ﴾ (All-Knowing) of everything, so He knows who deserves *ijtibāʾ*, and what follows from it of the mentioned teaching, and the completion of the general blessing in the manner mentioned. ﴿حَكِيمٌ﴾ (All-Wise): the doer of everything as wisdom and benefit require, so He does what He does as He does, following the course of His knowledge and wisdom. The mention of the title "Lord" in both places is to reinforce the certainty of the occurrence of the acts mentioned.

This is it. It has been said regarding the interpretation of this noble verse: that is, just as He chose you for such a dream, which indicates honour, might, and perfection of soul, your Lord will choose you for prophethood and kingship, or for great affairs. And He will complete His blessing upon you with prophethood, or by joining the blessing of this world to the blessing of the Hereafter, since He made them prophets and kings in this world and then transferred them from it to the high ranks in Paradise. Just as He completed it upon your two forefathers with messengership. So reflect. And God is the Guide.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 7:

﴿Indeed, in Joseph and his brothers﴾ That is, in their story. Here, "them" (al-muradu bihim) may refer either to all of them, since Benjamin also has a share in the story, or to the sons of his father by another mother (bani 'allatihi), who were mentioned earlier, since the story revolves around them. ﴿are signs﴾ great signs of great importance, indicating the overpowering power of God Most High and His dazzling wisdom, ﴿for those who ask﴾ for everyone who asks about their story and its account, or for those who seek the signs and take lessons from them, for they are the ones who comprehend them and benefit from them, to the exclusion of others who fall under the words of God Most High: ﴿And how many a sign in the heavens and the earth they pass by, yet they turn away from it﴾. So "the story" (al-qissa) refers to the narrated account itself, or to the Prophet's (ﷺ) prophethood, for those among the polytheists or Jews who asked him about their story, and he informed them of it as it truly was, without having heard it from anyone and without having studied any books. Thus "its narration" (iqtisasuha) is what is meant, and the plural "signs" (al-ayat) in this case is to indicate that the narration of each portion of the story is a clear sign sufficient to demonstrate his prophethood (peace be upon him), in the manner mentioned in the words of God Most High: ﴿the station of Abraham﴾, on the assumption that it is an explanatory apposition (atf bayan) to the words of God Most High: ﴿clear signs﴾, not as some have said, that it is due to the multiplicity of aspects of inimitability, both in wording and meaning.

Ibn Kathir recited: (ayatun) [in the singular], and in some codices it reads (ibratun) [lesson]. It has been said: God Most High related to the Prophet (ﷺ) the account of Joseph and the envy of his brothers toward him, because He saw the oppression his own people inflicted upon him, so that he might take comfort in it (li-ya'tasiya bihi).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 8:

﴿When they said: "Joseph and his brother"﴾ That is, his full brother, Benjamin. The reason he was not mentioned by name is an allusion that the basis of the love was his brotherhood with Joseph from both sides. Do you not see how they were content merely to remove Joseph from the scene without any attack on him? For they said: ﴿"Kill Joseph"﴾.

﴿"Dearer to our father than we are"﴾ The predicate is given in the singular despite the plurality of the subject, because (afʿalu min kadha, "more ... than such-and-such") is not differentiated between the singular and what is above it, nor between the masculine and the feminine. Yes, when it is definite the differentiation is required, and when it is in a construct phrase both forms are permissible. The benefit of the lam of emphasis (lam al-ibtida') on "Joseph" is to establish and reinforce the content of the sentence.

﴿"And we are a band"﴾ That is, while we are a group capable of loosing and binding, deserving of love. The ʿusba (band) and al-ʿiṣaba (troop) are ten men or more; they were so named because affairs are bound (tuʿṣabu, "gathered") by them. ﴿"Indeed our father is"﴾ in preferring the two of them over us in love, despite our superiority over them and their being far from sufficiency in affairs due to their youth and fewness, ﴿"in clear error"﴾ That is, going astray from the path of the fitting equity and of placing each of us in his proper station, ﴿"manifest"﴾ (p-256) evident from the outward state.

It is related that he loved him more because of the signs of goodness he saw in him, and his brothers envied him. When he saw the dream, he doubled his love for him to the point that he could not be patient without him, so their envy multiplied until it drove them to carry out what was recounted about them.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 9:**

﴿Kill Joseph or cast him out to some land﴾ is part of what is related after His saying, "When they said" (إذا قالُوا). Some of them said it, addressing the rest, as the form of the wording implies. It is as if they all consented to it. It is narrated that the speaker was Shim'un (Simeon) or Dan, and the rest were content, except for the one who said, ﴿Do not kill﴾ (verse 10), and so they were treated as though they were the speakers and were included under the saying attributed to all of them. Alternatively, each of them said it, addressing the others. This is more indicative of their haste toward that statement. The indefiniteness of أرضًا (ardan, "land") and its being free of a qualifier is for vagueness, meaning: a land that is unspecified, unknown, and far from inhabited areas. For this reason it is put in the accusative of the vague adverbial nouns (نصب الظروف المبهمة).

﴿Then the face of your father will be clear for you﴾ — يَخْلُ (yakhlu) is in the jussive (جزم, jazm, apocopate mood) as the answer to the imperative, meaning: يَخْلُصْ, "it will be purified for you". ﴿So he will turn to you with his whole self and will not turn away from you to anyone else, and no one will share with you in his love.⁠﴾ Thus mention of the "face" is to depict the meaning of his turning toward them. ﴿And you will be﴾ — وتكونوا (wa-takunu) is in the jussive, coordinated with يَخْلُ, or in the subjunctive (نصب, nasb) by implying أنْ (an) or الواو (wa) in the sense of مع (ma'a, "with"), like His saying, ﴿and conceal the truth﴾. The choice of the second-person address in لَكُمْ and what follows is for emphasis in moving them to accept, since a person's concern for his own affair and his attentiveness to obtaining its benefits is more complete and perfect. ﴿After him﴾ means after Joseph, that is, after finishing with his matter, or his killing, or his casting out. ﴿A righteous people﴾ means repentant to God, Exalted is He, for what you have committed; or righteous with your father, by reconciling what is between you and him through an excuse you prepare; or righteous in the affairs of your worldly life, as they become orderly after him, with the face of your father being free for you.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 10:**

﴿Said a speaker among them﴾: he was Yahudha (Judah), who was the best of them in opinion, and he is the one who said: ﴿I will not leave the land﴾ ... etc. It is also said that he was Ruwbil (Reuben). This is an resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*, a new sentence that answers an implied question), constructed in response to one who asks: "Did they agree on what was proposed to them of the two options of ruin, or did anyone among them oppose them in that?" So it is said: ﴿Said a speaker among them: "Do not kill Yusuf"﴾. He mentioned Yusuf by name in place of a pronoun to arouse their compassion for him, or to magnify the act of killing him, since he is the very one (who would be killed). It is narrated that he said to them: "Killing is a great matter," but he did not explicitly forbid them from the other option. He left that to the preference of what he had proposed to them, by his saying: ﴿and throw him into the depths of the well﴾. *Ghayabat* means its bottom and its depths, and it is so called because it is hidden from the eye of the one who looks. *Al-jubb* is the well that has not yet been lined with stones, since it is land that was dug (*jubbat*) as a pit, without anything further being added to it. Nafi' recited (*fi ghayabat al-jubb*, "in the depths of the wells") in both places, as if that well had several depths, or he meant by *al-jubb* the genus, i.e., "in some of the depths of the wells." It was also read as (*ghayabat*) and (*ghaybat*).

﴿will pick him up﴾: will take him in a manner of safekeeping from loss and destruction, for *al-iltiqat* is taking up a thing that is exposed to being lost. ﴿some of the caravan﴾: i.e., some group traveling through the land. The article *al-* in *al-sayyarah* is like that in *al-jubb*. The indefiniteness in these two words and in (*ba'd*, "some") serves to achieve what he intends in making his words attractive by agreeing with their purpose, which is that Yusuf be removed from them to a place where his trace will not be known and his news will not be related. It was also read (*taltaqith*) in the feminine, since "some of the caravan" is a caravan, as in the saying of the poet:

*As the chest of the spear was reddened with blood*

And from this usage: "some of his fingers were cut off."

﴿if you are going to act﴾: by my counsel. He did not make the matter a firm command upon them, but rather he only offered this to them in order to win their hearts, to direct them toward his opinion, and out of caution lest they attribute to him domineering and presumptuous conduct. Or (the meaning is): if you are going to do what you have resolved upon, namely removing him from his father, then do it without fail. Since this was liable to prompt a questioner to say: "What did they do after that? Did they accept this from him or not?", the answer is given by way of a resumptive sentence, in a manner that includes within it their acceptance, by what will come in His saying: ﴿and they resolved to put him into the depths of the well﴾. So it is said:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 11:

﴿They said: "O our father!"﴾ They addressed him thus in order to stir up the bond of kinship between him and them, and to remind him of the bond of brotherhood between them and Yusuf, peace be upon him, so that by this means they might lead him to relent from his opinion about guarding him from them, since he had sensed in them signs of envy and enmity. It is as if they had said: ﴿"What is the matter with you?"﴾ that is, what is wrong with you, ﴿"that you do not entrust us"﴾ that is, you do not make us trustworthy ﴿"with Yusuf,"﴾ even though you are our father and we are your sons, and he is our brother. ﴿"And indeed we are truly sincere toward him"﴾ desiring good for him and being compassionate toward him; there is nothing in us that ever undermines sincere advice and affection. The well-known reading is with idgham (assimilation) and ishmam (partial rounding), and it is narrated from Nafi', may Allah be pleased with him, that he omitted ishmam, while among the irregular (shadhdh) readings is the omission of idgham.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 12:

﴿Send him with us tomorrow﴾ to the desert, ﴿that he may enjoy himself and play﴾. That is, ﴿that he may enjoy himself (yarta')﴾: he may expand in eating fruits and the like, for al-ar-ta' (rata') is expansion in pleasures. ﴿And play﴾ with racing, wrestling and similar activities, which are counted among the preparations for warfare. They expressed this by "play" because it was in its (true) form, in order to achieve what they intended of taking Yusuf (peace be upon him) along, by presenting it to him in the form that suits his condition (peace be upon him). It was also read as (narta' wa-nal'ab) with nun. Ibn Kathir read (nurtie') from irta'a, and Nafi' read with kasra and ya' in it and in (yal'ab). It was also read (yurtie') from ar-ta'a mashiyatahu (he pastured his livestock), and (yarta') with kasra on the ayn, and (yal'abu) with damma as an inceptive (nominative) construction.

﴿And indeed we are truly its guardians﴾ from any harm befalling him. They emphasized their statement with several kinds of emphasis: presenting the sentence as a nominal clause, adorning it with inna and the lam, attributing the guarding to all of them collectively, and placing (lahu, "for him") before the predicate, in order to secure their aim through a stratagem.

**﴿He said﴾**: a resumptive clause (*istinaf*), answering an implied question: "What did Ya'qub (peace be upon him) then say?" So it is said that he said: ﴿Indeed, it grieves me﴾. The *lam* here is the *lam al-ibtida'* (the emphatic *lam* that opens a sentence), as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And indeed your Lord will judge between them﴾. ﴿That you take him away﴾, because of the severity of his separation from me and the scarcity of my patience regarding him. Yet, along with that, ﴿I fear that the wolf will devour him﴾, because the land was full of wolves (*madhabah*). Grief is the pain of the heart at the loss of the beloved, and fear is the agitation of the soul at the arrival of something disliked. For this reason, the first was attributed to the act of taking him away, which causes the loss, since it entails the continuation of his companionship and his constant association with Yusuf, while the second was attributed to what is expected to befall him, namely the wolf's devouring him. It is also said that he had seen in a dream that a wolf had attacked him, and he was wary of it, so he said this. Indeed, Allah had taught them the pretext.

؎ Indeed, calamity is entrusted to speech.

Ibn Kathir and Nafi' (in the narration of al-Bazzi) read ﴿الذئب﴾ with the hamza (*bil-hamzah*) according to the original form, and Abu 'Amr read it with the hamza when pausing (*waqfan*). 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir and Hamza read it without the hamza in continuous recitation (*darajan*). It is said that its derivation is from *tadha'abati al-rih*, meaning "the wind blew from every direction." Al-Asma'i said the matter is the reverse, and this is more evident both in wording and in meaning. ﴿And you were heedless of him﴾, either because you were occupied with pasturing and play, or because of your little concern for guarding him.

(p-258) ﴿They said: "If the wolf eats him while we are a group"﴾ That is: and the situation is that we are a large body, deserving that great affairs be entrusted to us ('ussibat, i.e., a band strong enough to be relied upon), and that calamities be averted by our opinions and our arrangements. The lam (al-lam) that enters upon the conditional is a preparatory lam (muwatti'a li-l-qasam, i.e., one that prepares for an oath). His saying: ﴿Indeed we would then be losers﴾ is a response that stands in place of the answer to the condition: that is, we would be doomed through weakness, feebleness and incapacity, or we would deserve destruction, since there is no use or benefit in our lives; or we would deserve to be cursed with loss and ruin. It is said: God the Exalted caused them loss and ruin (khassarahum and dammarahum) in that the wolf ate one of them while they were present. It was also said: if we fail to protect him, which is the dearest thing to us, then our livestock has perished and we have lost it. They confined themselves to answering Ya'qub's (peace be upon him) fear of the wolf's eating him, because that is the strong cause for prevention, rather than the sorrow, given that its duration is short, on the basis that they would bring him back soon.

﴿So when they took him away and resolved﴾, that is, determined, ﴿to put him﴾. The phrase ﴿أنْ يَجْعَلُوهُ﴾ (an yajʿalūhu) is the object (maf'ūl) of ﴿وأجْمَعُوا﴾ (wa-ajmaʿū). One says ajmaʿa al-amr (he resolved the matter), and from it comes ﴿فَأجْمِعُوا أمْرَكُمْ﴾ (fa-ajmiʿū amrakum), "So determine your affair." This usage is only applied to actions for which the motives to carry them out have become strong. ﴿into the depths of the well﴾ (fī ghayābat al-jubb): it was said that it is a well in the land of al-Urdunn (Jordan). It was also said that it lay between Egypt and Madyan, and that it was three farsakh (leagues) from the dwelling of Yaʿqub (peace be upon him) in Kanʿan (Canaan), which lies in the regions of al-Urdunn, just as Madyan is in that same area. As for what is said, that it is the well of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), the reasoning given refutes it: the caravan picked him up, and they came to their father in the evening of that same day, while the distance between the dwelling of Yaʿqub (peace be upon him) and Bayt al-Maqdis is several stages of travel. The answer to ﴿lammā﴾ (when) is omitted, to signal that it is evident and to indicate that its details cannot be contained within the scope of expression. Its summary is: they did to him what harm they did.

It is related that when they went out into the desert, they began to harm him and beat him until they nearly killed him. He began to cry out and call for help. Yahudha (Judah) said: "Did you not make a covenant with me that you would not kill him?" So they brought him to the well, and he clung to their garments, so they pulled them from his hands and lowered him into it. He clung to its edge, so they tied his hands and stripped off his shirt, because they had resolved to smear it with blood to deceive his father. He said: "O my brothers, return my shirt to me so that I may cover myself with it." They said: "Call upon the sun, the moon and the eleven stars, and they will keep you company." Then they lowered him into it, and when he reached halfway down they dropped him so that he would die. There was water in the well, and he fell into it. Then he took refuge on a rock, stood upon it weeping, and they called out to him. He thought that it was mercy that had reached them, so he answered them. They wanted to crush him, but Yahudha prevented them. He used to bring him food every day.

It is also related that when Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was cast into the fire and stripped of his clothes, Jibril (peace be upon him) came to him with a shirt of the silk of Paradise and dressed him in it. Ibrahim passed it on to Ishaq, and Ishaq to Yaʿqub. Yaʿqub put it in an amulet (tamīma) and hung it around the neck of Yusuf. Then Jibril (peace be upon him) came to him, took it out of the amulet, and dressed him in it.

﴿And We revealed to him﴾ at that moment, as good news to him of what his affair would come to, and to remove his loneliness and to give him comfort. It was said: this was before he reached maturity, just as revelation came to Yahya and Isa. It was also said: he was then of age. al-Hasan (may Allah be pleased with him) said: he was seventeen years old. ﴿You will surely inform them of this their affair﴾, that is: you will surely be freed from what you are in of bad condition and narrow circumstance, and you will surely tell your brothers what they did to you, ﴿while they do not perceive﴾ that you are Yusuf, because of the difference between your two states (the present one and your state on that day): due to the elevation of your rank, the majesty of your rule, and the distance of your present condition from their imaginings. It was also said: because of the long passage of time, which changes appearances and alters forms. The first interpretation is more fitting for consolation.

It is related that when they came to him seeking provisions, he recognized them while they did not recognize him. He called for the goblet (ṣuwāʿ) and placed it on his hand, then struck it so that it rang, and said: "This cup tells me that you had a brother from your father called Yusuf, whom he favored over you. You took him away and cast him into the depths of the well, and you told your father: 'The wolf ate him,' and you sold him for a paltry price." It is permissible for ﴿وَهم لا يَشْعُرُونَ﴾ (wa-hum lā yashʿurūn) to be connected to ﴿الإيحاء﴾ (the revelation) in the sense that We gave him companionship through revelation and removed from his heart the loneliness that they had caused him, while they did not perceive this and assumed that he was distressed and lonely, with no one to keep him company. It is also read as ﴿لَنُنَبِّئَنَّهُمْ﴾ (la-nunabbi'annahum) with the nūn, as a warning to them. In that case, the Exalted's words ﴿وَهم لا يَشْعُرُونَ﴾ are connected only to ﴿أوْحَيْنا﴾ (awḥaynā).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 16:

﴿And they came to their father in the evening﴾, at the end of the day. It is also read ('ushiyyan), which is the diminutive of 'ashiyy (ʿashiyy, "evening"). And 'ushan (ʿushan), with a damma on the first letter and without the madd, is the plural of a'sha (aʿshā, one who is weak-sighted at night), meaning: [they came] with their eyes dimmed from weeping. ﴿They were weeping﴾, feigning weeping.

It is related that when Ya'qub (ʿAlayhi al-Salam, peace be upon him) heard their weeping, he was alarmed and said: "What is the matter with you, my sons? And where is Yusuf?"

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 17:

﴿They said: "O our father, we went off racing one another (nastabiq)"﴾ That is: competing with one another in running and shooting (al-ramy), and the form (al-ifti'al) and the reciprocal form (al-tafa'ul) may share a meaning, as in al-intidal and al-tanadul and their like. ﴿And we left Joseph by our belongings﴾ That is: by what we use for enjoyment of clothing, provisions, and other things. ﴿Then the wolf ate him﴾ immediately after that, without the passing of a period of time in which one would customarily check and attend to (al-tafaqqud wa al-ta'ahhud) the belongings. Since goods are customarily not left except in a place where dangers are secure, his leaving them with him (peace be upon him) was not known to be out of negligence or a neglect of obligatory protection, especially since they did not depart from him or go out of his sight. So it is as if they said: "We did not fall short in guarding him, nor were we heedless of watching over him; rather, we left him in our place of safety and gathering, within our sight, because the field of a race is customarily only where its goals are visible. We parted from him only for a brief hour, with only a short distance between us and him, and so it happened what happened."

﴿And you will not believe us﴾ that is, you will not give credence to us in this statement, which indicates that we did not fall short in his matter. ﴿Even if we were﴾ in your sight and in your belief ﴿truthful﴾, described as honest and trustworthy; because of the intensity of your love for Joseph. How then, when you think ill of us and do not trust our word?!

The word (law, "even if") in such contexts is for indicating the certainty of what the preceding statement implies, of the affirmed or negated judgment, under every supposed state among the states accompanying it in general, by placing it upon the state furthest from it and most contrary to it; so that by its establishment or negation along with it, its establishment or negation along with other states becomes evident by way of priority (al-awlawiyyah), because whenever a thing is realized along with a strong contrary, it is all the more realized along with other things. For this reason nothing of the other states is mentioned with it, and it is sufficient to omit them by mentioning the conjunctive waw joining the clause to its counterpart which encompasses all states, differing from it when they are multiple. Its detailed explanation has already passed in Surat al-Baqarah at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Even though their fathers did not understand anything nor were they guided?﴾ and in Surat al-A'raf at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Even if we were unwilling?﴾.

(p-260) ﴿And they came upon his shirt﴾: its position (maḥall) is accusative as a circumstantial adverb (ẓarfiyyah) of ﴿with blood﴾, meaning: they came with blood above his shirt, just as one says, "He came upon his camels with loads." Or it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāliyyah) of it. There is disagreement over whether a ḥāl may precede the word it qualifies, a genuinely governed (majrūr) word, when the ḥāl is not itself an adverb.

﴿with false﴾ (kadhib) is a verbal noun (maṣdar) used to describe the blood for emphasis (mubālaghah). Or it is a verbal noun in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ūl), meaning "falsified in it" (makdhūb fīhi). Or it means "possessing falsehood" (dhū kadhib), that is, "accompanied by falsehood." It has also been read as kadhiban (كَذِبًا), which would be a circumstantial accusative from the pronoun, meaning "they came lying," or an accusative of purpose (maf'ūl lahu). ʿĀ'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, read it without the dotted letter (bi-ghayr al-mu'jamah), meaning "turbid" (kadir). It was also said to mean "fresh" (ṭariy). Ibn Jinni said: its root is from kadhib, which is the faint whiteness that appears on the nails of young children, as though it were blood that had marked his shirt.

It is related that they slaughtered a young goat (sakhlah) and smeared his shirt with its blood, but they forgot to tear it. When Ya'qub heard the news about Yusuf, peace be upon them both, he cried out at the top of his voice and said, "Where is the shirt?" He took it, threw it over his face, and wept until his face was stained with the blood of the shirt. He said, "By Allah, I have never seen a wolf more gentle than this one: it ate him and did not tear his shirt."

It was also said that there were three signs in Yusuf's shirt, peace be upon him: it was a proof for Ya'qub of their lying; he threw it over his face and his sight returned; and it was a proof of Yusuf's innocence when it was torn from behind.

﴿He said﴾ is a resumptive sentence (isti'nāf) built upon a question, as though it were asked: "What did Ya'qub say? Did he believe them about what they said or not?" So it was answered: "He said: That was not so. Rather, your souls have embellished a matter for you." ﴿Your souls have embellished (sawwalat) for you﴾ means: adorned and made easy, as Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said. Taswīl is the fixing of something in the soul together with hope of its accomplishment. Al-Azhari said: taswīl appears to be a form of tafʿīl from su'āl (asking) by a person, which is his wish that he seeks, and which adorns falsehood and other things for the one who seeks it. Its original form is hamzated. It was also said that it derives from sawal, which means slackness.

﴿a matter﴾ among the affairs, ﴿unusual﴾, which cannot be described or recognized. (fa-ṣabrun jamīl): that is, "so my affair is patient beauty," or "so patient beauty is most beautiful or most fitting." In a hadith: "Patient beauty is that which contains no complaint," meaning no complaint to the creatures. Otherwise, Ya'qub, peace be upon him, said: ﴿Indeed I complain of my anguish and my grief only to Allah﴾. It was also said: his two eyebrows fell over his eyes, so he would lift them with a band. It was asked, "What is this?" He said: "The length of time and the abundance of sorrows." Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed to him: "O Ya'qub, do you complain about Me?" He said: "O Lord, it is a sin, so forgive it for me." Ubayy read it as (fa-ṣabran jamīlan).

﴿And Allah is the One whose help is sought﴾: that is, the One from whom help is requested. This is a performative statement (inshā') from him, peace be upon him, seeking continuous help ﴿against what you describe﴾: against the manifestation of the state of what you describe, and the clarification that it is a lie, and the manifestation of its soundness, for it is a sign of falsehood. He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, above what they describe﴾. This is most fitting in light of what comes later in His words: ﴿So patience is beautiful; perhaps Allah will bring them all back to me﴾. Interpreting "the One whose help is sought" as referring to the possibility of what they describe, namely Yusuf's destruction and enduring the loss of him, is rejected by his, peace be upon him, denial of their claim in that matter, and the wording does not support it, for it has become predominantly used for describing a thing with what is not in it, as has been pointed out.

**(p-261)** ﴿And there came﴾ begins an account of what happened to Joseph in the well, after finishing the mention of what passed between his brothers and their father. The use of "coming" does not refer to their location, since Canaan is not on the Egyptian side of Madyan. It refers to Joseph's place. Choosing this verb over "passing by," "arriving," or similar expressions hints at his nobility and nearness to a mighty Sovereign, peace be upon him. It is apparent that the well was in an uninhabited, desolate region. The most evident reading of attributing "coming" to the caravan absolutely, in the words of the Exalted and Majestic: "And there came" ﴿a caravan﴾, meaning a company traveling from the direction of Madyan to Egypt, is that the event took place in accordance with their customary route. This is what the words of the Exalted in what preceded require: "some of the caravan will pick him up." It has been said that the well was in a remote wasteland far from settlements, frequented only by herders, so they lost their way and stopped near it. It has also been said that its water was salty, but became sweet when Joseph, peace be upon him, was thrown into it.

﴿So they sent their water-drawer﴾, the one who goes to the water and draws it for them. This was Malik ibn Dhu'r al-Khuza'i. The endpoint of the sending is not mentioned, just as the endpoint of the coming (namely, the well) is not mentioned, to signal that this is well known and is not passed over in silence. ﴿So he let down his bucket﴾, meaning he sent it down into the well. The omission is due to what you already know. Then Joseph grasped it and came out. ﴿He said﴾ is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf), i.e., a sentence that begins a new statement, responding to a question that the situation calls for. ﴿O good news! This is a boy!﴾ It is as if he called out, "Good news!" and said, "Come, for this is your time, since he has obtained a cool blessing." And what blessing is greater than what is found freely available, namely water? It has been said that "Bushra" is the name of a companion whom he called upon to help him bring Joseph out. Other than the Kufans read "Ya bushraya" (with the final ya), and Hamzah and al-Kisa'i inclined the fatha on the ra' (imalah). Warsh read it between the two pronunciations. It was also read as "Ya bushrayya" with assimilation (idgham), which is a dialect, and "Bushrāy" with the pause (waqf) intended.

﴿And they concealed him﴾, meaning the water-drawer and his companions hid him from the rest of the caravan. It has been said that they concealed his affair and their finding him in the well, and told the others: "The people of the water handed him over to us so that we might sell him for them in Egypt." It has also been said that the pronoun refers to Joseph's brothers. This is because Yahudha (Judah) used to bring him food every day. On that day he came to him but did not find him in it, so he informed his brothers. They went to the caravan and said, "This is our slave who ran away," and they bought him from them. Joseph remained silent, fearing that they would kill him. The weakness of this view is not hidden.

﴿as merchandise﴾: "Bidā'a" is in the accusative as a circumstantial (hal) state. The meaning is that they concealed him while he was in the state of being merchandise, that is, goods for trade, since a "bidā'a" is a portion of wealth cut off from one's property, i.e., set apart for trade. ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing of what they do﴾ is a warning to them for what they did in making someone like Joseph, who was (in truth) Joseph himself, a subject of being demeaned through buying and selling, and for the schemes they devised in that matter.

﴿And they sold him﴾, i.e., they sold him, and the pronoun refers to the water-drawer (al-warid) and his companions, ﴿for a paltry price﴾, debased coins of deficient purity, ﴿dirhams﴾, which is in apposition (badal) to "price", i.e., not dinars, ﴿counted﴾, i.e., not weighed. This is an explanation of its smallness and meagreness in quantity, after the explanation of its deficiency in itself, since what is customarily counted rather than weighed is that which does not reach forty. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that they were twenty dirhams, and it is related from al-Suddi, may Allah be pleased with him, that they were twenty-two dirhams.

﴿And they were﴾, i.e., the sellers, ﴿concerning him﴾, concerning Yusuf, ﴿among those who were indifferent﴾, among those who have no desire for what is in their hands. Therefore they sold him for the paltry price mentioned. The reason for this is that they had found him, and one who finds a thing treats it lightly or is not confident of its matter, fearing that a rightful claimant may appear and snatch it from him, so he sells it to the first bidder at the lowest price. It is also possible that the meaning of "they sold him" (sharawhu) is "they bought him" from his brothers, as has been related, and they were not desirous of buying him, fearing the loss of their property because of the runaway slave talk that had been spread about in their ears. The turning away from the form of ifti'al, which indicates taking for oneself, is because their taking him was only by way of merchandise (bida'a), not by gathering and keeping. The phrase ﴿concerning him﴾ (fihi) is linked to "those who were indifferent" if the lam is taken as the definite article (al-), and it is an explanation of what they were indifferent to if the lam is taken as a relative pronoun (ism mawsul), as if it were said: "Regarding what were they indifferent?" and it was answered: "They were indifferent concerning him", because what is linked to the relative clause (sila) does not precede the relative pronoun.

**Tafsir Abi al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim)**, on Surah Yusuf (12), verse 21:

﴿The one who bought him from Egypt said﴾ He is the *'Aziz* (the chief minister), who was in charge of its treasuries. His name was Qitfir or Itfir. The statement that he was "from Egypt" clarifies the matters that followed from his position, and it also signals that he was not one of those who had picked Yusuf up and sold him for the paltry price mentioned. The king at that time was al-Rayyan ibn al-Walid al-'Imliqi, who died during Yusuf's lifetime, after believing in him. He was succeeded by Qabus ibn Mus'ab, whom Yusuf invited to Islam, but he refused. It is also said that the king in Yusuf's days was the Pharaoh of Musa (peace be upon him). He lived four hundred years, based on the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And Yusuf had already come to you before with clear proofs﴾. It is also said that the Pharaoh of Musa was one of the descendants of the Pharaoh of Yusuf, and the verse is of the type where the children are addressed about the conditions of their fathers.

There is disagreement about the amount for which the *'Aziz* bought him. It is said: for twenty dinars, a pair of sandals, and two white garments. It is also said: they brought him into the market to display him, and they bid over his price until his price reached his weight in musk, his weight in silver, and his weight in silk. Qitfir bought him for that sum. At that time he was seventeen years old. He remained in the house, together with the period he spent in prison, for thirteen years. Al-Rayyan appointed him as minister when he was thirty years old. God gave him knowledge and wisdom when he was thirty-three years old, and he died at the age of one hundred and twenty.

﴿To his wife﴾: Ra'il, or Zulaykha. It is also said that her name is the first and the second is her epithet. The *lam* (the "to" in *li-imra'atihi*) is connected to *qala* (said), not to *ishtarahu* (bought him).

﴿Honour his lodging﴾: make the place of his residence noble and pleasing. The meaning is: take good care of him.

﴿Perhaps he will benefit us﴾ in our properties and our wealth, and we will rely on him in our affairs.

﴿Or we may take him as a son﴾: that is, we will adopt him. This was because she perceived in him signs of rectitude and nobility. For this reason it was said: the three most perceptive people are: the *'Aziz* of Egypt; the daughter of Shu'ayb who said, "O my father, hire him"; and Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him both) when he appointed 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) as his successor.

﴿And thus﴾: the *kaf* (the "thus" in *wa-kadhalika*) is in the accusative as an infinitive adverb (*masdariyyah*), and *dhalika* (that) refers to what is understood from the words of the *'Aziz* and the sense of distance contained in it, for the purpose of magnifying it. That is: like that wonderful establishment,

﴿We established Yusuf in the land﴾: that is, We gave him a place in it. It is said *makkanahu fihi* (he established him in it), meaning he settled him there, and *makkana lahu fihi* (he gave him a place in it). Because the two are close in meaning and mutually implicated, each of them is used in place of the other. The Mighty and Majestic said: "And how many generations We destroyed before them, whom We had established in the land as We have not established you." That is: as We have not established you in it; or, We established them in the land... etc. The meaning is: just as We gave him a noble abode in the house of the *'Aziz*, or an exalted place in his heart, so that he ordered his wife, apart from all his attendants, to honour his lodging, We gave him an elevated station in the land of Egypt. Perhaps this is an expression for making him respected among its people and beloved in all their hearts, as he was in the heart of the *'Aziz*, because that leads to the aim mentioned in the words of the Exalted: ﴿and that We may teach him the interpretation of events﴾, that is, We grant him success in interpreting some of the dreams, whose principal ones are the dream of the king and of the two companions of the prison, according to the words of the Exalted: ﴿That is of what my Lord has taught me﴾.

Whether we take it as coordinated with an implied goal toward which the discourse runs and which the arrangement calls for, as if it were said: "And like that establishment We established Yusuf in the land, and We made the hearts of (p-263) its people all places of his love, so that there would follow from it what followed of what happened between him and the wife of the *'Aziz*, 'and that We may teach him some of the interpretation of events'," which is the interpretation of the dream mentioned, and that leads to supreme leadership; or whether we take it as the cause of an omitted causative clause, as if it were said: "And for this profound wisdom We did that establishment, rather than others which have no praiseworthy outcome."

That said, it is not hidden from you that what these matters revolve around is the establishment in the side of the *'Aziz*. As for establishment in the side of all the people, its leading to that is only by way of its including that establishment. Therefore, the truth is that *dhalika* (that) should refer to the infinitive of His words, "We established Yusuf," on the basis that this infinitive is an expression for establishment in the heart of the *'Aziz* or in his house. That this is an establishment in the land, by way of his being honoured in it, not from another establishment compared to it, is as was previously said regarding His words: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation﴾, that *dhalika* refers to the infinitive of the verb mentioned after it, not to another making intended to be compared to this making. So the *kaf* is inserted to indicate the magnificence of the matter referred to, an insertion that is hardly avoided in the language of the Arabs or any other, and from this is their saying: "Someone like you does not stint." This is how the situation should be verified.

As for establishment in the sense of making him a king who disposes in the land of Egypt by command and prohibition, this is among the effects of that teaching and its consequences that branch from it, as you have understood, not among its beginnings that lead to it. So there is no way to make it the goal of that teaching. And it was not known of him, peace be upon him, in the course of his affairs, that he acted according to the dreams that alert to events before their occurrence, as a precedent that would validate making that the goal of his governorship.

And what occurred of the planning regarding the years was only action according to the previous, well-known dream, except that by "teaching the interpretation of events" might be meant what preceded: conveying the obscure secrets of the divine books and the subtle details of the ways of the prophets (peace be upon them). In that case the meaning becomes: We established him in the land of Egypt so that he would dispose in it with justice, and that We might teach him the meanings of the books of Allah the Exalted, their rulings, and the subtle details of the ways of the prophets (peace be upon them), so that he judges by them among its people. The general teaching of those meanings and rulings, although it is not later than his establishment in that sense, nevertheless the teaching of each particular meaning, which happens in the course of events and guidance to the truth in every occurrence, is later than that, and is fit to be a goal for it.

﴿And Allah is overpowering over His affair﴾: nothing disobeys Him and nothing prevents Him. Rather, ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾. So His concerns regarding Yusuf are included in this primarily, or He is the one who takes charge of the affair of Yusuf and does not leave it to another. By it was intended from the trial what was intended time after time, so nothing happened except what Allah intended for him of the praiseworthy outcome. ﴿But most of the people do not know﴾ that the matter is so; thus they come and go, supposing, from their own claim, that they have some share of the command, and how could they have that, when the whole matter belongs to Allah the Mighty and Majestic? Or they do not know the subtleties of His workmanship and the hidden aspects of His grace.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 22:

﴿When he reached his full strength﴾: that is, the limit of the strengthening of his body and his power. This is the age of standing firm, between thirty and forty. It was also said: the age of youth, and the beginning of reaching puberty (bulugh al-hulum). The first view is the more apparent, because of God's words: ﴿We gave him judgment﴾, meaning wisdom (hikma), which is knowledge supported by action; or judgment among people (hukm bayn al-nas), and understanding (fiqh); or prophethood. ﴿And knowledge﴾, that is, deep understanding of the religion (tafaqquh fi al-din). The indefinite form of both words is for magnification, meaning judgment and knowledge whose reality cannot be fully grasped and whose measure cannot be estimated. They are what God gave him when his powers had matured, whether they refer to prophethood and judgment among people or to something else. How could it be otherwise, when their giving has been made (p-264) a reward for his action, peace be upon him, where He said: ﴿And thus﴾, that is, like that wondrous reward, ﴿We reward the good-doers﴾, that is, everyone who does good in his deeds. Therefore it must be that this comes after the completion of his good deeds, among which is enduring sorrows and hardships. Knowledge has been explained as the knowledge of the interpretation of hadiths (ta'wil al-ahadith), but this is not sound unless it is restricted to the interpretation of the king's dream, for when that took place at the end of the days of trial, it was correct to count his being given it as part of the reward. As for the dream of the two companions of the prison, he remained in prison for several years after interpreting it, peace be upon him. Linking the mentioned reward to the good-doers indicates that good-doing is its cause, and it alerts that God, glory be to Him, gave him what He gave him because he was a good-doer in his deeds and God-fearing in the prime of his affair. ﴿Is the reward of good-doing anything but good-doing?﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 23:

﴿And she, in whose house he was, sought to seduce him﴾ This returns to explaining what happened in the house of the Aziz after he had instructed his wife to honour his lodging. The words of the Exalted, ﴿And thus We established Joseph﴾ up to here, form a parenthetical interjection (i'tiraD) brought in as a sample of the story, so that the listener may know from the outset that what he (peace be upon him) encountered of the trials, which will be recounted to him in detail, has a beautiful outcome and a praiseworthy end, and that he (peace be upon him) was a doer of good in all his deeds, and that nothing proceeded from him in times of ease or hardship that would detract from his integrity.

It is not hidden that the pivot of the fine transition (husn al-takhlis) to this interjection, before the completion of the noble verse, is nothing other than the complete establishment (al-tamkin al-baligh) understood from the words of the Aziz. Therefore, placing the earlier deliverance under the reference of "And thus We established" (in the words of the Exalted, "And thus We established"), as the majority have done, is far from proximity. So reflect.

Murawadah (ويد) means seeking, from (raada yarudu), when one comes and goes in search of something, and from it comes al-ra'id, one who seeks water and pasture. It is a form of mufa'alah from one party, like the creditor's demanding (mutalabat al-da'in), the debtor's procrastinating (mumaTalat al-madin), the physician's treating (mudawat al-Tabib), and their like, in which the act comes from one side and its cause from the other. For these acts, although they proceed from one side, since their causes proceed from the other side, they are treated as though they proceed from both. This is a subtle path, founded on a fine consideration, whose verification is that the cause of a thing is placed in its stead and its name is applied to it, as in the saying: "As you judge, so you will be judged" (kama tadin tudan), meaning: as you recompense, so you will be recompensed. The act of the initiator, although it is not a recompense, is named by it because it is the cause of the recompense. Likewise the intention to stand for prayer and the intention to recite the Qur'an, since they were the cause of standing and reciting, are expressed by them, so it is said: ﴿(When you stand up for prayer)﴾ ﴿(When you recite the Qur'an)﴾. This is a consistent and continuous rule. Since the causes of the acts mentioned in what we are dealing with proceed from the side opposite to the side of their doer, the creditor's demanding is caused by the debtor's procrastination, which comes from the debtor's side, and the procrastination comes from him in response to the demanding that comes from the creditor's side. Likewise the physician's treatment is for the sickness that comes from the patient's side. Similarly, her seeking to seduce him in what we are dealing with, for the beauty of Joseph (peace be upon him), has its proceeding from its locus placed in the position of the proceeding of its effects, which are those acts. So the form is built upon that, and the aspect of reality is observed by ascribing the act to its agent and making it fall upon the one who is the cause. So reflect.

It is permissible that the form of mughalabah be intended as mere intensification (mubalaghah). It has been said that the form retains its original meaning, in the sense that she demanded from him the act while he demanded from her abstention. It is also permissible that it be from ruwayd, which means gentleness and forbearance, and that its transitive construction with ʿan is because it implies the meaning of deception, so the meaning is: she deceived him.

﴿About himself﴾ meaning: she did what the deceiver does to his companion regarding something he does not wish to release from his hand, while he devises to take it from him. This expresses the contriving of intercourse with him, and the departure from explicitly naming her is either to keep the matter secret or out of distaste for mentioning it. The mention of the relative clause serves to establish the seeking, for her being in her house is among what calls to that. It was said to one woman: "What led you to what you are doing, which has no good in it?" She said: "The nearness of the cushion and the length of the night." It also serves to show the perfection of his integrity (peace be upon him), for his lack of inclination toward her, despite the constant sight of her beauties and his refusal of her while being under her authority, proclaims that he (peace be upon him) was at the highest ascents of chastity and integrity.

﴿And she locked the doors﴾. It was said there were seven of them, and for this reason the verb came in the form taffil rather than if'al. It was also said that it is for emphasis in securing and making firm.

﴿And she said: "Come, I am yours"﴾. It was read with fath and kasr of the ha' with fath of the ta', and its construction is like the construction of ayna and 'ayt; Hayta like jir; Hayta like haytu (haythu) is a verb-noun (ism fi'l) meaning "come forward" and "hasten"; the lam is for clarification, i.e., "I say this to you," as in halumma laka. It was also read (hi'tu laka) in the form of a verb meaning "I have prepared myself," as it is said: haa' yahi'u like jaa' yajī'u when one prepares oneself, and "hu'ayt laka," and the lam is a complement to the verb.

﴿He said: "I seek refuge in God"﴾ meaning: I seek refuge in God with a refuge from what you call me to. This is abstention from it in the most complete manner, and an indication of the reason, that it is a terrible abomination from which one must seek refuge in God Almighty for deliverance. This was only because he (peace be upon him) had witnessed it through the clear proof that God Almighty had shown him, regarding what it is in itself of utmost ugliness and extreme evil.

The saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Indeed, He is my Lord; He has made my dwelling good﴾ is a reason for refraining, by means of some external causes that might have an effect upon her and move her to consider it, after alerting her to its intrinsic cause, which she could hardly accept because of what her own soul had embellished for her. The pronoun is for the matter (li'l-sha'n), and the basis of placing it in that position is the claim of its fame, which dispenses with mentioning it. The benefit of beginning the sentence with it is to announce the grandeur of its content, together with the added firmness of its impression on the mind, for from the pronoun, at first, one understands only an undefined matter of importance, so the mind remains expectant of what follows it, and so it settles in more firmly upon its arrival. It is as if it were said: this great matter is that my Lord, that is my master the Aziz, has made my dwelling good, that is, he has taken good care of me by commanding you to honour me. How, then, could I wrong him by betrayal in his household? This contains guidance for her to observe the Aziz's right in the most gracious manner. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to God Almighty, and "my Lord" is the predicate of "indeed," and "has made my dwelling good" is a second predicate, or it is the predicate and the first is an appositive of the pronoun.

The meaning is that the situation is thus; how then could I disobey Him by committing that grave abomination? It contains a warning to her of God Almighty's punishment. On both interpretations, limiting the statement to mention of this state without addressing its requirement of refraining from what she called him to is a notice that this degree of clarification is sufficient to indicate its impossibility and that it is something that does not fall within the realm of occurrence at all.

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers will not prosper﴾ is a reason for the aforementioned refraining, following upon a reason. Al-falah means victory, and it has been said: remaining in good. The meaning of aflaha is that he entered into it, like asbaha and its sisters. By "the wrongdoers" is meant everyone who does wrong, whoever he may be, so it includes primarily those who repay good with evil and those who disobey God's command. It has been said: it refers to fornicators, because they wrong themselves and wrong the one whose family they violate.

﴿And she certainly desired him﴾, meaning she desired intimacy with him, since desire (al-hamm) does not attach to physical objects. That is, she intended him and resolved upon him with a firm resolve that no distraction could turn her from, after she had begun its preliminaries and done what she did of seductive solicitation (al-murawadah), locking the doors, and calling him, peace be upon him, to herself by saying: "Hayt lak" ("Come, I am yours"; a word of invitation). It is likely that she intended, at that point, other acts, such as extending her hand toward him and seeking an embrace, and so on, which would compel him, peace be upon him, to flee toward the door. The emphasis (al-ta'kid) serves to repel what might be suspected, namely the possibility that she might desist from her condition because of the admonitions in his speech, peace be upon him. ﴿And he desired her﴾, meaning he inclined toward intimacy with her, that is, he inclined to her according to the requirements of human nature and the desire and ardor of youth, an innate inclination that scarcely falls under obligation, not that he intended her by deliberate choice. Do you not see what preceded of his steadfastness (isti'sam), which indicates his complete aversion and repulsion from her, and his judgment that the wrongdoers will not prosper? Is this not a firm affirmation (tasjil) of the impossibility of desire arising from him, peace be upon him? The word "desire" was used for him only because his desire occurred in company with hers in the mention, by way of mushakalah (a rhetorical device of matching words), not because of any resemblance between them, as some have said. Their difference is indicated, since they were not joined in a single phrase of expression by saying "And they both desired one another," or "each of them desired the other." The first was introduced with what establishes its existence, namely the oath-form emphasis, and the second was followed by what removes its trace, in the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Had he not seen the proof of his Lord﴾, meaning his clear proof, which indicates the complete ugliness of adultery and the evil of its path. By his seeing it is meant his complete certainty in it, and his witnessing of it reaching the level of certainty of direct vision (ayn al-yaqin), at which point the realities of things are revealed in their true forms and are stripped of their borrowed forms by which they appear in this world.
