This is what the words of the Prophet (ﷺ) express: "Paradise is surrounded by hardships, and the Fire is surrounded by desires." It is as if he, peace be upon him, had witnessed adultery through that radiant proof, as it is in itself, at its most ugly and most deserving of caution. For this reason he did what he did of steadfastness and of judging that whoever commits it will not prosper. The answer to "had he not" (law-la) is omitted, indicated by the context, meaning: had he not witnessed the proof of his Lord concerning adultery, he would have acted according to the requirement of his innate inclination. But since he had witnessed it before, he remained in what he was in, by the necessity of the proof. The benefit of this conditional statement is to show that his abstention, peace be upon him, was not due to the absence of support from his nature, but purely to chastity and integrity, despite the strength of the internal motives and the arrangement of the external causes that necessitate the manifestation of natural judgments.

That said, the masters of the discipline (a'immat al-sina'ah, i.e., the grammarians) have stated that "law-la" (had it not been) in such contexts functions, in meaning but not in form, as a restriction of an absolute ruling, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿He almost led us astray from our gods, had we not been steadfast in them﴾. There, no desire is actually realized at all. It has also been permitted that "and he desired her" be the answer to "law-la," following the rule of the Kufan grammarians (al-Kufiyyun, the school of Kufa) regarding the permissibility of fronting the answer. In that case, the desire is in its literal meaning. The meaning would be: had it not been that he had witnessed the proof of his Lord, he would have desired her as she desired him. But since the non-witnessing is ruled out, as evidenced by his steadfastness and what follows from it, the desire is entirely negated.

That said, his desire, peace be upon him, has been interpreted as his untying the waistband and sitting in the position of the circumcised man, and that he untied the cord of his trousers and sat between her limbs. His seeing the proof has been interpreted as his hearing a voice saying: "Beware of her, beware of her," but he paid it no heed; then again and again, until Ya'qub, peace be upon him, appeared to him biting on his finger. It was also said that he struck his chest, and his desire came out through his fingertips. It was also said that a hand appeared between them, with no upper arm or wrist, on which was written: ﴿And indeed over you are guardians, noble recorders﴾, and he did not turn away. Then he saw on it: ﴿And do not approach adultery; indeed it is an indecency and evil is its way﴾, and he did not desist. Then he saw on it: ﴿And fear a Day when you will be returned to Allah﴾, and it did not avail. Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said to Jibril: "Reach My servant before he commits the sin." So Jibril, peace be upon him, descended, saying: "O Yusuf, will you do the deeds of the foolish while you are written in the register of the prophets?" It was also said: he saw the statue of the Aziz (the governor), and it was said and said. All of this is nothing but fables and falsehoods which the ears reject and the minds and intellects refuse. Woe to him who chews them over and fabricates them, or who hears them and believes them.

﴿Thus﴾: the kaf (ka) is in the accusative position (manṣūb al-maḥall). "Dhalika" (that) refers to the showing indicated by the words ﴿had he not seen the proof of his Lord﴾, meaning: in like manner of that insight and making known, We showed him Our proof previously. Or it refers to the firm establishment that is necessary for him, meaning: in like manner of that firm establishment, We established him, ﴿so that We might turn away from him evil﴾ in general, so that the betrayal of the master is included in it as a primary inclusion, ﴿and indecency﴾, which is adultery, because it is extremely ugly. In this there is a clear sign and a decisive proof that no desire toward sin ever arose in him, peace be upon him, nor did he ever turn toward it. Otherwise it would have been said: "so that We might turn him away from evil and indecency." Rather, that desire was directed at him from outside, and Allah the Exalted turned him away from it by means of what He placed in him of the requirements of chastity and protection. So reflect. It has been read as "liyasrifa" (that He may turn away), attributing the turning away to the pronoun of the Lord. ﴿Indeed he is among Our sincere servants﴾: this is a causal explanation of what preceded, of the content of the sentence, in the manner of affirmation. The sincere servants (al-mukhlasun) are those whom Allah the Exalted has purified for His obedience, by protecting them from whatever would damage it. It has also been read in the active form (al-mukhlisin), meaning those who sincerely devoted their religion to Allah, glory be to Him. In either meaning, he is counted in their ranks and included in their company from the beginning of his affair, by the nature of the nominal sentence, not that this happened to him after he had not been so. Thus the root of the possibility that desire for evil proceeded from him, peace be upon him, is entirely cut off.

﴿And they raced each other to the door﴾ is connected to His saying: ﴿And she certainly desired him, and he would have desired her, had he not seen the proof of his Lord﴾. His saying "Thus" through to its end is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraḍ, a clause placed between two conjoined elements) set between the two conjoined clauses, to affirm his purity, peace be upon him. It is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And thus did We show Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾. The meaning is: She desired him, and he refused, and they raced each other to the door, that is, to the outer door (al-burrani), which is the way out. For this reason "door" is in the singular after the plural used earlier. The preposition is dropped and the verb is connected directly to the noun it governs, as in ﴿and when they measure for them﴾ (the verb kala, "to measure", taking the object directly without "for"). Alternatively, the racing (istibaq) is given the sense of hastening (ibtidar). The attribution of the lead in the race to her, although her aim was merely to prevent Joseph and that does not require reaching the door, is because when she saw him hastening to the door to escape her, she too hastened to get ahead of him and stop him from opening it and leaving. Or the expression of her hastening after him is given in this form for emphasis (mubalaghah).

﴿And she tore his shirt from behind﴾: she pulled him from behind, and it split lengthwise. This is qadd (splitting along the length), just as shaqq (splitting) across its width is qatt. It has been said in describing ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, that when he went upward he qadda, and when he went across he qatta. The attribution of the qadd to her alone, although Joseph's strength also played a part in it, is either because she was the last component of the complete cause (al-ʿillah al-tammah), or to announce her exaggeration in preventing him from leaving and her exerting all her effort in that, for fear of losing the beloved, or for fear of being exposed.

﴿And they found her master at the door﴾: that is, they came upon her husband. Since his ownership of Joseph was not valid, it is not said "their master" (sayyidahuma). It has been said: they found him approaching, and it has been said: he was sitting with a cousin of the woman, ﴿at the door﴾, that is, the outer door, as has passed.

Kaʿb, may Allah be pleased with him, narrated that when Joseph, peace be upon him, fled, the bolts of the locks flew off and fell until he went out through the doors.

﴿She said﴾: this is a resumptive clause (istiʾnaf) answering an implied question: "What happened when they found the governor at the door?" So it is said: She said: ﴿What is the recompense for one who intended evil against your family﴾, namely adultery and the like, ﴿except that he be imprisoned or a painful punishment?﴾ Here "ma" is negating: there is no recompense for him except imprisonment or a painful punishment. It has been said the intended meaning is beating with whips. Or "ma" is interrogative, meaning: what is his recompense other than that or the like?

She came up, in that state in which minds are bewildered, when the governor saw her in that suspicious condition, with a stratagem in which she combined two aims: clearing her name from what appeared on the outward state of affairs, and drawing Joseph away from his stance in resisting her and his refusal to comply with her purpose, by instilling terror in his heart of her scheming, hoping to have him force himself upon her when she despaired of his willingly doing so. As she said: ﴿And if he does not do what I command him, he will certainly be imprisoned and will certainly be among the humiliated﴾. Then she made the occurrence of the aforementioned intention on the part of Joseph, peace be upon him, a settled and established matter, needing no report of its occurrence, and made her actions aimed at executing its recompense. She wants to carry out upon him what the governance's law requires (qanun al-iyalah, the law of the realm). In leaving the one who intends unspecified there is an exaggeration of the gravity of the stated penalty, presenting it as a law applying uniformly to everyone, whoever they may be. In mentioning herself with the title of the governor's household, there is an enhancement of the affair and an incitement to him to carry out what she desires, by the judgment of anger and zealotry.

﴿He said﴾ is a resumptive sentence, answering the implied question: "What did Yusuf say then?" So it is said that he said: ﴿It was she who sought to seduce me from myself﴾. That is, she solicited me to compliance, not that I intended any evil by her, as she claimed. He, peace be upon him, said this to clear himself of what had been attributed to him, namely betrayal and failure to recognize his master's right, and to repel the two grave matters she had put before him. Referring to her with the third-person pronoun rather than the second-person address or a demonstrative is an observance of good manners, while also hinting at turning away from her.

﴿And a witness from her own family testified﴾. It was said: he was her paternal cousin. It was also said: he was the one who was sitting with her husband by the door, and it was said: he was a wise man to whom the king would refer and whom he would consult. It is also permissible that one of her family had seen them without her knowing, so that Allah, exalted is He, made it manifest to Yusuf, peace be upon him, by the testimony in his favour and by standing for the truth. Allah, glorified is He, placed the testimony upon one who was from her own family so that it would be the stronger proof of his innocence, peace be upon him, and the more effective in negating the accusation.

It was also said: the witness was her maternal cousin, a child in the cradle, whom Allah, exalted is He, caused to speak in confirmation of his innocence. This is the most apparent view, for it has been narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Four spoke while they were infants: the son of the hairdresser of Pharaoh's daughter, the witness of Yusuf, the companion of Jurayj, and Jesus (peace be upon him)." Narrated by al-Hakim from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), and he said: it is sound according to the conditions of the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim). The mention that he was from her family is to state the fact, since the situation in this case does not differ whether the witness was from her family or from others.

﴿If his shirt is torn from the front﴾, that is: if it is known that it was torn from the front from before, and its parallel is: "If you do good to me, then I have done good to you previously," meaning: if you take account of your kindness to me, then take account of my previous kindness to you. ﴿Then she has told the truth﴾, with qad (a particle that here brings the past near to the present) understood, that is, "then she has indeed told the truth." The same applies to His words ﴿then he is lying﴾. And although she did not explicitly state that he intended evil toward her, yet since her speech clearly implied it, truthfulness and falsehood were attributed to her on that basis, for just as they apply to speech in terms of its explicit content, they apply to it in terms of what it implies, and on that basis they also apply to performative utterances.

﴿and he is one of the liars﴾. This conditional, since there is neither a rational nor a customary necessary connection between its antecedent and its consequent, is not part of the testimony at all. It was mentioned only to widen the scope and to give rein to the woman's side, by supposing what the situation might generally allow: that the shirt could be torn from the front through her resisting him, peace be upon him, in defence of herself when he wished to be intimate with her and to uncover her, treating this as the apparent and most common occurrence. This serves to bring closer what is actually intended by the giving of testimony, namely the content of the second conditional, which is His statement, mighty and majestic is He:

﴿And if his shirt is torn from behind, then she has lied, and he is of the truthful.﴾ ... up to acceptance and submission on the part of the listener, because it is closer to what actually happened and more clearly indicates what is sought. Even if there is no necessary connection between its two sides as well. The narration of the conditional (sharti, a conditional proposition) after the verb of testimony is because it belongs to the category of statements, or by supposing a verb of saying, meaning: he testified, saying... etc. Calling it a testimony, even though no judgment is made in it by the actual truth or falsehood, is because it performs the function of testimony, or rather because it is a testimony in the true sense and a judgment on its truth and falsehood. As for the case where the witness is the child, this is clear, since it is a report of both from the Knower of the Unseen. The expression in the form of a conditional is to indicate that this is also evident from the signs. As for the case where the witness is someone else, then because it is apparent that the true state of affairs is known to him as it is, either by direct observation or by report. So he is certain of the absence of the antecedent of the first conditional and the presence of the antecedent of the second conditional, and from this necessarily follows certainty of the negation of the consequent of the first and the occurrence of the consequent of the second. Thus it is a report of her lie and of his truthfulness, peace be upon him. However, he presented his testimony in a manner safe from disparagement and criticism, by framing it in the form of a conditional that apparently hovers between its benefit and his benefit. In reality, there is definitely no hovering in it, because the first conditional makes the truth of her claim depend on something whose occurrence is impossible, namely the shirt being torn from the front, so it is inevitably false, and from its necessity its falsehood is established. The second makes his truthfulness depend on something whose occurrence is certain, namely the shirt being torn from behind, so it is definitely established.

This is like what has been said about the man who said to a woman: "Marry yourself to me." She said: "I have a husband." He denied this to her. She said: "If I do not have a husband, then I have married myself to you." The man accepted, so since she has no husband, it is a valid marriage, for making something dependent on an established matter is an immediate effect on it.

It has been read as (min qubulun wa min duburun) with a ḍamma, because they have been cut off from being in a construct state, like qablu and ba'du; and with a fatḥa, as if they were made proper names for the two directions, so they are not declined because of feminine form and being proper nouns. It has also been read with a sukūn on the ʿayn.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 28:**

﴿So when he saw his shirt torn from behind﴾, as if he had not seen that yet, or had not considered it. Then, when he became aware of it and knew the true state of affairs, ﴿he said: "Indeed, it is"﴾, that is, the matter over which they had disputed, which is an expression for the intention of evil attributed to Yusuf and the plan for his punishment in her words: "What is the recompense for one who intended evil against your family...", to its end. But this is not from the standpoint of the origin of that intention and its attribution to him, rather regardless of that, lest His words, ﴿of your guile﴾, that is, of the kind of your scheming and cunning, O women, and not of anyone else's, be devoid of the benefit and the planning of punishment. Even though it is not possible to strip it of its attribution to them, yet when she gave it the form of truth, it conveyed the ruling that it is from their scheming, conveying this clearly. So reflect. The generalization of the address is to draw attention to the fact that this is an ancient trait of theirs:

*Do not think that Hind alone has treachery as her nature;
the disposition of every coquettish soul is Hind.*

The return of the pronoun to her words, "(What is the recompense for one who intended evil against your family)" alone, is a departure from investigating the root of what the dispute concerned, namely that the intention of evil is from whom it is, toward investigating one branch of its branches. It also makes the evil, or the matter expressed by it, her desire for Yusuf (peace be upon him), which the report refutes, since scheming requires that other faults on her part also be taken into account, as we have indicated.

﴿Indeed, your scheming is mighty﴾, for it is more subtle, clings more to the heart, and has a stronger effect on the soul. It is related from some scholars: "I fear from women what I do not fear from Satan, for He, exalted is He, says: ﴿Indeed, the scheming of Satan is ever weak﴾, and He said to the women: ﴿Indeed, your scheming is mighty﴾." And because Satan whispers secretly, whereas they confront men with it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 29:

﴿Yusuf﴾ The vocative particle has been omitted from it, owing to his nearness and the perfection of his alertness to the matter (al-hadith), and in this there is a bringing near to him and a gentle treatment of his station. ﴿Turn away from this﴾, that is: from this matter, and from speaking about it, and conceal it, for your truthfulness and innocence have become manifest. ﴿And ask forgiveness﴾, you yourself, O this woman, ﴿for your sin﴾ which proceeded from you and was established against you. ﴿Indeed, you were﴾ on account of that ﴿among the sinners﴾, from among the body of the people who deliberately commit sin, or from their kind. It is said: "khati'a" (to err, to sin) when one commits a sin intentionally. This is a reason given for the command to seek forgiveness. The masculine form (al-tadhkir) is used to give precedence to the males over the females. The Aziz was a forbearing man, so he was satisfied with this measure of reproach toward her. It is also said: he had little jealousy (ghayra).

﴿And women said﴾, that is, a group of women, and they were five: the wife of the cupbearer, the wife of the baker, the wife of the keeper of the beasts, the wife of the keeper of the prison, and the wife of the chamberlain. "Al-niswa" (the women) is a singular noun used as the plural of "imra'a" (woman), and its feminine marking is not real (ghayr haqiqi), like the feminine marking in "al-lumma" (a group of women) and "al-thubba" (a group of men). For this reason the verb attached to it does not take the feminine ending (ta' al-ta'nith). ﴿In the city﴾ is an adverbial complement of (qala), meaning: they spread the matter in Egypt. Or it is a description of "al-niswa." ﴿The wife of the Aziz﴾, that is, the king, meaning Qitfir. Their attribution of her to him by this title, without naming her or him, was not for the purpose of exaggerating the spreading of the news, on the principle that souls are more inclined to hear the news of those of high station, as has been said. Their purpose was not to expose the Aziz, but to intensify their blame of her, through their saying: ﴿She solicits her young man﴾, that is, she demands of him intercourse with her, contrives in that and deceives him ﴿concerning himself﴾. It was also said: she seeks from him immorality. Their choice of the present tense form (al-mudari') indicates the continuity of the solicitation. "Al-fata" (young man) among people is the young man, and its root is "fiy" (fi'y), as in their saying "fityan" (plural). "Al-futuwwa" (chivalry) is an anomalous form. Its plurals are "fatiyya" and "fityan." It is used metaphorically for the slave, which is what is meant here. In a hadith: "None of you should say, 'my slave (abdi) and my slave-girl (amati),' but let him say, 'my young man (fataya) and my young woman (fatati).'" Their referring to Joseph, peace be upon him, with this term, attributed to her and not to the Aziz, does not imply humiliation, since attribution to the Aziz would not necessarily imply humiliation. Rather, it may suggest a kind of honor, in order to show the clear disparity between them arising from ownership and slavehood. All of this serves to reinforce the exaggeration and intensified blame mentioned above, for a woman who has no husband, or who has a base husband, may be excused for soliciting lovers, especially if they are of high standing. But as for the one who has a husband, and what a husband, the Aziz of Egypt, her solicitation of another man, especially her slave, with whom there is no equality at all, and her persistence in that, is the utmost error and the extreme of misguidance.

﴿She has been seized by love﴾, that is, his love has pierced the covering (shaghaf) of her heart, which is its veil, or a thin skin called "lisan al-qalb" (the tongue of the heart), until it reached her inner heart (fu'ad). It was read as (sha'afaha) with the letter 'ayn, from (sha'afa al-ba'ir), when one smears a camel with tar and burns it. It is reported from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "al-shaghaf" is deadly love, and "al-sha'af" is love short of that. Al-Sha'bi used to say: "al-shaghaf" is love, and "al-sha'af" is madness. The clause is a second predicate, or a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of (turawidu) or from its object. Whichever it is, it is a repetition of the blame and an emphasis of the reproach, by showing the disturbance of her inner states as well as her outward states. Taking it as a cause for the continuity of the solicitation is, in terms of the "that" (inniyya, the fact), an inference from the less evident to the more evident, and in terms of the "why" (lumiyya, the reason), an inclination to prepare an excuse on her behalf, which these women were not in a position to do. The accusative of (hubban) is a specification (tamyiz) that transfers the action from the agent, since the original is: "his love has seized her," as has been pointed out.

﴿Indeed, we see her﴾, that is, we know her with a knowledge that approaches direct observation and sight, regarding what she did of solicitation and excessive love, ﴿in clear error﴾ away from the path of right guidance and correctness, or away from the ways of reason, ﴿manifest﴾, obvious, such that its being error is hidden from no one, or making her affair apparent among people. The clause confirms the content of the two preceding clauses, which were aimed at blame and reproach, and records against her that in her matter she is in grave error. They did not say, "Indeed she is in manifest error," in order to indicate that this judgment did not come from them by mere conjecture, but from knowledge and opinion, while also hinting that they themselves are far removed from the like of what she is in.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 31:**

﴿When she heard of their scheming﴾, that is, of their backbiting and their evil talk, and their saying: "The wife of the great man (al-'Aziz) has been infatuated with her slave, the Canaanite, and he has rejected her." They called it "scheming" because it was secret from her, like the scheme of a schemer, even though it was apparent to others. It is also said that she had asked them to keep her secret, but they divulged it against her. It is also said that they only said this so that she would show them Yusuf (peace be upon him). ﴿She sent for them﴾, inviting them. It is said that she invited forty women, among them the five mentioned. ﴿And prepared﴾, that is, she brought in and readied ﴿for them a reclining-place (mutaka')﴾, that is, what they would lean upon of cushions and pillows. Or she arranged for them a place for food and drink, because they used to recline for eating, drinking and conversation, as is the custom of the affluent. For this reason a man was forbidden to eat while reclining. It is also said that "mutaka'" means food, from their saying "we reclined (ittaka'na) at so-and-so's place," meaning we ate there. Jamil said:

*So we remained in blessing and reclined, and drank the lawful from its jars.*

It is related from Mujahid that "mutaka'" means food that is cut by knife, as though the meaning is that one leans on it with the knife while cutting, since the one cutting leans upon the thing being cut with the knife. It has been read without the hamza, and read with lengthening of the vowel of the kaf, like *muntazah* for *muntazah* and *yanba'* for *yanbu'*. It has also been read *mutka'* (مُتْكَأً), which is the citron, and they recited:

*She sent a citron to the sons of her father, which the stout, shameless one hastens with.*

Or it means that which is cut, from *matak al-shay'* when one cuts it off. And *matkan* (مَتْكًا) is from *taka* when one reclines (ittaka).

﴿And she gave each one of them a knife﴾, to use for cutting what is customarily cut among the meats, fruits and the like that were set before them and brought near to them, while they were reclining. Her purpose in this was what would come to pass of the cutting of their hands. ﴿And she said﴾ to Yusuf, while they were occupied with handling the knives and using them on the fruits and the like in their hands. The conjunction with *waw* perhaps indicates that her saying ﴿Come out before them﴾, that is, show yourself to them, did not come directly after she arranged their affairs, so that her purpose of diverting them might be accomplished. ﴿When they saw him﴾ is a conjunction with an implied element demanded by the command to come out, and the sentence is understood to include it. That is, he came out before them and they saw him. It was omitted to emphasize the suddenness of their seeing him, as though it would escape them at the mention of his coming out before them. Similarly it was omitted to emphasize speed in the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿When he saw it placed before him﴾, after His words: ﴿I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you﴾. In this there is an indication of the swiftness of his obedience (peace be upon him) to her command in matters whose harm is not visible among the deeds.

﴿They exalted him﴾, that is, they magnified him, and were overwhelmed by his surpassing beauty and his dazzling, exquisite handsomeness, for the excellence of his beauty over the beauty of every beautiful thing was like the excellence of the full moon on its night over the rest of the stars.

It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "I saw Yusuf on the night of the Mi'raj like the moon on the night of the full moon." It has also been said that the brightness of his face was seen reflected on the walls, as the light of the sun is seen on water. It is also said that the meaning of *akbarna* is that they menstruated (hadn), and the *ha'* is a pause marker, or it is a pronoun referring to Yusuf (peace be upon him) with the *lam* omitted, meaning they menstruated for him out of intense lust, as al-Mutanabbi said:

*Fear God and veil this beauty with a face-veil; for if you show yourself, the maidens in their chambers will menstruate.*

﴿And they cut their hands﴾, that is, they wounded them with the knives in their hands, because of the extreme of their astonishment, and the movements of their limbs departed from the course of choice and habit, so that they did not know what they had done. In expressing the wounding as "cutting" there is an evident indication of the great number of their wounds. Despite this, they did not care about it and were not aware of it.

﴿And they said: "Hashā lillāh"﴾, glorifying Him, exalted be He, above the attributes of deficiency and incapacity, and marvelling at His power to produce such a wondrous creation. Its origin is *hāshā*, as Abu 'Amr read it in running speech (fi al-darj), and its final alif was dropped for lightness. It is a preposition that conveys the meaning of exoneration (tanzih) in the context of exception, so nothing is excepted by it except what is necessarily a matter of exoneration. Thus it was placed in its position. The meaning of "hāshā Allāh" is the exoneration of God and the innocence of God. This is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him), and the *lam* indicates the one exonerated and declared innocent, as in *suqyan lak* (a blessing upon you). The evidence that it is placed in the position of the verbal noun is the reading of Abu al-Sammal, *hāshan* with tanwin, and the reading of Abu 'Amr, dropping the final alif, and the reading of al-A'mash, dropping the first. The use of it as a noun is characteristic of nouns, which indicates that it has been placed in the rank of a noun. Its not taking tanwin is to observe its original form, as in your saying "I sat from on his right" (jalastu min 'an yamīnihi) and the saying "I went from upon him" (ghadatu min 'alayhi), where the alif is changed to ya' with the pronoun. It has been read *hāsh lillāh* with a sukun on the shin, following the fatha in dropping the alif, and *hāsha al-Ilah*. It has also been said that *hāshā* is a verb (fa'il) from *al-hasha*, which is the side, and its subject is the pronoun of Yusuf, meaning he came to be on the side of avoiding what she accused him of, for God's sake, that is, for His obedience, or for His station, or he kept away from disobedience for the sake of God.

﴿This is not a human (bashar)﴾, by employing *ma* in the sense of *laysa* (is not). This is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, since both share in negating the present. It has been read *basharun* in the dialect of Tamim, and *bi-shir an* (بِشِرًى), meaning: a base purchased slave. They negated humanity from him because of the otherworldly beauty they witnessed in him, whose like had not been known among humans. They restricted him to angelhood by their saying: ﴿This is none but a noble angel﴾, based on what is fixed in minds, that no living being is more beautiful than an angel, just as it is fixed in them that no one is uglier than Satan. For this reason, everyone extreme in beauty or ugliness is still compared to these two. Their purpose was to describe him with the highest degrees of beauty and loveliness.

Abu al-Su'ud, *Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim*, on Surah 12, verse 32:

﴿She said: "That is the one about whom you blamed me.﴾ The *fa* (*fa-l-faṣīḥa*, the "eloquent fa," which signals an implied condition) is eloquent. The address is to the women, and the demonstrative refers to Joseph by the designation they had just used for him, namely his having gone beyond human rank in beauty and loveliness and being restricted to the status of an angel. Thus *ism al-ishara* (the demonstrative) is the *mubtada'* (subject of the nominal sentence), and the relative clause (*al-mawsul*) is its *khabar* (predicate). The meaning is: if the matter is as you have said, then that one, the noble angel far removed from human ranks, is ﴿the one about whom you blamed me﴾, that is, you reproached me for being infatuated with him, since you elevated my position by my connection to the Chief, and lowered his worth by describing him as a slave. Alternatively, the designation refers to what they had called him before, when they said: "The wife of the Chief has been overcome with love for her Canaanite slave," and so the relative clause is the *khabar* of an omitted *mubtada'*, meaning: "He is that Canaanite slave whom you imagined in your own minds and said about him and about me what you said. Now you know who he is and what your statement about us was." As for the view that the meaning is that you did not depict him as he truly is, and that had you depicted him as you witnessed him, you would have excused me for being infatuated with him, this does not suit the context. Her purpose in summoning them and paving the way for what she had prepared for them was to rebuke them and make them regret what had come from them of blame, and she has accomplished that completely. What was said in the way of excuse is the proper course for one who offers an excuse before his excuse becomes evident. It has also been said, regarding the reason for his being like an angel, that the combination of striking beauty, surpassing perfection, and complete protection from sin are special features of angels. This too does not suit her statement: ﴿that is the one about whom you blamed me﴾, for the designation of protection from sin is among the things that contradict the fulfillment of her aim. Then, after she had established the proof against them and made her excuse clear to them, and after they had suffered from the same cause that had afflicted her, namely him, peace be upon him, she revealed to them the remainder of her secret, and said:

﴿And indeed I sought to seduce him from himself﴾, as you said and heard. ﴿But he refused.﴾ He abstained, seeking chastity (*al-'iṣma*). It is the form *istaf'ala* used for intensification, indicating emphatic abstention and intense self-restraint, as if he were in a state of protection while striving to increase it, as in *istamsaka* (he held fast) and *istajma'a al-ra'y* (he gathered his opinion). In this there is clear proof that nothing harmful to his chastity came from him, peace be upon him, through his saying: ﴿"God forbid!"﴾ from anxiety or anything else. She first acknowledged to them what they had been hearing about her seeking to seduce him and affirmed it, displaying her delight in that. Then she went further, stating that he turned away from her in the most complete manner, and never inclined toward her at all. Then she added that she herself continued in her former state, not desisting from him, neither by the blame of the censurers nor by the rejection of the beloved. Thus she said:

﴿And if he does not do what I command him﴾, that is, what I command him to do in the future, just as he has not done it in the past. The preposition is omitted and the verb is connected directly to the pronoun, as in *amartuka al-khayr* (I commanded you the good). The pronoun refers to the relative clause, or *amri iyyahu* (my command to him), meaning the thing that my command requires and entails. In that case *ma* is a verbal-noun particle (*masdariyya*), and the pronoun refers to Joseph. She expressed her solicitation as a "command" to display the continuation of her authority over him and to demand obedience to her command.

﴿He will surely be imprisoned﴾, with the doubled *nun* (*al-nun al-muthaqqala*). She preferred the passive voice in accordance with the custom of kings, or to create the impression of the speed with which this would follow his failure to obey her command, as though no act of any agent intervened between them. ﴿And he will surely be among the humiliated﴾, with the light *nun* (*al-nun al-mukhaffafa*), that is, among the abject in prison. Both verbs have also been read with the doubled *nun*, but the well-known reading is preferred, because the *nun* was written in the codex as an *alif*, according to the rule of pausal pronunciation. The *lam* that enters upon the conditional particle is a *lam al-mutawatti'a* (the preparatory lam for an oath), and its response stands in place of both responses. She uttered this threat, which contains various forms of emphasis, in the presence of the women, so that Joseph, peace be upon him, would know that she was not acting in secret or out of fear of anyone, so that the stratagems would not constrict him and the pretexts would not wear him out, and so that the women would advise him and guide him toward agreeing with her. Since this flashing and thundering on her part was a likely occasion for a questioner to ask: "What did Joseph do at that time?", it was said:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 33:

﴿He said﴾, communing with his Lord, exalted is His authority: ﴿My Lord, the prison﴾ (sijn), the one you threatened me with casting into, ﴿is dearer to me﴾ (ahabb ila). Ya'qub recited it as bi-l-fath (with a fatha), as a verbal noun (masdar). ﴿Than that to which they invite me﴾ (p-274) — that is, more preferred by me, because it is a small hardship, followed by lofty, everlasting comforts, ﴿than that to which they invite me﴾, from their solicitation, which leads to misery and painful torment. This statement of his, peace be upon him, is based on what has preceded of the unveiling of realities before him and the manifestation of each of them in its fitting form. Therefore the form of comparison (sigha al-tafdil) is not on its usual basis, since he has no trace of love for what they call him to. Rather, he and the prison are two evils, the lesser of them and the closer to being preferred being the prison. The expression of preference as "love" serves to cut off the root of their hope for his assistance, out of fear of imprisonment. The restriction to mentioning the prison is because the humiliation is among its branches and consequences. The attribution of the invitation to all of them is because the women encouraged him to obey them and frightened him from opposing them. It was also said: they invited him to themselves. And it was said: he was tested with the prison only because of this statement, and it would have been better for him to ask God Most High for well-being; for this reason the Messenger of God ﷺ rejected the one who used to ask for patience.

﴿And unless You turn away﴾, that is: if You do not turn away ﴿from me their stratagem﴾ in making that beloved to me and beautifying it in my sight, by making me steadfast in what I am upon of chastity and modesty, ﴿I shall incline toward them﴾, that is: I shall lean toward answering them, or toward themselves, according to the dictates of nature and the rule of the appetitive faculty. This is a plea from him, peace be upon him, to the subtle graces of God Most High, following the custom of the prophets and the righteous in restricting the attainment of good and deliverance from evils to the threshold of God, exalted and majestic, and in denying power and capacity to themselves; and it is an exaggeration in soliciting His subtle grace to turn away their stratagem, by showing that he has no power to resist, like the words of one seeking help: "Rescue me, or I perish." It does not mean that he seeks compulsion and constraint toward chastity and modesty while in himself there is a motive calling him to their desire. The "sabwa" is inclination toward desire, and from it comes "al-saba" (the east wind), since souls incline toward it for the pleasantness of its breeze and its refreshment. It was also read as "asubbu ilayhinna", from "al-sababa", which is the tenderness of longing.

﴿And I would be among the ignorant﴾, those who do not act by what they know, since whoever's knowledge yields no benefit is the same as the ignorant; or among the foolish, by committing what they invite me to of abominations, since the wise does not do what is abominable.

Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 34:

﴿So his Lord responded to him﴾ regarding his supplication, which was contained in his saying: ﴿"And unless You turn away from me their scheming, I might incline toward them..."﴾ etc., for it includes a request for the turning away of their scheming in the most eloquent and most gracious manner, as has passed. And in attributing the responding to the Lord, with the addition to him - peace be upon him - is what is not hidden of the manifestation of gentleness. ﴿So He turned away from him their scheming﴾ according to his supplication, and kept him firm upon chastity and modesty. ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing﴾ of the supplication of those who humbly beseech Him, ﴿the All-Knowing﴾ of their conditions and what sets them right.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 35:

﴿Then it occurred to them﴾ That is: it became apparent to the Chief (al-'Aziz) and his companions, those who were in charge of loosing and binding (al-hall wa al-'aqd), after they had been content with the matter of Yusuf being kept secret and with turning away from it, ﴿after they had seen the signs﴾ which turned them away from that resolve (al-bada'), namely the evidences indicating his innocence, peace be upon him. The subject of "badā" (it occurred) is either its verbal noun (masdar), or the opinion (al-ra'y) understood from the context, or the verbal noun implied by His words ﴿they will surely imprison him﴾. The meaning: a resolve (bada') or an opinion occurred to them, or his imprisonment, which was decided, [came to them] as they said: "By God, they will surely imprison him." So the omitted oath and its answer are the object of the omitted saying, and it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from their pronoun. That resolve came about only through the woman's coaxing of her husband and her hold over him, leading him by the forelock and the hump, as he was submissive to her and she guided him wherever she wished.

Al-Suddi said: She said to the Chief: "This Hebrew slave has disgraced me among the people, telling them that I solicited him to himself. So either you permit me to go out and apologize to the people, or you imprison him." So he imprisoned him. She intended by this to realize her threat, so that his stubbornness would be softened by it and his neck would submit to her, since the cords of her hope had been severed concerning enticing him by displaying her beauty and by inclining towards herself and her helpers.

It is read ﴿they will surely imprison you﴾ (la-tasjununnahu) in the second-person form, by which some addressed the Chief and those around him, or addressed the Chief alone as a form of honour, or addressed the Chief and those with him among the men of opinion who directly carry out the imprisonment and confinement. ﴿For a while﴾ until the time when the people's talk would cease. This was the initial opinion of the Chief and his household. As for her, [it was] until the prison would subdue him and make him subservient to her, and the people would suppose that he was the guilty one. It is also read ﴿ʿattā ḥīn﴾ in the dialect of Hudhayl.

And there entered the prison with him (*ma'hu*, i.e., in his company) two young men (*fityan*) from among the king's young servants and slaves, one of whom was his cupbearer (*sharabi*) and the other his baker (*khabbazuhu*).

It is narrated that a group of the people of Egypt guaranteed them a sum of money so that they would poison the king in his food and drink. They agreed to this. Then the cupbearer backed out of it, but the baker went ahead and poisoned the bread. When the food was brought, the cupbearer said: "Do not eat, O King, for the bread is poisoned." The baker said: "Do not drink, O King, for the drink is poisoned." The king said to the cupbearer: "Drink it," and he drank it and it did not harm him. He said to the baker: "Eat it," but he refused. So he tested it on an animal, and it died. He then ordered that they both be imprisoned, and it so happened that they were put in prison with him.

The postponement of the agent (*al-fa'il*, the subject) after the object (*al-maf'ul*, the object) is for a reason already mentioned several times: to give attention to what is placed first and to create anticipation for what comes later, so that it settles in the soul, when it arrives there, with especially firm establishment. Its parallel is the placing of the adverbial phrase (*al-zarf*) before the explicit object in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So he sensed within himself a fear﴾. And the postponement of "the prison" (*al-sijn*) after the adverbial phrase is to create the impression of the reverse, namely that the adverbial phrase is a predicate (*khabar*) placed before the subject (*mubtada'*), and that the sentence is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) of the subject of (*dakhala*, "entered"). So reflect.

﴿One of them said﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*), built upon a question from someone who asks: "What did they do after they had entered the prison with him?" It is answered that one of them, namely the cupbearer, said: ﴿Indeed I see myself﴾, i.e., "I saw myself", and the use of the present tense is to bring the past scene vividly before the mind, ﴿pressing grapes into wine﴾, i.e., grapes. He named it by what it becomes, since pressing is aimed at it. It was said that *khamr* in the dialect of Oman is the name for grapes. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, it is (*a'siru 'inaban*, "pressing grapes").

﴿And the other said﴾, namely the baker: ﴿Indeed I see myself carrying bread upon my head﴾. The postponement of the object after the adverbial phrase is for the reason mentioned just above. And his saying: ﴿of which the birds eat﴾, i.e., they peck at it, is either an attribute of the bread or a resumptive sentence built upon the question.

﴿Inform us of its interpretation﴾, i.e., of the interpretation of the two visions mentioned, or of what was seen, by treating the pronoun as if it were that, by way of metaphor (*isti'arah*). For the demonstrative noun (*ism al-isharah*) is used to point to a plural, as in the poet's saying:

*In it are lines of black and white, as if on its skin is the mottling of vitiligo.*

That is: "as if that." The reason for resorting to treating the pronoun as a demonstrative noun, even though there is no need for it once the referent is interpreted as what has been mentioned or what was seen, is that a pronoun only refers to the referent itself as such, without concern for any of its states. Therefore its interpretation according to one of the two considerations is not possible except by treating it as a demonstrative noun, which indicates the thing pointed to under the consideration that was used in the speech. So reflect. This is when the two of them said it together, or when one of them said it on behalf of both together. As for when each of them said it after relating what he had seen, the mentioned address is not their expression, nor the expression of one of them on behalf of both, so that the referent would be plural. Rather it is the expression of each of them: "Inform me of its interpretation," asking for an explanation of what he had seen. The first-person plural form in the narration is used within the narration, not within what is narrated, in the manner of His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things﴾, for they were not addressed with that all at once, but each of them was addressed in his own time with a singular form specific to him.

﴿Indeed we see you﴾ is a justification for their presenting their dreams to him and asking him to explain them, peace be upon him, ﴿to be among the good-doers﴾, i.e., among those who excel in interpreting dreams, since some people of the prison had related their dreams to him and he interpreted them well. Or among the scholars, since they had heard him mention to the people what showed his knowledge and merit. Or among those who do good to the people of the prison. That is: "So do good to us by removing our distress, if you are able to do so."

It is narrated that when any man among them fell ill, he (peace be upon him) would attend to him; when his place became cramped, he would make room for him; when he was in need, he would gather for him. And it is narrated from Qatadah, may Allah be pleased with him, that there were people in the prison whose hope had been cut off and whose sorrow had lengthened, so he began to say: "Rejoice and be patient, you will be rewarded." They said: "May Allah bless you! How handsome your face is! How handsome your character is! Blessing has been bestowed upon us through your neighborhood. Who are you, young man?" He said: "I am Yusuf, son of Ya'qub the chosen of Allah, son of Is'haq the sacrificed one of Allah, son of Ibrahim the friend of Allah." The keeper of the prison said to him: "If I could, I would set you free, but I will treat you well as a neighbor, so stay in whichever of the prison's houses you wish."

It is related from al-Sha'bi that the two of them had dreams and tested him with them. The cupbearer said: "I see myself in a garden, and there is a vine on which are three clusters of grapes. I cut them, pressed them into the king's cup, and gave him to drink." The baker said: "I see myself with three baskets on my head, containing various kinds of food, and the birds of prey are pecking at them."

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 37:**

﴿He said: "No food will come to you that you are provided with in this place of yours, according to your habitual custom, except that I shall inform you of its interpretation﴾ before it comes to you." This is an *istithna' mufarragh* (an exhaustive exception, one with no stated object, whose sense is determined by the context) taken from the most general circumstances. That is, no food will come to you in any circumstance except in the circumstance in which I have informed you of it, by clarifying for you its essence, its manner, and all its other conditions. ﴿before it comes to you﴾.

The application of the term *ta'wil* (interpretation, explanation of what something will become) to this is either by way of *isti'arah* (metaphor), since with respect to food in general, which is indeterminate, it is in the position of the interpretation of what was seen in a dream and is similar to it; or by way of *mushakalah* (verbal correspondence, the use of a word because of its occurrence alongside another word), in line with what occurred in their own words, "Inform us of its interpretation." It is not far-fetched that by *ta'wil* is meant the thing that is to come about (*al-shay' al-a'il*), not the outcome (*al-ma'al*). For it is originally the making of one thing to revert to another thing. Just as it is permissible to mean the second by it, it is permissible to mean the first. The meaning then is: "Except that I shall inform you of what it will become, of the speech and news that corresponds to reality." He, peace be upon him, used to say to them: "Today there will come to you food of such and such a description," and they would find it so. His purpose, peace be upon him, in this is the clarification of everything of concern to them among the matters awaited before they occur.

The food is singled out for mention because it is most prominent in this matter given the circumstances, together with the consideration of achieving a smooth transition to it from what the two had related of the two dreams concerning drink and food. The pronoun has been made to refer to what the two had related of the two dreams, in the sense: "No food that you are provided with, according to your custom, will come to you except that I shall inform you of the interpretation of what you have related to me before that food, specified for that time, comes to you," intending by this the informing with haste in the announcement.

You should know that the noble composition clearly indicates the repetition of the coming of food and the informing of the interpretation, and their recurrence. The situation is one of displaying his excellence in the various branches of knowledge, such that the interpretation of their dream enters into this primarily. He, peace be upon him, did not restrict himself merely to the interpretation of their dream, although in it there is indication of his excellence, because when they described him, peace be upon him, as belonging to the ranks of the good-doers, and they knew this, since they said: ﴿Indeed, we see you to be among the good-doers﴾, he, peace be upon him, discerned in them goodness and an inclination to accept the truth. So he wished to go forth, the most eager of the eager, from what was incumbent upon him of calling creatures to the truth. He therefore prepared, before embarking on that, an introduction that would increase them in knowledge of the greatness of his station, in confidence in his affair, and in awareness of the height of his rank in the wondrous sciences. This was a means to achieving what he aimed at. The introduction had been drawn out from their own speech. It is as if he said: "The interpretation of what you related to me, in the nearest reach of completion, since you saw its likeness in the dream; and I explain to you every great and subtle matter of future affairs, even if there were no dream preceding it. Even the regular food that comes to you every day, I will explain to you before its coming." Then he informed them that his knowledge of this is not of the kind of the knowledge of the soothsayers and diviners, but rather it is a divine bounty that He grants to whomever He wills of those He chooses for prophethood. So he said:

﴿That is of what my Lord has taught me.﴾ That is: that interpretation and the informing of unseen things. The sense of distance in *dhalika* (that) is for indicating the loftiness of its rank and the remoteness of its station. ﴿Of what my Lord has taught me﴾ through revelation and inspiration, that is: part of it, or of that kind which the intellects do not approach to grasp. He indicated to them by this that he has many sciences, and that what they heard is a piece of their totality and a branch of their tree. Then he explained that attaining this honour was by means of his following the religion of his noble prophetic forefathers and his refraining from polytheism. So he said:

﴿Indeed, I have forsaken the religion of a people who do not believe in God﴾. This is a *isti'naf* (resumptive sentence) which came as an answer to a question arising from his saying: ﴿That is of what my Lord has taught me﴾, and as a justification for it. It is not an attribute (*sila*) of the relative pronoun for the teaching that occurred, leading to the meaning that it is of what my Lord taught me for this reason and not another. Nor is it [a justification] for the content of the declarative clause, because what is mentioned in the context of justification is not the cause for the mentioned interpretation being part of what his Lord taught him, or for its being of its kind; rather, it is the cause for the very act of teaching what he knew. It is as if it were said: "Why did your Lord teach you those wondrous sciences?" So it was said: "Because I have forsaken the religion of the disbelievers," that is, their religion upon which they agreed, of polytheism and the worship of idols. What is meant by forsaking it is refraining from it altogether, as his saying reveals: ﴿It is not for us to associate anything with God﴾, not abandoning it after having been involved in it. It was expressed in this way because it is, outwardly, more consistent with his following of his fathers, peace be upon him. The expression of their disbelief in God, exalted is He, by negating faith in Him is to specify that their worship of Him, exalted is He, together with the worship of idols, is not faith in Him, exalted is He, as is their false claim, in accordance with what has passed in the saying of God, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, it is an unrighteous deed﴾. ﴿And they, in the Hereafter﴾ and what it contains of recompense, ﴿they are disbelievers﴾ specifically, and not others, because of their excessiveness in disbelief.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, *Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim ila Mazaya al-Kitab al-Karim*) on surah 12, verse 38:**

﴿And I follow the religion (*millah*) of my forefathers, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.﴾ That is: he attained these perfections and won these honours only because he followed the religion of his noble forefathers, and did not follow the religion of a people who disbelieved in the Originator (*al-mabda'*) and the Return (*al-ma'ad*). He (peace be upon him) said this to encourage his two companions toward faith and *tawhid* (affirmation of God's oneness), and to repel them from the *shirk* (association of partners with God) and error in which they were. The mention of his abandoning their religion is placed before the mention of his following the religion of his forefathers, because *takhliyah* (emptying, clearing away) precedes *tahliyah* (adorning).

﴿It is not for us﴾, that is: it is not correct, nor is it proper, let alone that it should occur, ﴿for us﴾, the company of prophets, because of the strength of our souls and the abundance of our knowledge, ﴿to associate anything with God﴾, whatever it may be, whether an angel, a jinn, or a human, let alone inert matter. ﴿That﴾, that is: the *tawhid* indicated by his saying: (It is not for us to associate anything with God), ﴿is from the bounty of God upon us﴾, that is: it arises from His support of us with prophethood and His designating us to lead the community (*ummah*) (p-278) and guide them to the truth. This, although it is among the requirements and motives of *tawhid*, is a magnificent blessing and a great favour upon us in particular, ﴿and upon the people﴾ generally through us. And since this is expressed by that title, *tawhid*, which it requires, is expressed by gratitude, so it is said: ﴿but most people do not give thanks﴾, that is: they do not affirm God's oneness. For *tawhid*, although it is one of the effects of the support mentioned, is also gratitude to God, Mighty and Majestic, for the blessing. The apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun referring to "people" in order to add clarification and explanation, and to cut off the supposition that it refers to the collective, which would imply that the non-grateful are not restricted to people.

It has also been said: that *tawhid* is from God's bounty upon us in that He set up for us proofs which we examine and by which we reason to the truth; He has set up similar proofs for all other people as well, but most of them do not examine them or reason by them, following their own desires, and so they remain disbelievers, not thankful. You may also say: that *tawhid* is from God's bounty upon us, in that He gave us intellects and faculties which we use for the proofs of *tawhid* that He laid out in the souls and the horizons; He has given all other people similar ones too, but most of them do not give thanks, that is, they do not direct those powers and faculties to that for which they were created, and do not use them for the proofs of *tawhid* mentioned, the horizon-based, the soul-based, the rational and the transmitted.

"O two companions of the prison!" That is: O my two companions in the prison, just as you say, "O thief of the night." He addressed them with the title of companionship in the place of sorrows and the house of griefs, in which affection becomes pure and sincere counsel is unmixed, so that they would turn to him and accept his speech. He set forth for them an example by which the truth would become clear to them in the fullest clarity, and said: ﴿Are multiple lords, separate from one another, better, or Allah, the One, the Irresistible?﴾ Lords with no connection among them and no agreement, each of whom enslaves you as he wills, without any of them overseeing the others, while none of them is independent. ﴿Better﴾ for you ﴿or Allah﴾, the God worshipped in truth, ﴿the One﴾ who is singular in divinity, ﴿the Irresistible﴾, the Victorious whom no one can overcome. And after he had alerted them to the corruption of a plurality of lords, he made clear to them that their gods had fallen from the level of consideration altogether, let alone divinity. So he said, generalizing the address to them and to those who follow their religion:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 40:

﴿What you worship besides Him﴾ means: besides Allah, anything, ﴿except names﴾ that are empty, having no referent in external reality. This is because that to which the name has no actual referent has no existence at all; so their worship was directed only at those names. ﴿Which you have named﴾ means: which you have made into names. The objects named were not mentioned, out of consideration for what the context requires, namely their removal from the rank of existence, and as an indication that their naming is in falsehood just as their worship is, since the names have no named object, just as their worship has no object of worship. ﴿You and your fathers﴾ [have named them] out of sheer ignorance and misguidance on your part. ﴿Allah has sent down no authority for them﴾ means: for that naming, which entails worship; ﴿no authority﴾ means no proof indicating its validity. ﴿Judgment belongs only to Allah﴾ means: regarding the matter of worship that branches from that naming, judgment belongs only to Allah, may His authority be exalted, because He alone deserves it essentially, since He is the Necessary Existent in Himself, the Originator of all things, and the Owner of their affair. ﴿He has commanded﴾ is a resumptive statement, built upon a question arising from His saying "Judgment belongs only to Allah." It is as if it were said: "What has Allah judged in this matter?" And it was answered: He has commanded, through the tongues of the prophets, peace be upon them, ﴿that you worship not except Him﴾, meaning: that you not worship except Him, as the dictates of reason also require. ﴿That is the upright religion﴾, meaning: the restriction of worship to Him, Exalted is He, is the established, straight religion, upon which proofs by reason and by transmission have combined. ﴿But most people do not know﴾ that this is the upright religion, due to their ignorance of those proofs; or they know nothing at all, so they worship names they have invented of their own accord, turning away from rational proof and transmitted authority. Having established the truth, called them both to it, and explained to them its lofty worth and the breadth of His knowledge, he (the commentator) began to explain what the two of them had asked about; and because this is a topic different from what preceded it, he separated it from that by repeating the address, and so he said:

O two companions of the prison, as for one of you﴾ (﴿يا صاحِبَيِ السِّجْنِ أمّا أحَدُكُما﴾), namely the cupbearer (al-Sharabi), he did not specify him out of confidence in what the interpretation indicates, and as a means of keeping the matter of his companion ambiguous, lest he address him directly with what would distress him. ﴿Will give his lord﴾ (﴿فَيَسْقِي رَبَّهُ﴾), i.e., his master, ﴿wine to drink﴾ (﴿خَمْرًا﴾). It is reported that he (peace be upon him) said to him: "What you saw of the vine and its goodliness: the king, and the goodness of your state with him. As for the three branches, they are three days that pass in prison, after which you will come out and return to what you were." Ikrimah read (فَيُسْقى رَبُّهُ), in the passive voice (al-bina' lil-maf'ul), meaning: "he will be given to drink what he is watered with."

﴿As for the other﴾ (﴿وَأمّا الآخَرُ﴾), namely the baker, ﴿he will be crucified and birds will eat from his head﴾ (﴿فَيُصْلَبُ فَتَأْكُلُ الطَّيْرُ مِن رَأْسِهِ﴾). It is reported that he (peace be upon him) said to him: "What you saw of the three baskets: three days will pass, then you will come out and be executed." ﴿The matter is decreed﴾ (﴿قُضِيَ﴾), i.e., completed and made certain, ﴿the matter about which you both inquire﴾ (﴿الأمْرُ الَّذِي فِيهِ تَسْتَفْتِيانِ﴾), namely what the two of them saw in their dreams, as a definitive matter, not its outcome, which is an expression for the salvation of one of them and the destruction of the other, as the attribution of the decree to it might suggest. This is because istifta' (seeking a legal opinion) occurs concerning an incident, not concerning its ruling. One says: "He sought a legal opinion from the jurist concerning the incident" (istaftaa al-faqih fi al-hadithah), meaning he requested from him an explanation of its ruling. One does not say: "He sought from him a ruling on its ruling" (istaftaahu fi hukmiha). Likewise ifta' (issuing a legal opinion): one says, "So-and-so issued a legal opinion concerning such-and-such incident with such-and-such," and one does not say, "He issued a legal opinion concerning its ruling or its answer with such-and-such." Among what is a clear indicator of this is His, exalted be He, saying: ﴿O chiefs, give me your opinion concerning my vision﴾ (﴿يا أيُّها المَلأُ أفْتُونِي في رُؤْيايَ﴾). The meaning of their seeking a legal opinion here is their request for its interpretation (ta'wil, explanation of meaning), by their saying: ﴿Inform us of its interpretation﴾ (﴿نَبِّئْنا بِتَأْوِيلِهِ﴾). The matter was expressed with the word "matter," and the request for its interpretation with the word "istifta'," in order to magnify its importance and exalt its status, since istifta' occurs in grave, problematic cases whose ruling is obscure and whose answer is unclear. His choice of the future form (ṣīghat al-istiqbal), despite their having already sought an opinion on it, is because they were on the verge of it, until (peace be upon him) would give them the answer they desired (yaqdiya ... min al-jawab wataruhu). The attribution of the decree to him, although it belongs to the states of its outcome, is because in reality it is identical with that outcome, and it had appeared in the world of images (alam al-mithal) in that form. As for His using the singular (tawhid) despite the plurality of their dreams, it comes in accordance with what He made singular in their saying: ﴿Inform us of its interpretation﴾ (﴿نَبِّئْنا بِتَأْوِيلِهِ﴾). This is not because the matter was what they were accused of and imprisoned for, namely the poisoning of the king, for they did not seek an opinion concerning that, nor concerning what is its form, but concerning what is a form of its outcome and consequence. So reflect upon this.

He (peace be upon him) informed them of this in order to confirm his interpretation and to emphasize it. It has been said: when he interpreted their dreams, they denied them and said: "We saw nothing." So he informed them that this would come to pass, whether you believed or disbelieved. Perhaps the denial came from the baker, since there is no reason for the cupbearer to deny, except that this was out of consideration for his side.

(p-280) That is, Joseph (peace be upon him) said: ﴿to the one of the two whom he thought would be saved﴾. The expression is phrased in the present tense (*mudari'*) rather than the way it could have been stated, "to the one whom he thought to be saved," for emphasis on the certainty of the deliverance. This is what the noble wording indicates, as in the Almighty's saying: ﴿The matter has been decided about which you both inquire﴾ (12:41). This is the secret behind choosing the wording of the noble text over saying "to the one he thought was saved." ﴿From the two of them﴾, meaning from his two companions. He was identified by the attribute of deliverance only to prepare for the basis of the recommendation, that he be mentioned before the king. The sense of seeking nearness (*taqarrub*) that is understood from the phrasing mentioned, although it is more inclusive of that and more conducive to fulfilling what he (Joseph) enjoined on him, is not a distinguishing attribute on which the distinction between him and his companion, who was described by the attribute of perishing, depends. The one who thought (the matter) was Joseph (peace be upon him), not his companion, because the recommendation mentioned does not depend on the supposition of the one who was saved, but on the supposition of Joseph, and it carries the meaning of certainty, as in the Almighty's saying: ﴿I was certain that I would encounter my account﴾ (69:20). So the expression "by revelation" is as indicated by the Almighty's saying ﴿The matter has been decided﴾ … etc. It has also been said that it means "by his own reasoning," and the expression "by ijtihad (independent judgment)" and the judgment that "the matter has been decided" is also a matter of ijtihad.

﴿Mention me﴾ with what I am in terms of condition and attribute, ﴿before your lord﴾, meaning your master. Describe me to him with the attribute I have that you have witnessed. ﴿But Satan caused him to forget﴾, meaning he caused the cupbearer to forget through his whispering and by placing in his heart preoccupations that hindered him from remembering. Otherwise, causing to forget is in reality from God, Mighty and Majestic. The *fa* (in ﴿fa-ansāhu﴾) indicates causation, for his (Joseph's) request, which included seeking help from other than Him, glorified be He, was the impetus for what was mentioned about the causing to forget. ﴿The remembrance of his lord﴾, meaning the cupbearer's mention of him (Joseph) before the king. The attribution (of "remembrance" to "lord") is by the slightest connection, or it means the mention of his lord's news. ﴿So he remained﴾, meaning Joseph (peace be upon him), because of that forgetting or that saying, ﴿in prison for several years﴾. *Bid'* (several) is what lies between three and nine, from *al-bad'*, which means cutting. Most of the sayings are that he remained in it seven years.

It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "May God have mercy on my brother Joseph. Had he not said, 'Mention me before your lord,' he would not have remained in prison seven years after the five." Seeking help from people, although it is permitted (*murakhkhasa*, a concession), yet what befits the stations of the prophets (peace be upon them) is to adhere to the resolute courses (*'aza'im*, the firm obligations, as opposed to concessions).

﴿And the king said﴾, that is, al-Rayyan (the king), ﴿"Indeed I see"﴾, that is, "I saw." The use of the present form serves to narrate a past state as if it were happening before the listener. ﴿"Seven fat cows"﴾, the plural of سَمِينٌ (samīn) and سَمِينَةٌ (samīnah), just as كِرامٌ (kirām) is the plural of كَرِيمٌ (karīm) and كَرِيمَةٌ (karīmah). One says رِجالٌ كِرامٌ (rijālun kirām, "noble men") and نِسْوَةٌ كِرامٌ (niswatun kirām, "noble women"). ﴿"Eating them"﴾, that is, who ate them. The shift to the present form (يَأْكُلُ) is to make the image present in the mind, expressing wonder. This clause is either a circumstantial clause (ḥāl, a clause describing the state of the subject at the time of the action) referring to the cows, or a descriptive clause (ṣifah) modifying them. ﴿"Seven lean ones"﴾, that is, seven lean cows. عِجافٌ (ʿijāf) is the plural of عَجْفاءُ (ʿajfāʾ), and by analogy it should be عُجْفٌ (ʿujf). This is because فَعَلاءُ and أفْعَلُ are not pluralized on the pattern فِعالٌ. Yet it was deviated from analogy, treating one of two opposites as though it were the other. The reason it was not said سَبْعُ عِجافٍ (sabʿu ʿijāfin) in the construct form is that the specification (tamyīz, the noun that specifies the number and clarifies the kind) is meant to explain the genus, and an adjective is not suitable for this purpose. Thus one does not say ثَلاثَةُ ضِخامٍ وأرْبَعَةُ غِلاظٍ (thalāthatu ḍikhāmin wa-arbaʿatu ghilāẓ, "three big ones and four thick ones"). As for your saying ثَلاثَةُ فُرْسانٍ وخَمْسَةُ رُكْبانٍ (thalāthatu fursānin wa-khamsatu rukbān, "three knights and five riders"), it is because فارِس (fāris, "knight") and رَاكِب (rākib, "rider") function as nouns.

It is reported that he saw seven fat cows coming out of a dry river, and after them came out seven lean cows in extreme emaciation, and the lean ones swallowed the fat ones.

﴿"And seven green ears of grain"﴾, whose grain had formed. ﴿"And others dry"﴾, that is, and seven others dry, which had ripened and twisted around the green ones until they overcame them, according to what has been reported. Perhaps the reason for not mentioning them in detail is that what was said about the condition of the cows is sufficient. ﴿"O chiefs"﴾, an address to the nobles, among the scholars and the wise. ﴿"Give me your opinion regarding my vision"﴾, this one, that is, interpret it, explain its ruling, and what outcome it leads to. The expression of "interpretation" (taʿbīr, explaining the meaning of a dream) by "giving an opinion" (iftāʾ) is to honor them and to magnify the matter of his vision.

﴿"If you are able to interpret dreams"﴾, that is, if you know the interpretation of the genus of dreams with continuous knowledge. This is the transition from the imaginary forms witnessed in sleep to what they are as symbols and examples of external or internal matters that actually occur, from العُبُورُ (ʿubūr, "crossing over"), which is passing beyond. You say عَبَرْتُ النَّهْرَ (ʿabartu al-nahr, "I crossed the river") when you cross it and pass beyond it. Similarly أوَّلْتُها (awwaltuhā, "I explained its outcome"), that is, I mentioned its final outcome. عَبَرْتُ الرُّؤْيا عِبارَةً (ʿabartu al-ruʾyā ʿibāratan) is more firmly established than عَبَّرْتُها تَعْبِيرًا (ʿabbartuhā taʿbīran). The combination of the past and the future (in تَعْبُرُونَ, which is present, and إنْ كُنْتُمْ, which is past) is to indicate continuity, as has been pointed out. The lām (لِ in لِلرُّؤْيا) is for specification, or to strengthen the delayed element for the sake of the rhyme endings (fawāṣil, the closing words of verses). Or the verb تَعْبُرُونَ is given the meaning of a transitive verb with the lām, as though it were said: "If you are appointed to interpret it." It is also permissible for لِلرُّؤْيا to be the predicate of كانَ (kāna), as one says فُلانٌ لِهَذا الأمْرِ (fulānun li-hādhā al-amr, "so-and-so is for this matter") when he is independent in it and capable of it. And تَعْبُرُونَ is another predicate.

**﴿They said﴾** is a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*) answering an implied question, as if it were said: "What did the chiefs say to the king?" The answer is: **﴿They are a jumble of dreams﴾**, meaning their confused mixtures. The word *aḍghāth* (أضغاث) is the plural of *ḍigth* (ضِغْث), which originally refers to a bundle of mixed plants tied together. It was then used metaphorically for what the imaginative faculty (*al-quwwa al-mutakhayyila*) gathers from the soul's whisperings, the suggestions of Satan, and their appearance in sleep. The word *aḥlām* is the plural of *ḥulm*, meaning false dreams that have no reality. The construction is an *idafa* in the sense of *min* ("of"): they are *aḍghāth min aḥlām*, "bundles from among dreams." They removed the dream from the category of true visions, which have a consequence that they lead to and whose matter is attended to. They used the plural, although it was a single dream, to exaggerate its falsehood, as in the saying "So-and-so rides horses and wears turbans," said of someone who owns only one horse and one turban. Alternatively, the plural reflects that the dream contained different things: the seven fat cows, the seven lean cows, the seven green ears of grain, and the other dry ones. Consider the fitness of the placement of *aḍghāth* alongside *sanābil* (ears of grain). How admirable is the discipline of the revelation!

**﴿And we are not versed in the interpretation of dreams﴾**, that is, the false visions that have no basis, **﴿knowers﴾**. This is not because they have an interpretation that they do not know. Rather, it is because they have no interpretation at all. Interpretation (*ta'wil*) applies only to true visions. It is possible that this is their acknowledgment of the shortcomings of their knowledge, and that they are not experts in interpreting dreams, even though dreams do have an interpretation. This is suggested by their avoidance of the expression used in the king's speech, which conveys merely the movement from the signifier to the signified. They did not say "the interpretation (*ta'bīr*) of dreams" or "its explanation (*'ibāra*)," but used *ta'wil*, which indicates manipulation and effort in that matter, because of the great distance between the starting point (*al-ā'il*) and the outcome (*al-ma'āl*). This is confirmed by the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: **﴿I will inform you of its interpretation﴾**.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 45:

﴿And the one of the two who had been saved said﴾, that is, from the two companions of Yusuf, and he was the cupbearer (al-Sharabi), ﴿and he remembered after a time﴾. The verb is read with an unpointed dal (ادّكر, with no dotted letter), which is the eloquent reading. It is also reported from al-Hasan with a dotted letter (ادّكر, dhal), meaning he recalled Yusuf (peace be upon him) and his affairs which he had witnessed, and his instruction regarding the interpretation of the king's dream and the difficulty of its interpretation before the chiefs. ﴿After a time﴾ means after a long period. It is also read as (immatin) with a kasra, meaning blessing, that is, after he had been granted deliverance by blessing; and (amahin), meaning forgetfulness. The clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the relative pronoun, or to its pronoun in the relative clause. It has been said that it is coordinated with (najā), but this is not correct, because the rule for each of the attribute (sifah) and the relative clause (silah) is that its attribution to the described or the relative noun should be known to the addressee as it is known to the speaker. For this reason it has been said: attributes before they are known are information, and information after it is known is attributes. You know that his remembering after a time is known only through this clause, so there is no room to place it in the same string of the relative clause together with his deliverance, which was already known beforehand.

﴿I will inform you of its interpretation﴾, that is, I will tell you by way of transmission from one who has its knowledge, not from my own opinion. For this reason he did not say, "I will give you a verdict on it." He followed this with his words: ﴿So send me forth﴾, that is, to Yusuf. He did not mention him explicitly, relying on what had preceded of the remembrance and what followed of his words.

﴿Yusuf, O truthful one (al-Siddiq)﴾. That is, he was sent to him, came to him, and said: "Yusuf," and described him with intensive truthfulness, according to what he had witnessed of him, experienced his conditions, and tested them, because he was intent on seizing his traces and drawing from his lights. So this is of the kind of brilliant opening (bara'at al-istihlal). ﴿Give us your interpretation concerning seven fat cows that seven lean ones devour, and seven green ears of grain and others dry﴾.
