That is, concerning the vision of that. He did not state it explicitly because its aim was clear, by the indication of what had preceded of their dealings and because the content of the incident pointed to it, since it could not occur in the world of witnessing. That is: explain to us its outcome and its judgment. And since he observed the high rank of his (peace be upon him) excellence, he expressed that by seeking a ruling (iftaʼ), and he did not say, as he and his companion had said at first: ﴿(Inform us of its interpretation)﴾. In his saying ﴿Give us a ruling﴾, although he alone was the one asking for the ruling, there is an indication that the vision was not his own but belonged to others who were concerned with public affairs, and that he was in this matter a interpreter and a messenger, as he signaled when he said: ﴿Perhaps I may return to the people﴾. That is: to the king and those around him, or to the people of the city if the prison was outside it, as has been said; then I will inform them of that. ﴿Perhaps they will know﴾ that and act according to its requirement, or they will know your merit and your standing together with your present condition, so that you may be freed from it. He did not give a definite answer on that out of deference to him, following the path of courtesy and guarding against rash speculation, since they did not know for certain that he would return, so he might die before it, (perhaps the fates will pass beyond what the two of you are reaching for), nor from their knowledge of that, so perhaps they did not know it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 47:

﴿Said﴾ is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) built upon a question, as if it were said: "What then did Yusuf (peace be upon him) say in the interpretation?" So it was said: He said: ﴿You will sow for seven years, consistently.﴾ It has been read with a fatha on the hamza and with a sukun on it, and both are a verbal noun (masdar) of da'aba fi al-'amal, meaning he persisted in the work and exerted himself in it. Its accusative (intisab) is in the circumstantial (hal) position from the subject of ﴿you will sow﴾, i.e., persevering, or "you will persevere with perseverance," with it being an emphatic verbal noun for a verb that is the circumstance. He (peace be upon him) interpreted the fat cows and the green ears of grain as seven years of abundance, and the lean ones and the dry ones as seven years of drought. He directed them, by means of their persistence for seven years in cultivation and their exertion in it, since through that the abundance is realized, which is the fulfilment (misdaq) of the fat cows and their interpretation. Within the course of that, he guided them to a matter beneficial for them, so he said: ﴿Whatever you harvest﴾, i.e., in every year, ﴿leave it in its ear﴾, and do not thresh it, lest the weevil eat it, as is the case with the grain of Egypt and its surroundings. Perhaps he (peace be upon him) inferred this from the green ears of grain. He commanded them to do so only because it was not customary among them, and since they were accustomed to farming he did not command them to it, but made it a matter of certain occurrence and an interpretation of the dream, a fulfilment of what was in it of the fat cows. ﴿Except a little of what you eat﴾ in those years. In this there is guidance from him (peace be upon him) to them toward reducing consumption, and the limitation to the exception of what is eaten, excluding the seed, is because that is known from his saying: ﴿(you will sow for seven years)﴾. After completing what he commanded them, he began to explain the remainder of the interpretation, from which the wisdom of the aforementioned command becomes apparent, so he said:

(p-283) ﴿ثُمَّ يَأْتِي﴾ ("Then there will come") is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to (تَزْرَعُونَ) ("you will sow"). There is no reason to read it as an imperative, urging them to exert themselves and go to great lengths in sowing, since the meaning is also attained by informing them of this. ﴿مِن بَعْدِ ذَلِكَ﴾ ("after that") means after the seven years mentioned. The speaker did not say (مِن بَعْدِهِنَّ) ("after them," in the feminine plural) but chose to point to their description, since the pronoun is entirely silent about the attributes of its referent. ﴿سَبْعٌ شِدادٌ﴾ ("seven hard [years]") means seven years difficult for the people. ﴿يَأْكُلْنَ ما قَدَّمْتُمْ لَهُنَّ﴾ ("they will eat what you have stored up for them") refers to the grains left in their ears of grain. This implies that his (peace be upon him) command to do this was for a time of necessity. The attribution of eating to the years, although it is in fact the people who eat during them, is metaphorical (majāz), as in the expression (نَهارُهُ صائِمٌ) ("his day is fasting"). It also hints that this is an interpretation (taʾwīl) of the eating of the lean cows by the fat ones. The preposition in (لَهُنَّ) ("for them") is a supporting reinforcement (tarshīḥ) of this, as if what was saved in the ears of grain were something prepared and presented to them, as is presented to a guest. Otherwise, in reality, it is presented to the people during them. ﴿إلا قَلِيلا مِمّا تُحْصِنُونَ﴾ ("except a little of what you store away") means what you keep safe (تُحْرِزُونَ) of the seed grain intended for sowing.

Then after that there will come a year (ʿām) in which people will be granted relief, and in which they will press (juice) out of the fruit. Here is the passage in full, with the Qur'anic quotation rendered as its meaning:

Then there will come after that (i.e., after the years described above with the hardship and the consumption of the stored grain) a year (ʿām) in which people will be given rain (ghayth), and in which they will press. The word for year was not expressed as sanah, to avoid its original connotation of a year of drought, and as an early indication from the outset of the difference in condition between it and the years that preceded it. "People will be given rain" (yughathu al-nās) is from ghayth, meaning they will be rained upon, as it is said: the lands were given rain (ghīthat al-bilād) when they were rained upon at a time of need; or it is from ghawth (relief), as it is said: God gave us relief (aghāthanā Allāh), that is, He supported us by removing hardships when they overshadowed us. "And in it they will press" (wa-fīhi yaʿṣirūn) means: whatever is pressed from grapes, sugarcane, olives, sesame and similar fruits, because of their abundance. The mention of pressing, though it could have been dispensed with by mentioning rain, which normally entails it (just as the handling of grains was dispensed with), is either because rain's entailing pressing is not like its entailing grain, since harvested crops depend on other causes besides rain for their goodness, or in consideration of the one asking the question, taking account of his particular circumstance as glad tidings to him. This is what the excellence of his being given precedence over the people in the reading with the second-person (tāʾ) form depends upon.

It is said: the meaning of yaʿṣirūn is that they milk the udders. The repetition of fī-hi is either to indicate the difference in the times of what occurs in it of rain and pressing in time, which is evident, and in heading, since rain and relief are from God's bounty, while pressing is from people's action; or because the context is one of enumerating the benefits of that year, and for this reason both benefits were placed before the verbs in both places, since the principal purpose is to explain that this benefit and that benefit will occur in that year, not to state that these two occur in that year, as the delay would indicate. It is also possible that the fronting is for restriction (qaṣr), meaning that their rain and their pressing in all the other years are as nothing compared to that year of theirs; and that the latter is for the sake of the rhyme (fawāṣil), while the former is for the sake of his condition. It was also read as (yuʿṣarūn), in the passive, from aʿṣarahu, if he delivered him (anjāhu), which suits the notion of relief. It is also possible that the active form is from it likewise, as if it were said: in it people are given relief and in it they bring relief, that is, God gives them relief and they give relief to one another. It is also said: the meaning of (yuʿṣarūn) is that they are rained upon, from aʿṣarat al-saḥāba (the cloud rained), either by implying that aʿṣarat carries the meaning of maṭarat and transitivizing it, or by deleting the preposition and making the verb reach its object, the original being aʿṣarat ʿalayhim.

The rulings of this blessed year are not derived from the king's dream; rather, he (peace be upon him) received them through revelation, and so he gave them the good news of them after interpreting the dream as he interpreted it, and commanded them with the fitting management in such matters, to make clear the loftiness of his station and the firmness of his foot in excellence, and that he encompasses what has not occurred to anyone's mind, let alone what its form is seen in a dream, in the manner of his saying to his two companions when they inquired of him about their dreams: (No food will come to you that you are provided with except that I will inform you of its interpretation). And it completes the blessing upon them, since none shared with him, peace be upon him, in knowledge of its occurrence, not even through seeing in a dream what indicates it.

And the king said, after the envoy had come to him with the interpretation and he had heard from him what he had heard about the smallest details (*naqir* and *qitmir*): ﴿Bring him to me.﴾ This was because of what he knew of his knowledge and excellence. ﴿So when the messenger came to him﴾, that is, Joseph, and invited him to the king, ﴿he said: Return to your lord﴾, that is, your master, ﴿and ask him what was the matter with the women who cut their hands﴾, that is, investigate their affair for me. He did not say "ask him to investigate that," but rather urged the king to strive earnestly in the inquiry so that his innocence would become clear and his purity would be manifest, since a question stirs a person to take up investigation in earnest in order to uncover what is directed at him, whereas a mere request is something that may be overlooked, tolerated, and not taken seriously. He did not mention the wife of the Governor, despite what he had suffered from her of the bearing of griefs and the endurance of sorrows and anxieties, out of observance of the obligations of rights and as a precaution against her plotting, since he believed her to be still standing on the edge of enmity. As for the women, he hoped to bring about their speaking the truth and their testimony, through her own confession that she had solicited him against his self and that he had refused. For this reason he confined himself to describing them by the cutting of hands and did not explicitly mention their soliciting him or their saying: "Obey your mistress." He contented himself with alluding to that by his saying: ﴿Indeed my Lord is Knower of their plot﴾, out of courtesy toward them and as a precaution against the evil of their speech before the king and their standing up to dispute in defense of themselves, should they hear of his attributing corruption to them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 51:

﴿He said﴾ is a resumptive clause (istinaf, a clause that begins a new sentence) built upon a implied question, as if it were said: "What happened after that?" So it is said: The king said, after the messenger had conveyed the report to him and had brought them (the women) before him: ﴿What was your affair?﴾ That is, what was your matter, which is the kind of matter whose gravity makes it right for one person to address another about it. ﴿When you solicited Joseph﴾ and deceived him ﴿concerning himself﴾ and enticed him to obey his mistress. Did you find in him anything of evil or suspicion? ﴿They said: Far is God from imperfection﴾, exalting Him and marvelling at his purity and chastity. ﴿We know no evil in him.﴾ They strongly negated the category of evil from him by using the indefinite form and by adding min (the particle used to strengthen negation).

﴿The wife of the chief minister said﴾, and she had been present in the assembly. It is also said that the women turned to her to question her, and it is also said that she feared they would testify against her by what she had said to them: ﴿And indeed I solicited him concerning himself, but he refrained. And if he does not do what I command him, he will certainly be imprisoned and will be among the humbled.﴾ So she confessed, saying: ﴿Now the truth has become manifest﴾. That is, it became established and settled, or it became clear and apparent after being hidden, as al-Khalil said. It is also said that it is derived from ḥiṣṣah, which is a portion of a whole, meaning that the portion of truth became distinguished from the portion of falsehood, just as the shares of land and other things are distinguished. It is also said: it became clear and appeared, from "ḥaṣṣa sha'rahu" when he shaved it off so that the skin of his scalp appeared. It was also read in the passive form, from "ḥaṣḥaṣa al-ba'ir mabarakahu," meaning that the camel set its chest down on the ground to kneel. The poet said:

"So it settled, on the hard rocks, its chest-bone and knees, and it sank down with Salma's burden, then it became still."

The meaning is: the truth was confirmed in its place and set in its proper position. By this she did not mean merely the appearance, through their testimony, of the absolute purity of him (peace be upon him) in what their knowledge encompassed, without touching upon his purity in all other circumstances, especially in what the dispute had concerned in the presence of the chief minister. Nor did she mean an inquiry into her own condition and what she had done in this matter. Rather, she meant the manifestation of what is actually established in reality and the affirmation of his purity (peace be upon him) in the place of dispute, and of her treachery. So she said: ﴿It was I who solicited him concerning himself﴾, not that he solicited me concerning myself, ﴿and indeed he is among the truthful﴾. That is, in his saying when I falsely accused him: ﴿"It was she who solicited me concerning myself"﴾. By ﴿Now﴾ she meant the time of her speaking this speech, not the time of their testimony. So reflect, O fair-minded reader, whether you see any purity above this rank, since the adversaries could not restrain themselves from testifying to it, and excellence lies in what the adversaries testify to. He (peace be upon him) only undertook to lay the groundwork for this premise before going out, so as to manifest the innocence of his reputation from what had been charged against him, especially before the chief minister before he resolved what the latter had tied, as his saying (peace be upon him) indicates when the messenger returned to him and informed him of their words:

(p-285)

﴿That﴾, i.e., that verification which leads to the manifestation of the reality of the matter, ﴿so that he [the Chieftain] may know﴾, i.e., the Chieftain, ﴿that I did not betray him﴾ in his household, as he had alleged. This is not knowledge in an absolute sense, for that does not require giving priority to the investigation over his release from prison. Rather, it [the investigation] came before the undoing of what he had firmly decided. Perhaps this was out of regard for the rights of the lordship (al-siyada), because proceeding to take him out of his confinement before the falsity of what had caused it became evident, even if that was by the king's command, would give the impression of acting presumptuously (al-iftiyat) against his judgment. As for it being so that he could not be given the chance to disparage his affair before the king, in a contrived manner, in order to carry out what he had decided, that is not fitting for his standing, peace be upon him, in trusting in his affair and relying upon his Lord, exalted is His majesty.

﴿in secret﴾, i.e., in the absence of the sight of others (bi-zahr al-ghayb). It is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the doer or from the object: I did not betray him while I was absent from him, or while he was absent from him, or while he was absent from me. Or it is an adverbial of place (zarf), i.e., in a place of absence, behind curtains and locked doors. Whichever of these it is, the intended meaning is to show the completeness of his innocence from betrayal and the utmost of his avoidance of it when the causes of it come together. ﴿And that God﴾, i.e., and so that He, exalted is He, ﴿does not guide the plot of the betrayers﴾, i.e., He does not let it take effect or make it succeed, but rather nullifies it and causes it to vanish. Or it means He does not guide them in their plot, the verb being applied to the plot for the sake of emphasis, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They imitate the saying of those who disbelieved﴾, i.e., they imitate them in their saying. In this there is an allusion to his wife in her betrayal of his trust, and to himself in his betrayal of God's trust when he helped her to imprison him after they had seen the signs of his innocence, peace be upon him. It is also possible that this is for the confirmation of his trustworthiness, and that if he had been a betrayer, God, mighty and majestic, would not have guided his affair and made his end good.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 53:

﴿And I do not absolve myself﴾ meaning: I do not declare myself free of evil. He, peace be upon him, said this out of humbling himself (hadm) before his noble soul, which is innocent of every evil, and out of elevating its station above self-praise (tazkiyah) and self-admiration (i'jab) at the manifestation of the perfection of its purity, in the manner of his, peace be upon him, saying: "I am the master of the descendants of Adam, and I say so without boasting" (wa la fakhr), or as a recounting of the blessing of God, Mighty and Majestic, upon him, and a disclosure of His hidden secret regarding the actions of His servants. That is: I do not declare my soul free of evil in and of itself, nor do I attribute this virtue to it by its own nature without the grace (tawfiq) of God, Mighty and Exalted.

﴿Indeed, the soul﴾ the human soul, of which my soul is a part, in and of itself, ﴿is certainly one that commands to evil﴾, inclined toward desires (ash-shahawat) (p-286), employing the faculties and instruments in attaining them. Rather, that is only by the grace (tawfiq) of God Most High, His protection (i'smah), and His mercy, as His saying indicates: ﴿except those upon whom my Lord has mercy﴾, from among the souls whom He protects from falling into ruin, and of whom my soul is one. Or, it is one that commands to evil at every time except the time of my Lord's mercy and His protection of it. It has been said: the exception is disjunctive (munqati'), meaning: rather, the mercy of my Lord is what turns evil away from it, as in His saying, Exalted: "and they cannot save me, * except by mercy" (50). ﴿Indeed my Lord is Forgiving, Merciful﴾, of great forgiveness toward what befalls souls by virtue of their natures, and abundant in mercy toward them by protecting them from being driven by that requirement. The use of the apparent noun in place of the pronoun, together with the mention of the title of Lordship (rububiyyah), is to cultivate the principles of forgiveness and mercy.

It has been said: up to this point is the speech of the wife of the Minister (imra'at al-Aziz), and the meaning is: that which I said was so that Joseph, peace be upon him, would know that I did not betray him, and did not lie about him in his absence, and brought what is the true reality; and I do not absolve myself, even so, of treachery, since I said about him what I said and did to him what I did. Indeed every soul is certainly one that commands to evil, except those upon whom my Lord has mercy, that is, except a soul which God has shown mercy by protecting it, like the soul of Joseph. Indeed my Lord is Forgiving to whoever seeks forgiveness for his sin and acknowledges it, Merciful to him. Accordingly, his, peace be upon him, deliberateness in leaving the prison, due to his, peace be upon him, lack of contentment with meeting the king and his order to be sent for in an intermediate manner, is explained: he did what he did so that his innocence would become clear, and that he had been imprisoned through great injustice, together with his excellence and eminence of standing; so that the king would receive him with what befits him of honor and reverence, and this indeed occurred.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 54:

﴿And the king said, "Bring him to me; I will take him for myself."﴾ (I will make him pure, i.e., exclusively) ﴿for myself.﴾ (And special to me.) ﴿So when he spoke with him﴾, that is: then they brought him. The verb is omitted to indicate the swiftness of bringing him, as though there was no time at all between the command to bring him and the conversation with him. The hidden pronoun in (kallamahu, "he spoke with him") refers to Yusuf, and the explicit pronoun refers to the king. That is: when Yusuf spoke with him, following his coming to him, and he questioned him and witnessed from him what he witnessed. ﴿He said, "Indeed you are today with us established, trusted."﴾ Possessing high rank and standing, ﴿trusted﴾ entrusted with everything. The word (al-yawm, "today") is not a measure of the duration of rank and trustworthiness; rather, it is the moment of speaking. The intent is to specify their beginning, to guard against the possibility that they would come after some time.

It is narrated that when the messenger came to him, peace be upon him, he left the prison, prayed for his family, bathed, and wore new clothes. When he entered upon the king, he said: "O Allah, I ask You for Your good from its good, and I seek refuge in Your might and Your power from its evil and the evil of others." Then he greeted him with peace and supplicated for him in Hebrew. He said: "What is this tongue?" He said: "The tongue of my forefathers." The king knew seventy languages, so he spoke to him in them, and he answered him in all of them, and the king marvelled at him. He said: "I love to hear my dream from you." So he related it and described for him the cows and the ears of grain and their places as he had seen them. So he seated him upon the throne and entrusted his affair to him.

It was also said: Qitfir died during those nights, so he appointed him to his position and married him to Ra'il, and he found her a virgin, and she bore him Ifrayim and Misha. Perhaps that was only after his appointment, peace be upon him, to what was assigned to him concerning the affairs of the treasuries, as his saying, Mighty and Majestic is He, indicates:

He said, "Appoint me over the storehouses of the land," meaning the land of Egypt, that is, give me charge of its affairs of revenue and expenditure. ﴿Indeed I am a guardian﴾ of it against one who does not deserve it, ﴿knowing﴾ the ways of managing it.

In this is evidence for the permissibility of seeking authority (wilayah) when the seeker is able to establish justice and implement the rulings of the Shari'ah, even if the authority is from the hand of an oppressor or a disbeliever.

It is reported from Mujahid that the king embraced Islam at his hand (peace be upon him). Perhaps his (peace be upon him) preference for that particular authority was only for undertaking what was most important among the matters of sovereignty at that time, namely the management of the affairs of the years, as detailed in the ta'wil (interpretation), since it is among the branches of that authority, for the sake of the generality of benefit and the comprehensiveness of its return, as it is said. He did not mention the king's acceptance of what he (peace be upon him) asked, namely being placed over the storehouses of the land, as an indication that this is a matter that cannot be refused and needs no explicit statement, especially after mentioning before it all that falls under it of the rulings of sovereignty, in His saying: ﴿Indeed you today are with us established, trustworthy﴾. It also alerts that all of that is from Allah, mighty and majestic, and that the king is merely an instrument in it. It is said:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 56:

﴿And thus﴾, i.e., like that thorough establishment, ﴿We established Joseph﴾, i.e., We made for him a place ﴿in the land﴾, i.e., the land of Egypt.

It is related that it was forty farsakh by forty. In expressing the aforementioned granting as "establishment in the land," attributed to His own Essence—exalted is His authority—there is an honouring of him, peace be upon him, an emphasis on the perfection of his authority, and an indication that this came about from the very beginning and not after the request, which is not hidden.

﴿He settles therein﴾, i.e., he descends from its lands ﴿wherever he wills﴾, and takes it as a dwelling place. This is an expression for the perfection of his capacity to dispose of it and its coming under his dominion and authority, so that it is as if it were his home, which he disposes of as a man disposes of his own home. Ibn Kathir read it with the nun (﴿natabawwa'u﴾).

It is related that the king crowned him, sealed him with his ring, girded him with his sword, and placed for him a throne of gold adorned with pearls and rubies. Then he, peace be upon him, said: "As for the throne, I will strengthen your kingdom with it; as for the ring, I will manage your affairs with it; as for the crown, it is not from my garment nor the garment of my fathers." The king said: "I have placed it out of honour for you and in acknowledgement of your virtue." So he sat upon the throne, the kings submitted to him, the king delegated his affairs to him, he established justice in Egypt, and men and women loved him. In the years of famine he sold food to the people of Egypt: in the first year for dinars and dirhams, in the second for jewellery and gems, in the third for livestock, then for estates and property, then for their persons, until he enslaved them all. They said: "We have never seen a king more majestic and greater than him today." Then he freed them and returned their property to them. He would not sell to any one of the buyers more than a camel's load, distributing it fairly among the people.

﴿We bestow Our mercy﴾, i.e., Our gift in this world of kingship, wealth and other blessings ﴿upon whom We will﴾, in accordance with the wisdom that calls for the will ﴿and We do not waste the reward of the good-doers﴾, but We pay it in full. In this there is an indication that the basis of the aforementioned will is the good-doing of the one upon whom the aforementioned mercy falls, and that it is a reward for him. And to remove the supposition that the fruits of good-doing are restricted to the immediate reward mentioned, it was said by way of emphasis:

And the reward of the Hereafter [is] better, meaning: their reward in the Hereafter. The idafa (construction of possession/association) here is for mulabasa (connection/association), and it is the lasting bliss that has no end. [It is] "better" for them, i.e., for the muhsinin (those who do good) mentioned. The relative clause was placed in its position, so it says: "those who believed and were God-fearing," as an alert that what is meant by ihsan (excellence/doing good) is in fact faith and steadfastness in taqwa (God-consciousness), which is derived from combining the two verb forms, the past and the future.

﴿And the brothers of Joseph came﴾ seeking provisions, when the famine that had struck the land of Canaan and the lands of Syria had struck the land of Egypt as well. Ya'qub, peace be upon him, had sent them all except Benjamin. ﴿So they entered upon him﴾, that is, upon Joseph, who was in his seat of rule. ﴿And he recognized them﴾ because of the strength of his understanding, and because their earlier circumstances did not differ from their condition at that time, since he had parted from them when they were men, and their forms and appearance were similar in both states. He was also preoccupied with them and with knowing their circumstances, especially in a time of famine. It is related from al-Hasan: "He did not recognize them until they made themselves known to him."

﴿But they did not recognize him﴾, that is, while they were not recognizing him, owing to the long interval and the difference between his two states, peace be upon him, in his person, his rank and his dress, and because they believed that he had died. Since their failure to recognize him was a continuing matter both in his presence and in his absence, it was expressed by the nominal sentence (al-jumla al-ismiyya), in contrast to his recognition of them, peace be upon him.

﴿And when he had furnished them with their provisions﴾, i.e., he equipped them with their supplies of food and what the traveller needs, and he loaded their camels with the grain they had come for. It is also read with a kasrah on the jim (*jihāzihim*). ﴿He said: "Bring me a brother of yours from your father"﴾. He did not say "from your brother," in order to emphasise that he did not recognise them. Perhaps he (peace be upon him) only said this because it was reported that they asked him for an extra load beyond the usual for Binyamin, and he gave them that and stipulated that they bring him. It was not because of what is reported, that when they saw him and spoke to him in *'Ibriyyah* (Hebrew), he said to them, "Who are you? For I do not recognise you!" They said to him, "We are a people from the people of al-Sham, herdsmen. Hardship has befallen us, so we have come to seek provisions." He said to them, "Perhaps you have come as spies?" They said, "God forbid! We are brothers, sons of one father, and he is an elderly, truthful prophet from among the prophets, whose name is Ya'qub." He said, "How many are you?" They said, "We were twelve, and one of us perished." He said, "How many are you?" They said, "Ten." He said, "Where is the eleventh?" They said, "He is with his father, who consoles himself with him for the one who perished." He said, "Who will testify for you that you are not spies and that what you say is true?" They said, "We are in lands where no one knows us, so no one will testify for us." He said, "Then leave one of you with me as a pledge, and bring me your brother from your father, who carries a message from your father, until I believe you." So they cast lots, and the lot fell upon Shim'un, so they left him with him. This is because the command to bring him at the time of the provisioning does not support it, nor does the urging to give full measure, nor the kindness in lodging them, nor restricting the grain to a prohibition on measure on the assumption that they intended to bring him, nor placing their merchandise in their saddlebags so that they would return, nor their promise to bring him by way of enticement, nor their giving their father the reason for sending their brother as the withholding of grain without mention of the message. Moreover, if Shim'un's detention had occurred, it would have been a calamity (*ṭāmmah*) in which every saying and every speaker would be forgotten.

﴿Do you not see that I give full measure﴾, I complete it for you. The choice of the present-tense form, although this speech came after the provisioning, indicates that this is a continuous habit of his. ﴿and I am the best of hosts﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*jumlah ḥāliyyah*), i.e., "Do you not see that I give you full measure continuously, while I am in the utmost kindness in lodging you and entertaining you?" And this was indeed the case. The sight is restricted to the giving of full measure because the address occurred in the midst of it. As for kindness in lodging, it was continuous before and after, and for this reason it is expressed by a nominal sentence (*jumlah ismiyyah*). He (peace be upon him) did not say it as a boast, but to urge them to fulfil what he had commanded them. The restriction in the matter of measure to mention of giving full measure is because his (peace be upon him) treatment of them in this respect is like his treatment of others in observing the requirements of justice. As for hospitality, people have no right to it, so he singled them out in that with what he willed.

(p-289) ﴿But if you do not bring him to me, then there will be no measure (of grain) for you with me﴾ from now on, let alone its full measure, ﴿and do not approach me﴾ by entering my land, let alone (receiving) kindness in lodging and hospitality. This is either a prohibition or a negation, conjoined to the place of the conditional clause (in its grammatical position). It indicates that they intended to obtain provisions (al-imtiyar) time and again, and that this was known to him, peace be upon him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 61:

﴿They said: "We will try to seduce him away from his father"﴾ That is: we will deceive him concerning him, and we will devise a stratagem to wrest him from his hand, and we will exert ourselves in that. In this there is an indication of the high value of the request and the difficulty of attaining it. ﴿And indeed, we will surely do it﴾ that, without being negligent in it or lax, or: we are indeed capable of it, and we will not exert ourselves in vain over it.

﴿And he said﴾ Yusuf ﴿to his young men﴾, meaning his servants who measured out the grain. The word is the plural of فَتًى (fatan, "young man"), i.e. ﴿فِتْيانِهِ﴾ (fityānihi). It was also read as ﴿لِفِتْيَتِهِ﴾ (li-fityatihi), which is the plural of paucity (jam' qilla, a plural form used for small numbers) of the same word. ﴿Put their merchandise back in their saddlebags﴾. He appointed a man for each saddlebag to put back their merchandise with which they had bought the food. It consisted of sandals and leather. He did this, peace be upon him, out of generosity towards them and out of fear that his father might not have anything for them to return with a second time. All of this served to secure what he hoped for, namely their return with their brother, as his words indicate: ﴿so that they may recognise it﴾, that is, so that they may recognise the right of returning it and the nobility involved in that. Or it means: ﴿so that they may recognise it﴾, and this is the more evident connection with his words ﴿when they return to their family﴾, since their recognition of it is necessarily conditioned upon returning and emptying the sacks. As for recognising the right of nobility in returning it, although in itself it is not conditioned by that, nevertheless, since its beginning was at that time, it was conditioned by it.

﴿so that they may return﴾ as I have instructed them, for conferring favour upon them by giving the two exchanges, especially when the merchandise is scarce, is among the strongest motives for returning. As for what has been said, that he, peace be upon him, did this because he saw it as ungenerous to take a price from his father and brothers, that statement is true in itself, but the stated reason rejects it. As for the claim that the cause of placing the merchandise for their return was that their religion compelled them to return it, because they did not consider it lawful to keep it, its basis is their supposing that it had remained in their saddlebags through forgetfulness. It is evident that this would never occur to anyone at all, since the manner of placing it indicates that it was done as a favour. Do you not see how they were certain of this when they saw it, and took it as evidence of the earlier favours, as you will learn in detail?

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 63:

﴿When they returned to their father, they said﴾ before they busied themselves with unpacking their goods, ﴿O our father, the measure has been withheld from us﴾, i.e., in future. In this there is an evident indication that it was customary between them and him (peace be upon him) that they obtain grain repeatedly, time after time. ﴿So send with us our brother﴾, Binyamin, to Egypt. In this there is a notification that the basis of the refusal was his not being with them, ﴿that we may measure﴾ by means of him from the food what we wish. Hamzah (p-290) and al-Kisa'i read it with the yā' (yaktal, "he will measure"), attributing it to the brother because he was the cause of the measuring; or it means that he will measure for himself along with our measuring. ﴿And indeed, we will surely be its guardians﴾, from any harm befalling him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 64:

﴿He said: "Shall I entrust him to you except as I entrusted his brother to you before?"﴾ Yusuf ﴿before﴾, and you had said concerning him too what you said, then you did to him what you did. So I do not trust you, nor your guarding. I entrust the matter only to Allah. ﴿But Allah is the best guardian﴾. It is also read as (hifzan), and their being in the accusative is as a specification (tamyiz) and as a circumstantial qualifier (hal). According to the first reading, it would give the impression that the superiority of being the best guardian is restricted to that state. ﴿And He is the Most Merciful of the merciful﴾. So I hope that He will show mercy to me by guarding him, and not combine two calamities upon me. This, as you see, is an inclination from him, peace be upon him, toward permitting and sending (the son) for what he saw in it of benefit.

And when they opened their belongings, they found that their merchandise had been returned to them. That is, out of His bounty. They had known this from the indication of the situation that had already passed. It is also read with the vowel of the assimilated dal transferred to the ra', as is said of *qīla* and *kīla* (قِيلَ وكِيلَ).

"And they said" is a resumptive clause (*istīnāf*, a new sentence that answers an implied question), as if it were asked: "What did they say then?" It was said: they said to their father, and perhaps he was present at the opening: ﴿O our father, what more could we seek?﴾ If *al-baghy* is interpreted as seeking (*ṭalab*), then *mā* is either an interrogative governing it, so the meaning is: "What more do we seek beyond what we have described to you of the king's kindness toward us and his generosity, which calls us to obey his command and to return to him with our needs?" They had already informed him of this, saying to him: "We came to the best of men, who lodged us and honored us with a honor such that, if a man from the family of Ya'qub had been in our place, he would not have been honored as we were honored."

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿This is our merchandise, returned to us﴾, it is a new sentence (*jumla mustanafa'a*) clarifying what the denial implies, namely that the kindness has reached its utmost limit. It is as if they said: "How could it not be so, when this is our merchandise, which he has returned to us as a bounty from a source we did not know of, after he has bestowed upon us great favors? Is there anything more than this that we could seek?" They did not mean by this to be content with it absolutely, nor to refrain from seeking its like. Rather, they meant to be content with it as a reason for obeying his command and for turning to him in seeking more, as we have pointed out.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿(returned to us)﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) relating to ﴿(our merchandise)﴾, and its governing element is the sense of the demonstrative. The choice of the passive form is to indicate the completeness of the kindness, which arises from the completeness of the concealment implied by the completeness of their unawareness of it, to the extent that they did not perceive it nor its doer.

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿and we will bring provisions for our family﴾, that is, we will bring them food from the king's presence. It is coordinated (*ma'ṭūf*) upon an implied element to which the return of the merchandise extends, that is: "So we will rely on it and bring provisions for our family, ﴿and protect our brother﴾ from harm, as we have promised, so whatever harm may befall him [will be averted], ﴿and gain an additional﴾, that is, through him. For this reason the report of his protection was placed between the basic provision and the additional one. ﴿A camel's load﴾, that is, a camel's load in addition to the loads of our camels, according to the principle of equal division. ﴿That﴾, that is, what our camels carry, ﴿is a small measure﴾, that is, a small quantity that does not burden us. So this is a new sentence that came as a justification for what preceded, as if it were said: "What need is there for the additional amount?" So it was said what was said. Or: that additional measure is a small thing, which the king will not begrudge us, or an easy matter for him that he does not regard as great, or whatever object we seek from our affairs. The clause that follows it (p-291) is an explanation and clarification of what the denial implies, namely that they were successful in obtaining some of their requests, or were able to achieve them. It is as if they said: "Our merchandise is present, so we rely upon it, and we bring provisions for our family, and we protect our brother, so that no harm befalls him, and we gain through him an additional camel's load beyond what we measure for ourselves. What then could we seek beyond these desired things?"

It is also read as *mā tabghī* (what do you seek?), addressed to Ya'qub, peace be upon him, meaning: "What do you seek beyond these favorable outcomes, which include the safety of our brother and the abundance of our means, or beyond what the king has done for us of kindness that calls us to turn to him?" The resumptive clause clarifies this. Or: "What do you seek as a witness to the truth of what we have described to you of his kindness?" The clause mentioned is an expression of the witness indicated by the implication of the denial. If *mā* is negative, then the meaning is: "We do not seek anything other than what we have seen of the king's kindness, which makes it obligatory to return to him," or "We do not seek other than these favorable outcomes." It has also been said: "We do not ask you for any other merchandise," and the resumptive clause is a justification for it.

If, however, *al-baghy* is interpreted as exceeding the limit, then *mā* is only negative, and the meaning is: "We do not exceed in speech, nor do we add to what we have described to you of the king's kindness toward us and his generosity, which requires what has been mentioned." The resumptive clause explains what they claimed regarding the absence of transgression. His saying: ﴿and we will bring provisions for our family﴾ is coordinated upon ﴿(what we seek)﴾, that is: "We do not exceed in what we have mentioned of his kindness, and in obtaining its like: bringing provisions for our family and protecting our brother. For that is the least of things through his kindness." It has also been permitted that it be an independent utterance, that is, a parenthetical concluding clause (*jumla i'tirāḍiyya tadhyīliyya*, a parenthetical clause that sums up the sense) with the meaning: "And it is fitting that we bring provisions for our family." This is likened to your saying: "I have striven for the need of so-and-so, and it is incumbent upon me to strive." You know that the nature of concluding parenthetical clauses is to confirm and establish the content of the preceding statement, as in the example given, and your saying: "So-and-so speaks the truth, so the truth is clear." However, his saying "and we bring provisions…", etc., even if we are assisted in interpreting it as meaning "it is fitting that we bring provisions for our family," is far from that. Or the meaning is: "We do not go astray in judgment, nor do we deviate from the right course in what we advise you concerning sending our brother with us." The clauses to the end are an elaboration and explanation of their not transgressing and of their soundness of judgment. That is: "Our merchandise is present, so we rely upon it, and we bring provisions for our family, and we act thus and so. So consider this carefully."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 66:

﴿He said: "I will never send him with you"﴾ after I have witnessed from you what I have witnessed, ﴿until you give me a solemn pledge in the name of Allah﴾. That is, a pledge by which I may bind myself with respect to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. He called it a pledge "from Him, exalted" because confirming covenants by Him is permitted by Him, so it is a permission from Him, Mighty and Majestic. ﴿that you will surely bring him back to me﴾ is the answer to the oath, since the meaning is: "until you swear by Allah that you will surely bring him back to me." ﴿unless you are encircled﴾ means: unless you are overpowered and are unable to do so, or unless you are destroyed. Its origin is the encirclement of an enemy, for whoever is encircled by an enemy is generally destroyed. This is an exception from the most general of circumstances, or from the most general of causes, according to the interpretation of the sentence by the negation toward which it leads. That is: "You will surely bring him back to me and you will not refrain from bringing him in any circumstance, or for any cause, except in the circumstance of being encircled by you," or "for the cause of being encircled by you." A parallel to this is their saying: "I have sworn upon you that you do such-and-such, unless you do so-and-so," meaning: "I want from you nothing but your doing it."

The first reading is also permitted without any interpretation, that is: "You will surely bring him back to me in every circumstance except the circumstance of being encircled by you." You know that, since bringing him back is not among the continuous actions that encompass all circumstances in the sense of accompaniment, as in your saying, "I will certainly stay with you unless you give me my right," and since his peace be upon him did not intend that it be accompanied in the sense of alternation for all circumstances other than the excepted one, as when you say, "Pray unless you are in a state of impurity," but rather merely that its realization and occurrence be without any hindrance to it, as in your saying, "I will certainly perform Hajj this year unless I am prevented," for your intention is only to inform that nothing other than the circumstance of being prevented will stop you from Hajj, not to inform of its accompaniment with those circumstances in the sense of alternation, as is your intention in the example of prayer. It is as if the consideration of the circumstances with it is in terms of their not preventing it, and so the meaning returns to the aforementioned interpretation.

﴿So when they had given him their pledge﴾, that is, their covenant from Allah, as Ya'qub, peace be upon him, had desired, ﴿he said: "Allah is Witness over what we say"﴾, that is, over what we said during the request for the pledge and its giving from both sides. The use of the present-tense form is to bring its image to mind, which leads them to firmness and to guarding and watching over its remembrance. ﴿Trustee﴾ means a watchful, vigilant Overseer. By this he intends to display his trust in Allah, Exalted, and to urge them to observe their covenant.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 67:

﴿And he said﴾, offering them counsel when he had resolved to send them all off together: ﴿"O my sons, do not enter﴾ Egypt ﴿by one gate, but enter by different gates."﴾ He forbade them this out of caution against the striking of the evil eye (al-'ayn). They were people of beauty and fine bearing, and on this occasion they had dressed more finely than on the first, and in Egypt they had become known for honour and closeness to the king, unlike their first visit. Thus they were a cause for every onlooker to gaze at them and for every aspirant to covet them. The striking of the evil eye by the decree of the Mighty, the Wise, is not something to be denied. It has been related from him (ﷺ): "The evil eye is real." And from him (ﷺ): "The evil eye can bring a man into the grave and a camel into the cooking pot." And he (ﷺ) used to seek refuge for al-Hasan and al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with them both, by saying: "I seek refuge in the perfect words of Allah from every devil and venomous creature, and from every envious eye." He (ﷺ) also said: "Your father used to seek refuge with them for Isma'il and Ishaq, peace be upon them." Al-Bukhari related it in his Sahih. Experience also bears witness to this. Since not entering by one gate did not necessitate entering by separate gates, and since entering by two or three gates still contained some of the gathering that entering by a single gate involves, which would facilitate the occurrence of what is feared, he said: ﴿"But enter by different gates."﴾ This was an explanation of what the prohibition actually intended. He did not suffice with this command, though it entailed the prohibition, in order to show complete concern and to make clear that this is what was meant by the command mentioned, not to establish something else.

﴿"Yet I cannot avail you anything against Allah."﴾ That is: I cannot benefit you, nor can I ward off by my planning ﴿anything﴾ of what Allah has decreed for you, for caution does not prevent divine decree (al-qadar). He, peace be upon him, did not intend by this the complete abandonment of caution. How could he, when the Mighty One has said: ﴿"And do not cast yourselves into destruction with your own hands"﴾ and said: ﴿"Take your precaution"﴾? Rather, he intended to show that what he had enjoined upon them is not something that necessarily secures the intended outcome; it is a measure taken in general, and the actual effect and the realisation of benefit from it come from the Mighty, the Powerful. This is not a repelling of decree, but rather seeking help from Allah the Exalted and fleeing to Him. ﴿"Judgement belongs to none but Allah"﴾ absolutely, having no partner, and nothing can prevent Him. ﴿"In Him I have placed my trust"﴾ in all that I do and forgo, and in this is an indication that the arrangement of means does not impair reliance (tawakkul). ﴿"And in Him alone"﴾, not in anyone else, ﴿"let those who rely upon Him rely."﴾ He combined the two particles in conjoining one sentence to another, with the prior mention of the complement for restriction, bound by the conjunction (wa). He coupled the act of others, namely the restriction of reliance to Allah the Exalted, with his own act, and by attributing the causal role of his action to his being a prophet, to the act of others who follow him. Thus his sons enter among them as a primary entry. In this is what is not hidden of the goodness of their guidance and of directing them to place their reliance upon Allah the Exalted in what they were about to face, not being deceived (p-293) by the precaution he had enjoined upon them.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 12, verse 68:**

﴿And when they entered from the gate their father had ordered﴾: from the separate gates of the city. It is said that it had four gates, and they entered through them. The mention of it was limited to this because it implies refraining from what they had been forbidden. ﴿It did not avail them at all﴾: that entering would not avail, in what was to come when what happened did happen, ﴿against Allah﴾ meaning against the entering ones, because its purpose was to ward off harm from them. The combination of the past tense and the future tense (in the verb forms) is to establish the required connection between the answer of *lamma* (when, a conditional particle) and what follows it. The non-availing in fact is realized only when the harm descends, not at the time of entering. What is realized at that time is what the aforementioned combination conveys: that the said entering was not going to avail in what was to come. So reflect.

﴿From Allah﴾: from His side. ﴿Any thing﴾: meaning, anything of what He had decreed for them, even though it was likely in the first view, since Ya'qub (peace be upon him) had instructed them with it, and they acted upon its requirement, trusting in its benefit from the grace of Allah the Exalted. So the intent is not to explain that the said entering was the cause of its not availing, as in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Then when a warner came to them, it increased them only in aversion﴾, where the coming of the warner was the cause of the increase in their aversion. Rather, the intent is to explain that it was not a cause of availing, even though availing was expected in the first view, as in your saying: "He swore that he would give me my right at the arrival of the term, and when it arrived he gave me nothing." The intent is to explain that the arrival of the term was not a cause of giving, though giving was hoped for by the requirement of the oath, not to explain that its arrival was a cause of non-giving. So the outcome is the explanation of the non-occurrence of the intended purpose from the known plan, though its occurrence was hoped for, not the explanation of the occurrence of its non-occurrence from it.

It is also permissible that this be meant on the basis of what he (peace be upon him) mentioned within his instruction, that it would not avail them anything from Allah. So it is as if it were said: "And when they did what he had instructed them with, that did not benefit anything, and the matter happened as he (peace be upon him) said, so they met what they met." Then it is from the category of the occurrence of what was expected. So reflect.

﴿Except a need﴾: this is a disconnected exception (*istithna' munqati'*, an exception not of the same kind as what precedes it), meaning: but rather a need and a concern existing ﴿in the soul of Ya'qub, which he fulfilled﴾, that is, he expressed it and instructed them with it to dispel a passing thought, without believing that planning has any effect in changing the decree. The pronoun of the subject in (*qadaha*, "fulfilled it") has been made to refer to the entering, in the sense that that entering fulfilled a need in the soul of Ya'qub, namely his wish that their entering be from separate gates. The meaning then is: that entering did not avail them anything from Allah the Exalted, but it fulfilled a need present in the soul of Ya'qub by its occurrence according to his wish. So the exception is also disconnected. On both readings, the planning had no benefit except the dispelling of the passing thought. As for striking by the evil eye, it did not occur because it was not decreed against them, not because it was averted by that, even though it was [otherwise] required against them.

﴿And indeed he is one of great knowledge﴾ ﴿for what We taught him﴾: for Our teaching him through revelation and the establishment of proofs, since he did not believe that caution averts decree, nor that planning has a share of influence, so that the flaw in his opinion would become evident when the effect did not follow. Or, since he definitively said that it would not avail them anything from Allah, so the situation was as he said. In the emphasis of the sentence with *inna* (indeed) and the *lam* (of emphasis), and the indefiniteness of "knowledge," and its being attributed to the teaching ascribed to His own Self, glorified is He, there is an indication of the greatness of the status of Ya'qub (peace be upon him), and the loftiness and magnificence of the rank of his knowledge, which is not hidden.

﴿But most people do not know﴾: the secrets of the decree, and they suppose that caution avails against it. As for what is said, that the meaning is "they do not know the obligation of caution together with its not availing anything against the decree," this is rejected by the context of explaining the non-fulfilment of the sought outcome from its antecedents.

(p-294)﴿When they entered upon Joseph, he drew his brother to himself﴾, meaning Binyamin (Benjamin). That is, he took him to himself, either at the meal, or in the house, or in both. It is narrated that when they entered upon him, they said to him: "This is our brother; we have brought him to you." He said to them: "You have done well, and you will find that (honour) with me." So he honoured them, then hosted them and seated them in pairs. Binyamin was left alone, so he wept and said: "If my brother Joseph were alive, he would have seated me with him." Joseph said: "Your brother has been left alone," and he seated him with himself at his table and began to eat with him. Then he lodged each two of them in a room, saying: "This one has no second with him, so he will be with me." Joseph spent the night holding him close and smelling his scent until morning. He asked him about his children, and he said: "I have ten sons. I named them after the name of a brother of mine who perished." Joseph said to him: "Would you like me to be your brother in place of your lost brother?" He said: "Who would find a brother like you? But Ya'qub and Rahil did not give birth to you." Joseph wept, rose to him, embraced him, and made himself known to him. At that point ﴿he said: "Indeed I am your brother"﴾, Joseph, ﴿so do not grieve﴾, that is, do not be sad, ﴿over what they used to do﴾ to us in the past. Allah the Exalted has indeed been good to us and has gathered us together in goodness. "And do not inform them of what I have informed you." This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them.

It is also narrated from Wahb that he did not make himself known to him, but said to him: "I am your brother in place of your missing brother." The meaning of ﴿(so do not grieve)﴾ is: do not be sad because of what you used to suffer from them of envy and harm, for you are safe from them. It is narrated that he said to him: "I will not leave you." He said: "You know of my father's grief over me. If I detain you, his grief will increase, and there is no way to that except that I attribute to you what is not becoming." He said: "I do not mind; do as you see fit." He said: "I will put my drinking cup into your baggage, then announce concerning you that you have stolen it, so that I may have a means of getting you back after you have been sent away with them." He said: "Do it."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 70:

﴿So when he had furnished them with their provisions, he placed the drinking-cup﴾ That is, the cup (al-mishraba). It is said it was a drinking vessel that was made into a measure (sa') with which grain is measured. It is said that animals were watered with it and grain was measured with it. It is said it was made of silver, and it is said of gold, and it is said of silver overlaid with gold. It is said it was an elongated vessel resembling the Persian makkuk (a measuring vessel whose two ends meet), which non-Arabs use. It is said it was set with jewels.

﴿in the saddlebag of his brother﴾ Benjamin. It is read as (wa-ja'ala) with the answer of "lamma" omitted, its implied sense being: he gave them respite until they set off. ﴿Then a crier called out﴾ a caller cried out, ﴿"O caravan, you are thieves!"﴾ The "'ir" (caravan) is the camels bearing the loads, so called because they go back and forth (yu'iru), that is, they go and come. It is said it is a caravan of donkeys. Then the usage broadened until every caravan was called "'ir," as if it were the plural of "'ayr." Its original form is fa'l, like saqf and suqf, and it was treated as what was done to bid and ghid. The intended meaning is its people, as in his words, peace be upon him: "O horsemen of God, mount!"

It is reported that they set off, and Yusuf gave them respite until they had gone a distance from the settlement. It is said they went out of the inhabited area, and then he ordered them to be pursued and they were overtaken and called out to: ﴿"Indeed you are thieves."﴾ If this address was by Yusuf's command, then perhaps by "theft" was meant their taking him (Benjamin) from his father, and Benjamin's inclusion in it is by way of predominance (taghlib); otherwise it comes from the crier, according to his assumption, and the first is the more apparent and better suited to the context. And al-Yamani read (sariqun) without the lam (laam).

(p-295) ﴿They said﴾, i.e., the brothers, ﴿and turned to them﴾: this is a circumstantial clause (jumla haliyya) referring back to the subject of "they said." It was brought in to show their alarm at what they had heard, because it contradicted their condition. ﴿"What is it that you are missing?"﴾ That is: what are you losing? One says "faqadtu al-shay'" (I lost the thing) when one has become without it, in such a way that it strayed from you and not through your own action. The implied meaning is: "What has gone astray from you?" The imperfect form is used to bring the scene vividly before the mind. It has also been read as "tufqidūn" (you are deprived of), from "afqadtuhu" when you find him missing. Under both readings, the departure from what the apparent wording would require, namely their saying "What has been stolen from you?", serves to demonstrate the completeness of their innocence by showing that nothing had been stolen from them, let alone that they themselves were the thieves. Rather, what could possibly happen is that something of theirs goes missing, so they ask them: "What is it?" This also contains guidance for them to observe good manners, to avoid rashness, and to refrain from attributing innocence to matters in which there is no good, especially by way of emphatic assertion. For this reason they altered their speech, when...

They said, in reply: "We are missing the king's drinking-vessel" — they did not say "you stole it" or "it was stolen." It was also read as ṣā‘ (صاعَ), ṣawʿa (صَوْعَ) and ṣuwʿa (صُوعَ), with the ṣād vowelled with a fatḥa or a ḍamma, and with the ʿayn unpointed or pointed (ʿayn with a dot, from ṣiyāgha, "goldsmithing"). Then they said, as a way of sustaining what they had received from their side and of showing the belief that it had remained in their baggage only by coincidence: "And for him who brings it" — from his own accord, showing it before the search — "is a camel's load" of provisions, as a reward for him, not with the intention of fulfilling the promise, since they were certain the condition could not occur and were resolved upon what is not hidden, namely seizing whoever is found with it in his baggage. "And I am its guarantor" — a surety who will pay it to him. This is the words of the crier (al-mu’adhdhin, "the one who calls out").

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 73:**

﴿They said: "By God!"﴾ The majority of scholars hold that the *tā'* (تاء) is a substitute for the *wāw* (واو) of the oath, which is why it is used only with the exalted Name of God (al-Jalala al-Mu'azzama), or with "the Lord" (al-Rabb) when it is joined to the Ka'ba, or with "the Most Merciful" (al-Rahman) according to a weak opinion. Had you said *tārrahīm* (تالرَّحِيمِ), it would not be permitted. It has also been said that the *tā'* is substituted for the *bā'* (باء), and it has been said that it is an original particle in itself. Whatever the case, there is an expression of wonder in it. ﴿You certainly know﴾ with a certain knowledge that corresponds to reality ﴿that we did not come to cause corruption in the land﴾, that is, to steal, for theft is among the greatest kinds of corruption; or, "to cause any kind of corruption in it, whether great or small," which is more comprehensive than the theft you attribute to us. The negation of coming *for* corruption, although it does not necessarily entail what the context demands (the negation of corruption absolutely), nevertheless they treated the coming that results in that, even by way of coincidence, as a coming for the purpose of corruption, as an object of purpose (*mafʿūl li-ajlihi*), by way of claim, to show the full extent of its ugliness in their eyes and to affirm the impossibility of its issuing from them. This is like what has been said concerning His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Word is not changed before Me, and I am not unjust to the servants﴾, whose apparent meaning negates excessive injustice rather than negating injustice in general, which is what the context demands. The meaning is: if I punish one who does not deserve punishment, I would be an extremely unjust oppressor. Thus it is as if they said: "If corruption should issue from us, then our coming would be for that," intending by it to disparage its nature and to show the perfection of their innocence of it. They mean that what we are is widely known among you, through our two comings, and they were in the utmost degree of religious integrity and chastity in what they did and abstained from. It is even narrated that they entered Egypt with the mouths of their mounts muzzled, lest they graze upon anyone's crop or food, and they were persistent in various kinds of acts of obedience. And you know by this that no corruption issues from us.

﴿Nor were we thieves﴾, that is, we were never described as thieves at any time. They judged by their knowledge of this, because knowledge of their present conditions necessitates knowledge of their absent conditions. They did not suffice with negating the two matters mentioned, but rather they called upon their knowledge of this as a witness, to impose the proof upon them and to realize the wonder implied by the *tā'* of the oath.

(p-296) ﴿They said﴾: that is, the companions of Yusuf, peace be upon him, said: ﴿"What is the recompense for it?"﴾ The pronoun refers to the drinking-bowl (al-suwa'), with an elided noun (al-mudaf being omitted), i.e., "What is the recompense for its theft, according to you and in your law?" ﴿"If you are liars"﴾ not in the claim of innocence from theft, for they were truthful in that, but rather in what that entails of denying that the bowl was among them, as is indicated by the words of Him, Mighty and Majestic:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 75:

﴿They said: "The recompense for him is: he in whose saddlebag it is found, he himself is its recompense."﴾ That is: the seizing of him in whose saddlebag the drinking-vessel (al-suwa') is found, where it is mentioned under the heading of being found in the saddlebag rather than under the heading of theft, even though that entails theft in their belief, which is founded on the rules of custom. Therefore they answered as they answered, for seizure and enslavement for a year is indeed the recompense of the thief, not of one in whose hand the property of another is found, however it may be. So reflect, and interpret the words of each party in a way that does not conflict with their opinion, for this is closer to the meaning of guile and further from fabrication.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so he himself is its recompense﴾ is an affirmation of that ruling; that is, his seizure is his recompense, as when you say: "The right of the guest is that he be honored, so it is his right." It is also permissible that (jaza'uhu) be the subject, and the conditional clause as it is be its predicate, by placing the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun. The original would be: "Its recompense is: he in whose saddlebag it is found, he himself is it," with the first (jaza'uhu) referring to "he in whose," and the second referring to the apparent noun that was placed in its position.

﴿Thus﴾ that is: like that recompense, the most complete one, ﴿We recompense the wrongdoers﴾ by theft. It is an emphasis on the mentioned ruling after an emphasis, and a statement of the ugliness of theft. Indeed they acted that way out of confidence in their complete innocence of it, while they were heedless of what had been done to them.

﴿So he began﴾ Joseph, after they had returned to him for the search, ﴿with their sacks﴾, meaning the sacks of the ten brothers, that is, by searching them ﴿before﴾ the search of ﴿the sack of his brother﴾ Benjamin, in order to clear away the accusation.

It is related that when the turn came to his sack, he said: "I do not think this one has taken anything!" They said: "By God, we will not let him go until you search his baggage, for that is better for your soul and for ours."

﴿Then he brought it out﴾, meaning the drinking cup, or the goblet, for it is used both as masculine and feminine, ﴿from his brother's sack﴾. He did not say "from it," referring the pronoun back to the sack, nor "from his sack," referring it back to his brother, intending thereby greater disclosure and clarification. It is also recited with a ḍammah on the waw and with the waw changed to a hamzah, as in ashāḥ for wishāḥ.

﴿Thus﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), and the kāf is superfluous (muqḥamah), to indicate the grandeur of what is pointed to, and likewise what is implied in "that" of distance. That is: like that wondrous stratagem, which is an expression for guiding the brothers to the aforementioned ruling, by causing it to be uttered by their own tongues and by moving them toward it through those who sought the ruling, in a way they did not anticipate. Accordingly, the meaning of His words, mighty and majestic is He, ﴿We devised for Joseph﴾, is: We arranged and planned for him, for the sake of attaining his purpose, through the preliminaries which he arranged, such as planting the goblet and what follows it. Thus the lām is not as in His words, "so that they may plot against you a plot," for it introduces the one who is harmed, according to the common usage.

His exalted words: ﴿He could not have taken his brother under the king's law﴾ are a resumptive clause (isti'nāf) and a causal explanation of that stratagem and its contriving, not an exegesis or clarification of it as has been said. It is as if it were said: "Why did he do that?" It was answered: "Because he could not have taken his brother by what he did under the king's law," that is, in his authority, as Ibn 'Abbas said, (p-297) or in his judgment and ruling, as Qatadah said, ﴿except that God wills﴾. For the penalty for theft in his religion was only to beat the thief and to make him pay double what he took, not enslavement and servitude, as was the Shari'ah of Jacob, peace be upon him. Thus he could not, by what he had done, take his brother by the theft he attributed to him in any state whatsoever.

﴿Except that God wills﴾, that is: except in the state of His will, which is an expression for His desire for that stratagem, or except in the state of His will for taking him in that manner. It is permissible that the stratagem refers to that and to all its antecedents leading to it, namely the guidance of Joseph and his people toward the words and deeds that issued from them, as explained in sequence. However, this is not on the basis that the restriction derived from fronting the prepositional phrase is understood in relation to something else absolutely, in the sense of "such a stratagem We devised, not another stratagem," for there is no sense in explaining it by Joseph's inability to take his brother under the king's law in the matter of the thief, since there is definitely no connection between a stratagem in general and the king's law concerning the thief at all. Rather, it is in relation to part of it, in the sense of "such a stratagem reaching this extent We devised for him, and We did not suffice with part of that," for he could not have taken his brother under the king's law by it except in the state of Our will for him, through bringing about what functions as a formal recompense, a complete cause, namely guiding his brothers to the aforementioned ruling. On this basis the restriction should be understood in the interpretation of those who explained His words, ﴿We devised for Joseph﴾, by His words "We taught him it and inspired him with it," that is, such teaching as entails what has been explained in sequence: We taught him that, not merely part of it... and so on.

In any case, the exception is from the most general of states, as has been indicated. It is also permissible that it is from the most general of causes and means, that is: he could not have taken his brother for any cause or by any means except for the cause of His will, exalted is He, or except by the means of His will, exalted is He. Whichever is the case, it is a contiguous exception (muttaṣil), for taking a thief is not contrary to the king's religion when the one who takes him regards that as religion and believes in it, especially when he consents to it and gives the ruling accordingly.

It has been said: the meaning of the exception, ﴿except that God wills﴾, is that God wills to make that ruling the king's ruling. But you know that what is meant by "his religion" is what he then followed, so changing it would undermine the contiguity. And intending the absolute sense of whatever one follows as religion, which is more general than that and than what is newly introduced, leads to the exception being of the type of an application to the impossible, since the aim is to explain Joseph's inability, peace be upon him, to take his brother at that time, and the will did not concern the aforementioned decree at that time. And intending his inability absolutely leads to the opposite of the intended meaning, for the exception of the state of the mentioned will from the states of his inability, peace be upon him, indicates that there is no need for the aforementioned stratagem. So reflect. It has also been permitted that the exception is disjunctive (munqaṭi'), that is: but his taking him by God's will and permission was in a religion other than the king's religion.

﴿We raise by degrees﴾, that is, many lofty ranks of knowledge. Its accusative is as a verbal noun or as an adverb of time or place, or by dropping the preposition, that is: to degrees. The object is His words, ﴿whom We will﴾, that is: We will to raise him as wisdom requires and the interest demands, just as We raised Joseph. The choice of the imperfect form indicates that this is a continuous practice not restricted to this matter. The clause is resumptive and has no place in i'rab (grammatical analysis). ﴿And above every possessor of knowledge﴾ among those raised, ﴿is one who knows﴾, whom they cannot reach. Know that if the stratagem is taken to refer to the first two meanings, then the raising of Joseph, peace be upon him, refers to what was considered in it by the conditional or the component clause, namely his, peace be upon him, guiding them to plant the goblet in his brother's sack and what follows from it of the preliminaries arranged to keep his brother, which is accomplished on his part. The meaning is: We guided his brothers to the aforementioned ruling, for he could not have taken his brother without it; or We guided each of them, and Joseph and his companions, to what issued from them, and We did not suffice with what was accomplished from Joseph alone, for he could not have taken his brother by that alone. Thus His words, ﴿We raise by degrees﴾ up to His words, ﴿knower﴾, explain that, meaning that the aforementioned raising does not bring about the full attainment of his aim, since it is not such that nothing escapes His knowledge. Rather, We raise each one We raise according to his preparedness, and above each one of them is a Knower whose knowledge cannot be measured and whose essence cannot be grasped, who raises each of them to what befits him of the ladders and stages of knowledge. He raised Joseph to what befits him of the lofty ranks, and knew that what his circle of knowledge contained did not suffice for his aim, so he guided his brothers to the aforementioned ruling, and so it was what it was. It seems that he, peace be upon him, was not certain that the aforementioned ruling would issue from his brothers, though he was hopeful of it, since that is up to God, mighty and majestic is He, existence and non-existence alike. The mention of the attribute of knowledge is to specify the direction of superiority. In the intensive form together with the indefiniteness and the shift to the third person there is a clear indication of the grandeur of His exalted and sublime Majesty and of the magnitude of His all-encompassing knowledge.

As for if it is taken to refer to the teaching that entails the aforementioned ruling, then raising refers to that teaching and to the ruling, even though it was not within Joseph's power, peace be upon him, but it was within his knowledge through revelation and instruction. The meaning is: We taught him such teaching reaching this extent, and We did not restrict ourselves to teaching what lies beyond the ruling that would issue from his brothers, since he could not have taken his brother except by that. Thus His words, ﴿We raise by degrees whom We will﴾, explain His words, ﴿We devised﴾, and clarify that this is of the category of raising to the lofty degrees of knowledge, and praise Joseph for being raised to them. And His words, ﴿and above every possessor of knowledge is one who knows﴾, are a concluding statement to it, that is: We raise lofty degrees of knowledge to whom We will, and above each of them is a Knower who is higher in rank.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: "Above every scholar is a scholar, until knowledge ends with God, exalted is He."

The meaning is: the brothers of Joseph, peace be upon him, were scholars, but Joseph, peace be upon him, was more excellent than them. It is recited as "degrees of whom We will" with the construct form, and the first is more suitable to the concluding statement, since the raising is attributed there to the one to whom the superiority is attributed, not to his degree. It is also permissible that the Knower in this interpretation refers to God, mighty and majestic is He, that is: and above each of those raised is a Knower who raises each of them to the degree befitting him. And God, exalted is He, knows best.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 77:

﴿They said: "If he steals,﴾ meaning Binyamin, ﴿then indeed a brother of his stole before.﴾ They mean by this Yusuf, peace be upon him, and what befell him from the direction of his paternal aunt, according to what has been said, namely that she used to nurse him. When he grew up, Ya'qub, peace be upon him, wanted to take him away from her, and she could not bear to be parted from him for an hour. She had a belt (mintaqah) that she had inherited from her father Ishaq, peace be upon him. So she devised a plan to keep Yusuf, peace be upon him. She took the belt and tied it around him under his clothes. Then she said, 'The belt of Ishaq, peace be upon him, has been lost, so search for whoever took it.' They found it tied around Yusuf, and she said, 'He is my slave (salam), I will do with him as I wish.' So Ya'qub, peace be upon him, left him with her until she died. It has also been said that in his youth he took an idol belonging to his maternal grandfather, broke it, and threw it among the carcasses.
