It has also been said that he entered a church, took a small golden statue that they worshipped, and buried it.

﴿So Yusuf kept it⁠﴾ — that is, he concealed the resentment arising from what they had said ﴿within himself⁠﴾, not that he confided it to some of his companions, as in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿and I have confided to them in secret⁠﴾. ﴿And he did not reveal it to them⁠﴾, neither by word nor by deed, forgiving them and showing forbearance. This is an emphasis on what preceded. ﴿He said⁠﴾, that is, to himself, and this is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf, a new clause that begins a fresh statement) built upon a question arising from the report of the concealment mentioned, as if it were said: 'What did he say to himself in the course of that concealment?' So it is said, he said: ﴿You are worse in position⁠﴾, that is, in rank, since you stole your brother from your father, then you began to fabricate lies against the innocent. It has also been said that it is a substitute (badal, a grammatical substitution) for (kept it), and the pronoun refers to the statement explained by his words: "You are worse in position." ﴿And Allah knows best what you describe⁠﴾, that is, He has knowledge reaching the utmost degree that the matter is not as you describe, that the theft came from us. Rather, it is only a fabrication against us. The form (of the word) is for mere intensification, not to make His knowledge, may He be exalted and glorified, superior to theirs. How could it be otherwise, when they have no knowledge of that at all?﴾

﴿They said﴾ when they saw signs that he [Benjamin] was about to be detained, pleading: ﴿O chief of the land, he has a father, an aged old man﴾. They did not mean by this to inform him that Benjamin had a father, for that was already known from what had preceded. Rather, they meant to inform him that the father is ﴿an aged old man﴾ in years, who can hardly bear to be separated from him, and he is a solace to him, by which he consoles himself for his lost brother (the one who perished). ﴿So take one of us in his place﴾, for we are not in his station of love and compassion [toward the old man]. ﴿Indeed, we see you to be of the doers of good﴾ toward us. So complete your goodness with this completion, or [the phrase means] "those accustomed to goodness," so do not change your habit.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 79:

﴿He said: "We seek refuge in Allah"﴾, i.e., "We seek refuge in Allah, a seeking of refuge, from ﴿taking﴾" — the verb has been omitted and the verbal noun (maṣdar) put in its place, annexed to the object after the preposition has been dropped — ﴿except him with whom we found our property﴾, because our taking him is only in accordance with your own judgment (fatwa), so it is not for us to violate what it requires. The use of the first-person plural form, although the address comes from his brothers in the singular, is (a) a way of following the customs of kings (sulukan ila sunan al-muluk, lit. "a way of conducting oneself according to the customs of kings") or (b) to indicate that taking and giving is not something one may act on alone, but is entrusted to the opinions of those who loose and bind (ulu al-hall wa al-'aqd). The choice of "with whom we found our property" rather than "who stole our property" is for the sake of establishing the truth and avoiding a lie in speech while still achieving the aim, for they would not interpret the finding of the drinking-cup in the saddlebag as anything other than theft. ﴿Indeed, we would then be wrongdoers﴾, i.e., if we took someone other than him with whom we found our property, even with his consent, ﴿wrongdoers﴾ according to your own doctrine; and this is not for us. This is the meaning intended by the words during the course of the dialogue. It also has an inner meaning: that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, commanded me through revelation to take Benjamin for purposes which Allah knew in this matter; so if I took someone else, I would be a wrongdoer and would be acting contrary to the revelation.

﴿فَلَمّا اسْتَيْأسُوا مِنهُ﴾ means: when they despaired of him, that is, they despaired of Joseph and of his granting their request, with the utmost despair, as shown by the form *istif'āl* (the Arabic verbal pattern expressing seeking or reaching a state). This degree of despair came about for them because they witnessed his seeking refuge in God from what they had asked of him, which indicates that this matter was, in his view, at the furthest extreme of abhorrence, something to be avoided and to be sheltered from by God, Mighty and Majestic, and that he called it wrongdoing in his saying: (Indeed, we would then be wrongdoers). ﴿خَلَصُوا﴾ means they withdrew and separated themselves from the people, ﴿نَجِيًّا﴾ meaning: possessors of secret consultation (*najwā*), taking it as meaning the consultation and private conversation itself; or "a group apart" (*fawjan najiyyan*), taking it to mean one who converses privately, like *sha'īr* and *samīr* meaning one who keeps company and one who converses by night. Among its occurrences is His saying: ﴿وَقَرَّبْناهُ نَجِيًّا﴾ (And We brought him near as a confidant). It is also permissible to say: "they are *najiyy*," as one says "they are *ṣadīq*," since it is in the pattern of verbal nouns like *zafīr* and *za'īr*.

﴿قالَ كَبِيرُهُمْ﴾ (The eldest among them said). The eldest in age was Ruwbil; or the eldest in intellect was Yahudha; or their leader was Shim'ūn. ﴿ألَمْ تَعْلَمُوا﴾ (Do you not know?). It seems they had agreed during their private conference to return entirely, and he did not approve of this, so he said, rebuking them: Do you not know ﴿أنَّ أباكم قَدْ أخَذَ عَلَيْكم مَوْثِقًا مِنَ اللَّهِ﴾ (that your father has taken from you a solemn pledge in God's name), a covenant by which one is bound, namely their oath by God. That it was "from God" is because He permitted it and because the oath was sworn by His noble name. ﴿وَمِن قَبْلُ﴾ (and before this) means: and before this too, ﴿ما فَرَّطْتُمْ في يُوسُفَ﴾ (you neglected Joseph), you were remiss regarding his affair, and you did not keep your father's covenant, though you had said: ﴿(وَإنّا لَهُ لَناصِحُونَ)﴾ (indeed we are sincere advisers to him) and ﴿(وَإنّا لَهُ لَحافِظُونَ)﴾ (indeed we are his guardians). The "*mā*" here is either superfluous (*zāʾidah*, an added particle with no grammatical role) or verbal (*maṣdariyyah*, forming a verbal noun with the following verb). The position of the verbal noun is in the accusative, coordinated with the object of (*taʿlamū*, you know), meaning: Do you not know your father's taking a covenant from you and your earlier neglect regarding Joseph, peace be upon him? There is no defect in separating the conjunction from what it conjoins by an adverbial expression. It has also been permitted to put it in the accusative as coordinated with the subject of *inna* and its predicate, *fī Yūsuf*, or with *min qablu*, with the meaning: Do you not know that your earlier neglect occurred regarding Joseph, peace be upon him, or that your neglect which exists or is existing regarding Joseph, peace be upon him, occurred before this? Against this: the context requires only the report that this neglect occurred, not that your earlier neglect was regarding Joseph, as the first reading implies, nor that your neglect regarding him occurred before, as the second implies. Moreover, an adverbial expression cut off from its genitive complement cannot be a predicate, an attribute, a relative clause, or, according to some, a circumstantial adjunct, as is established in its proper place.

It was said: its position is nominative, as a subject, with *min qablu* as the predicate, and there is much to be said about that. It was also said: *mā* is relative (*mawṣūlah*) or descriptive (*mawṣūfah*), and its position is accusative, coordinated with the object of *taʿlamū*, meaning: what you did to him of betrayal, by way of pre-empting it regarding him. As for the accusative coordinated with the subject of *inna*, and the nominative as a subject, you know their status.

﴿فَلَنْ أبْرَحَ الأرْضَ﴾ (So I will not leave the land) is a consequence of what he mentioned and reminded them of: their father's covenant, and his saying: ﴿لَتَأْتُنَّنِي بِهِ إلا أنْ يُحاطَ بِكُمْ﴾ (you shall surely bring him to me unless you are encompassed by disaster). That is: I will not leave the land of Egypt, acting in accordance with the terms of the covenant, ﴿حَتّى يَأْذَنَ لِي أبِي﴾ (until my father gives me leave) to depart and return to him. It seems their oaths had been bound on not returning without Jacob's permission, peace be upon him, ﴿أوْ يَحْكُمَ اللَّهُ لِي﴾ (or God decides for me) to leave in a manner that does not lead to breaking the covenant, or to free my brother by some means.

It is related that they spoke to the Governor about releasing him, and Ruwbil said: "O King, you shall surely return our brother to us, or I shall cry out a cry that will leave no pregnant woman in Egypt without miscarrying her child, and every hair on his body stood up and came out of his garments." The sons of Jacob, when angered, could not be withstood, except that if someone touched a man who was angry among them, his anger would subside. Joseph said to his son: "Stand by his side and touch him," and he did so. Ruwbil said: "Who is this? Indeed in this land there is a seed of the seed of Jacob," ﴿وَهُوَ خَيْرُ الحاكِمِينَ﴾ (and He is the best of judges), since he judges only by truth and justice.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 81:

﴿Return﴾ you (plural) ﴿to your father and say: "O our father, your son has stolen"﴾ according to the outward appearance of the situation. It is also read as "suriqa" (he has been made to appear a thief), meaning he has been attributed with theft. ﴿And we did not testify﴾ concerning him ﴿except to what we knew﴾ and witnessed, namely that the drinking vessel (al-suwa') was taken out of his bag. ﴿And we were not guardians of the unseen﴾ i.e., of the inner reality of the matter, ﴿so we do not know whether the true state of affairs is as we witnessed or otherwise.﴾ Or it means: we were not aware, when we gave you the covenant (al-mawthiq), that he would steal; or: we would encounter this matter; or: you would be afflicted with it just as you were afflicted with Joseph.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 82:

﴿Ask the town in which we were﴾ That is, Egypt; or a town near it, where the crier overtook them. That is: send to its people and ask them about the story. ﴿And the caravan in which we came back﴾ That is, its people, for the story is well known among them. They were a people from Kan'an (Canaan), neighbours of Ya'qub (peace be upon him). It was also said: from Sana'a. ﴿And indeed we are truthful﴾ This is an emphatic statement in the place of an oath.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 83:

﴿Qala﴾ (He said): i.e., Ya'qub (peace be upon him). This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) built upon a question arising from what preceded. It is as if it were said: "What was his response when the one who stayed behind said to his brothers what he said?" So it was said: Ya'qub said when they returned to him and told him what they told him. The reason it was omitted is to signal that their hastening to accept it and their returning with it to their father is a settled matter, independent of explanation; what is needed is only the answer of their father.

﴿Bal sawwalat﴾ (Rather, your souls have made it seem fair to you): i.e., adorned and facilitated. This is a turning away (idrab) not from the explicit statement of theirs, for they were truthful in that, but from what it implies of claiming innocence of causing what befell him and that nothing had proceeded from them, by word or deed, that would lead to it. It is as if it were said: "The matter was not as you say; rather, your souls adorned for you a matter (amran) among the matters, so you did it," intending by that their ruling to seize the thief for his theft. ﴿Fa-sabrun jamil﴾ (So patience is beautiful): i.e., so my matter is beautiful patience, or: so beautiful patience is the most beautiful. ﴿'Asa Allahu an ya'tiyani bihim jami'an﴾ (Perhaps Allah will bring them all to me): with Yusuf, his brother, and the one who stayed behind in Egypt. ﴿Innahu huwa al-'Alim﴾ (Indeed He is the All-Knowing) of my condition and theirs, ﴿al-Hakim﴾ (the All-Wise), who has not tested me except for a far-reaching wisdom.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 84:

﴿And he turned away from them﴾, i.e., he turned away from them, out of aversion to what he heard from them. ﴿And said: "Oh, my grief over Joseph!"﴾ Al-asaf (grief) is the most intense sorrow and regret. He attributed it to himself, and the alif is a substitute for the ya' (of the possessive), so he called upon it, i.e., "O my grief, come, for this is your time." He grieved over Joseph, even though the event was the affliction of his two sons, because the loss of Joseph was the foundation of all losses, fresh in his heart even though his time had long passed, taking hold of the core of his heart so that he could not forget it. And because he was confident of the life of both of them, knowledgeable of their whereabouts, and hopeful of their return.

As for Joseph, nothing in his situation stirred the chain of his hope except the mercy and grace of Allah the Exalted. And in a report: "No nation among the nations has been given (Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un) [We belong to Allah and to Him we return] except the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ). Do you not see that Ya'qub, when he was afflicted with what he was afflicted with, did not say it, but said what he said." The assonance between the words asaf (grief) and Yusuf (Joseph) adds beauty to the noble composition, as in the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿and they forbid others from it and keep away from it themselves﴾, and His words: ﴿you cling heavily to the earth, are you content﴾, and His words: ﴿then eat of all the fruits﴾, and ﴿I have come to you from Saba' with certain news﴾, and their likes.

﴿And his eyes turned white from the grief﴾ which necessitates weeping, for when tears become abundant, they dissolve the blackness of the eye and turn it into a turbid whiteness. It was said: his sight had become blind; and it was said: he could perceive only weakly.

It is narrated that the eyes of Ya'qub did not dry from the day of separation from Joseph until the time of their reunion, eighty years, and there was none on the face of the earth more honored by Allah the Mighty and Majestic than Ya'qub, peace be upon him. And it is narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he asked Jibril, peace be upon him: "How intense was Ya'qub's (peace be upon him) longing for Joseph?" He said: "The longing of seventy bereaved mothers." He said: "What reward did he have?" He said: "The reward of a hundred martyrs." And his opinion of Allah never worsened for a single moment. In this is evidence of the permissibility of grieving and weeping at calamities, for refraining from that does not fall under obligation, since few can control themselves in severe trials. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wept over his son Ibrahim and said: "The heart grieves and the eye sheds tears, and we do not say what displeases the Lord. Indeed, we are grieved for you, O Ibrahim." What is impermissible is what the ignorant do of wailing and shrieking, slapping cheeks and chests, tearing collars and rending garments.

And it is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he wept over the son of one of his daughters while he was in his last breaths. It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, you weep though you have forbidden us from weeping?" He said: "I did not forbid you from weeping, but I forbade you from two foolish sounds: a sound at joy and a sound at sorrow."

﴿So he was kazim﴾ filled with suppressed anger over his sons, holding it within his heart and not showing it. It is an fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, as evidenced by His words: ﴿and he was maksum﴾, from kazama al-siqa' when he tied it tight over its contents; or it is in the sense of fa'il, like His words: ﴿and those who restrain anger﴾, from kazama al-ghayz when he swallowed it; and its origin is kazama al-ba'ir jirrata when he returned it into its belly.

"They said, 'By God, you will not cease remembering Joseph'", meaning: you will not cease and will never stop remembering Joseph, mourning over him, so the negative particle has been omitted, as in the line of poetry:

"So I said, 'By God's oath, I will not cease sitting'"

It is omitted because there is no confusion with the affirmative, since when an oath is not accompanied by a sign of affirmation, it is definitely negative. ﴿Until you become one who is wasting away﴾: ill, close to destruction. It was also said: the ḥaraḍ (wasted one) is the one whom grief or sickness has melted away. It is originally a verbal noun, and for this reason it is not made feminine, dual or plural. Its adjectival form is with a kasra, like danif (gravely ill), and it has been recited that way, and also with two dammas, like junub and gharub. ﴿Or you become among those who perish﴾: that is, among the dead.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 86:

﴿He said: "I only complain of my anguish and my grief to Allah"﴾ Al-bathth (anguish) is the most severe kind of worry, which its bearer cannot bear, so he spreads it out to people; that is, he makes it public. So they had said to him what they said by way of consolation and solace. He said to them: "I do not complain of what I suffer to you, nor to others, so that you would undertake to console me; rather, I complain of my worry ﴿and my grief to Allah﴾, the Exalted, seeking refuge at His side and humbly beseeching at His door for its removal." It is also read with two fathas and two dammas. ﴿And I know from Allah what you do not know﴾ of His kindness and mercy, so I hope that He will have mercy on me, be gentle with me, and not disappoint my hope. Or: I know, by revelation or inspiration from Him, what you do not know of the life of Yusuf. It is said: he saw the Angel of Death in a dream and asked him about him, and he said, "He is alive." It is also said: he knew from the dream of Yusuf, peace be upon him, that his parents and brothers would bow down to him in prostration.

O my sons, go and seek out news of Joseph and his brother. (Tafsir note: "tahassasu" here means "seek to know" — it is a tafa''ul form derived from al-hass, sensory perception.) It is also read with the letter jim (tajassasu), from al-jass, which means seeking; i.e., search for them. "From Joseph and his brother" means: from their news. He did not mention the third, because his absence was by choice and its removal is not difficult.

"And do not despair of the mercy of Allah." Do not give up hope in His relief and deliverance. It is also read with a damma on the ra' (rawh), i.e., from His mercy by which He gives life to His servants. This is guidance to them toward some of what was left unspecified in His saying: "And I know from Allah what you do not know" (p-303). Then He warned them against abandoning the action required by His prohibition, with His saying: "Indeed, none despair of the mercy of Allah except the disbelieving people," because of their lack of knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, and His attributes, for the one who truly knows Him never despairs in any circumstance.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 12, verse 88:**

﴿When they entered upon him﴾, i.e., upon Yusuf, after they had returned to Egypt in accordance with their father's command. That this is not mentioned signals their haste in doing what they were commanded, and indicates that this is a certain matter that needs no mention or explanation. ﴿They said: O 'Aziz﴾, i.e., the king, the mighty and unassailable, ﴿adversity has touched us and our family﴾, the emaciation from severe hunger. ﴿And we have brought merchandise that is meagre﴾ (*muzjah*, "pushed away," "inferior"), which every merchant pushes away out of disinterest in it and contempt for it. It derives from *azjaytuhu*, when you push and drive something away, as the wind drives the clouds (*tuzji al-sahab*). It was said: their merchandise consisted of Bedouin goods, wool and clarified butter. It was said: it was pine nuts and *habbat al-khadra'*. It was said: it was roasted doum-fruit flour and dried curd (*aqit*). It was said: it was debased dirhams that are accepted only at a loss. They mentioned this first so that it would serve as a means to achieve their aim, by arousing compassion, stirring tenderness and mercy, and setting in motion the chain of compassion. Then they said: ﴿So give us full measure﴾, i.e., complete it for us, ﴿and be charitable to us﴾ by returning our brother to us. This was said by al-Dahhak and Ibn Juraij, and it is the most fitting to their situation, in view of their father's command. Or it means by giving full measure, or by overlooking the inferiority of the goods and accepting them, or by giving more than their value as an act of grace. They called it charity out of humility. Or they intended charity beyond what he gives them in exchange for the price, based on the belief that the sanctity of charity is specific to our Prophet (ﷺ). They did not begin with what they were commanded to say, seeking to win compassion and kindness, so that by the tenderness of their condition they would stir the tenderness and affection of the heart. Moreover, what they said has two possible meanings, for their words ﴿and be charitable to us; indeed, God rewards the charitable﴾ admit of being taken in either of the two senses. Thus, perhaps he (peace be upon him) understood it in the first sense, and for this reason…

﴿He said﴾, responding to what they had put forward and included in their speech of seeking the return of their brother: ﴿Do you know what you did to Joseph and his brother?﴾ The apparent expectation was that he would mention only what they had done to his brother, but he mentioned what they had done to Joseph because both were subjected to the same act. The intent behind this is their isolating him from Joseph and humiliating him, to the point that he could speak to them only in weakness and abasement. The meaning is: have you repented of that after knowing how ugly it is? This is a question about the necessary consequence, and what is intended is its implication: ﴿when you were ignorant﴾ of its ugliness, which is why you went ahead with it. Or [it means] you were ignorant of its consequence. He said this out of counsel for them and encouragement toward repentance, and out of compassion for them when he saw their helplessness and humility, not as reproach or rebuke. It is also permissible that this statement from him, peace be upon him, was separate from their speech, serving as an admonition to them regarding what is their right and duty: turning away from all demands and devoting themselves wholly to seeking Binyamin. Moreover, it is permissible that he, peace be upon him, learned by way of revelation (wahy) or inspiration (ilham) of his father's instruction and his sending them to seek news of him and his brother. So when he saw that they had become preoccupied with other things, he said what he said.

It was said: They gave him the letter of Ya'qub, peace be upon him, in which he had written: "A letter from Ya'qub Isra'il, the Prophet of God, son of Ishaq, the sacrificed one of God, son of Ibrahim, the Friend of God, to the Aziz of Egypt. To proceed: we are a household upon whom afflictions have been imposed. As for my grandfather, his hands and feet were bound and he was thrown into the fire, but God Most High saved him, and made it cool and safe for him. As for my father, the knife was placed on his nape to be slaughtered, but God Most High ransomed him. As for me, I had a son who was the most beloved of my children to me, and his brothers took him away to the desert; then they brought me his shirt stained with blood, saying: 'The wolf has eaten him.' My eyes went blind from weeping for him. Then I had another son, who was his brother from the same mother, and I used to console myself with him, but they took him away. Then they returned and said: 'He has stolen, and you have detained him. We are a household that does not steal, nor do we give birth to a thief. So if you return him to me, well and good; otherwise I will invoke a supplication against you that will overtake the seventh of your descendants. And peace." When he read it, he could not contain himself and his patience was exhausted, so he said to them what he said. It was also said: when he read it, he wept, and he wrote the reply: "Be patient as they were patient, and you will triumph as they triumphed."

﴿They said: Are you indeed Joseph?﴾ It is an interrogative of affirmation (*istifham taqrir*, a question that seeks confirmation). For this reason they emphasized it with *inna* and the *lam*. They said it out of astonishment and wonder. It has also been read as (إنَّكَ) in the affirmative form (*bi-al-ijab*), meaning "You are indeed Joseph." It was said that they recognized him by his appearance and bearing (*ruwa'ihi wa-shama'ilihi*) when he spoke to them. It was also said that he smiled and they recognized him by his front teeth (*thana-ya*). It was also said that he lifted the crown from his head and they saw a mark on his forehead (*qarn*) resembling a white birthmark (*al-shama al-bayda'*), and that Sarah and Ya'qub had a similar mark. It has also been read as (أئِنَّكَ) or (أنْتَ يُوسُفَ), with the meaning "Are you indeed Joseph?" or "You are Joseph." In the latter case the first (interrogative) element is omitted because the second indicates it, and this adds to the sense of astonishment.

﴿He said: I am Joseph﴾ in answer to their question. He added to it his saying: ﴿and this is my brother﴾, that is, from my two parents. This is for emphasis in identifying himself, for magnifying the status of his brother, and as a completion of what his saying ﴿Do you know what you did to Joseph and his brother?﴾ conveyed, as indicated by his saying ﴿God has bestowed favor upon us﴾. It is as if he said: Do you know what you did to us by separating us and humiliating us? So I am Joseph and this is my brother, and God has bestowed favor upon us by delivering us from what we were afflicted with, by reuniting after separation, by honor after humiliation, and by intimacy after loneliness. It is not unlikely that this contains an indication of a reply to their request for the return of Benjamin: that he is my brother, not your brother, so there is no basis for your demand. Then he gave a reason for this by way of the explanatory resumptive clause (*istinaf ta'lili*) in his saying: ﴿Indeed, whoever fears God﴾, that is, does what is pious in all his conditions, or protects himself from what brings down God's wrath and punishment, ﴿and is patient﴾ in trials, or in the hardship of acts of obedience, or in refraining from sins that the soul desires, ﴿then indeed God does not waste the reward of the good-doers﴾, that is, their reward. The explicit noun was placed in the position of the pronoun (*al-muzhar mawdi' al-mudmar*) to draw attention to the fact that those described by piety and patience are also described by good conduct (*ihsan*).

﴿They said, "By God, God has certainly preferred you over us"﴾: He chose you and favored you over us, by the noble qualities you have mentioned. ﴿"And indeed we were"﴾: indeed, the matter is that we were ﴿sinners﴾, deliberately committing sin, since we did to you what we did. For this reason He honored you and humbled us. In this is an indication of repentance and seeking forgiveness, and for this reason.

"He said: 'No reproach upon you today.'" That is, no blame and no rebuke ﴿upon you﴾. It is a form of tafʻīl from al-tharb (تَثْرِيب), which is the fat covering the stomach (kirsh), and its meaning is its removal, just as tajlīd (التَّجْلِيد) is the removal of the skin and taqrīʻ (التَّقْرِيع) is the removal of the ... [sic: the removal of the knocking/striking, i.e., severe rebuke]. For when the fat is gone, that is the utmost emaciation, so it was used as a metaphor for the rebuke that takes away the sheen of faces. As for His saying, Mighty and Exalted: ﴿today﴾, it is in the accusative case governed by al-tathrīb (the reproach), or by a implied predicate of "lā" (no), meaning: "no effect upon you," or "no reproach is established upon you today," the day which is the likely occasion for it, so what then do you suppose about the other days? (p. 305) Or it is governed by His saying: ﴿May God forgive you﴾, because at that time he pardoned their offense and overlooked their wrongdoing, on account of what they did of repentance. ﴿And He is the Most Merciful of the merciful﴾: He forgives minor and major sins, and bestows His favor on the penitent by accepting them. And from his generosity, peace be upon him, was that his brothers sent to him: "You invite us to your food morning and evening, and we are ashamed before you because of what passed from us toward you." He, peace be upon him, said: "The people of Egypt—even though I have become their ruler—used to look at me with the first eye, and would say: 'Glory be to Him who raised a slave who was sold for twenty dirhams to what he has reached!' Now you have honored me, and I have become great in the eyes, since the people have come to know that you are my brothers and that I am from the descendants (ḥafada) of Abraham, peace be upon him."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 93:

﴿Go with this shirt of mine⦆ It is said: it is the one he was wearing at that time. And it is said: it is the inherited shirt that was in the amulet (ta'widh). Gabriel commanded him to send it to him, and revealed to him that the fragrance (fayh) of the wind of Paradise does not fall upon any afflicted person except that he is healed. ﴿Then cast it over the face of my father; he will regain his sight⦆: that is, he will become seeing, or he will come to me seeing. The following supports this: ﴿And bring me all your family﴾, that is, my father and others included under the word "family" (ahl) collectively, from women and offspring.

It is said: it was Yahudha (Judah) who carried the shirt, and he said: "I was the one who grieved him by bringing the shirt smeared with blood to him, so I will gladden him just as I grieved him." And it is said: he carried it barefoot and bareheaded from Egypt to Kan'an (Canaan), and between them is a distance of eighty farsakh.

The Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 94:

﴿When the caravan departed⁠﴾ it set out from the outskirts of Egypt. It is said: "faṣala min al-balad fuṣūlan" (he departed from the town) when he separated from it and passed its walls. Ibn 'Abbas - may Allah be pleased with them both - recited: (انْفَصَلَ العِيرُ) [infaṣala al-'Ir]. ﴿Their father⁠﴾ Ya'qub - upon him be peace - said to those who were with him: ﴿"Indeed I smell the scent of Yusuf⁠"﴾. Allah, glorified is He, caused him to perceive the fragrance that clung to the shirt from a distance of eighty farsakh (parasangs), when Yahudha brought it. ﴿"Were it not that you would think me senile⁠"﴾, i.e., you would attribute to me "al-fanad," which is senility, the loss of reason, and corruption of judgment from old age. It is said: "shaykh mufannid" (a senile old man), but it is not said "'ajuz mufannida" (a senile old woman), since she was not a person of judgment in her youth, so she would not be deemed senile in her old age. The answer to "lawla" (were it not) is omitted, meaning: you would have believed me.

"They said: 'By God, you are still in your old error,'" meaning: those present with him said, "By God, you are indeed in your ancient error (ḍalāl al-qadīm), that is, in your long-standing departure from what is right, in your excessive love for Joseph, your constant mention of him, and your hope of meeting him." They thought he had died.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 12, verse 96:**

﴿So when the bearer of good news arrived﴾, who was Yahudha (Judah), ﴿he cast it﴾, meaning the bearer of good news cast the shirt ﴿upon his face﴾, meaning the face of Ya'qub (Jacob). Or Ya'qub cast it upon his own face. ﴿And he regained his sight﴾, meaning he returned to seeing, because of the strength that revived in him. ﴿He said: Did I not tell you﴾, meaning his saying: ﴿Indeed, I find the scent of Yusuf (Joseph)﴾. The address is then to those who were with him in Kan'an (Canaan). Or it refers to his saying: "And do not despair of the mercy of God," and then the address is to his sons, which is the more fitting reading given his saying: ﴿Indeed, I know from God what you do not know﴾. (p-306) For the basis of the prohibition mentioned is only the knowledge that Ya'qub was given from God, glory be to Him. On this reading, it is permissible for this to be the content of the saying, meaning: Did I not tell you when I sent you to Misr (Egypt), and ordered you to search, and forbade you from despairing of the mercy of God the Exalted: ﴿(And I know from God what you do not know)﴾, concerning the life of Yusuf, peace be upon him.

It is narrated that he asked the bearer of good news: "How is Yusuf?" He said: "He is the king of Misr." He said: "What do I do with kingship? On what religion did you leave him?" He said: "On the religion of Islam." He said: "Now the blessing is complete."

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿They said, "O our father, ask forgiveness for us for our sins. Indeed, we were wrongdoers."﴾

And it is due to one who acknowledges his sin that he be pardoned and that forgiveness be asked for him. So it was as though they were confident of his pardon, peace be upon him, and therefore they limited themselves to requesting the seeking of forgiveness, and they included that within the seeking of forgiveness.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 98:

﴿He said: "I shall ask my Lord for forgiveness for you. Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful."﴾ This indicates His pardon. It has been said: he delayed the seeking of forgiveness until the time of the pre-dawn (sahar). It has been said: until the night of Friday, so that he might seek out the time of response (in supplication). It has been said: he delayed it until he had asked Yusuf, peace be upon him, to absolve them (istihlal), or knew that he had pardoned them, for the pardon of the wronged party is a condition of forgiveness. This is supported by the report that he faced the qiblah standing and supplicated, while Yusuf stood behind him saying "Amin," and they stood behind the two of them, humbled and submissive, for twenty years, until their exertion reached its limit and they thought it was destruction. Then Jibril, peace be upon him, descended and said: "Indeed Allah has answered your supplication concerning your son, and has taken their covenants after you concerning prophethood. If this is sound, their prophethood is established, and what proceeded from them occurred before they were appointed as prophets (al-istinba'). " It has been said: the meaning is continuing in supplication, for it is reported that he would seek forgiveness every Friday night for over twenty years. It has been said: he stood to pray at the time of the pre-dawn, and when he finished he raised his hands and said: "O Allah, forgive me my anguish over Yusuf and my lack of patience with regard to him, and forgive my sons what they did to their brother." So Allah revealed to him: "Indeed Allah has forgiven you and them all."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 99:

﴿When they entered upon Yusuf﴾ It is related that Yusuf had sent to his father a provision and two hundred mounts so that he and those with him could equip themselves to come to him. Yusuf went out to meet him with the king, with four thousand of the soldiery, the dignitaries, and all the people of Egypt. They received Ya'qub, peace be upon him, as he was walking, leaning on Yahudha. He looked at the horses and the people and said: "O Yahudha, is this the Pharaoh of Egypt?" He said: "No, rather it is your son." When he met him, he said, peace be upon him: "Peace be upon you, O remover of sorrows." It is also said that Yusuf said to him: "O father, you wept over me until your sight was lost. Did you not know that the Resurrection will gather us?" He said: "Yes, but I feared that your religion would be stripped from you, and that I would be prevented from you and you from me." It is also said that Ya'qub and his sons entered Egypt, and they were seventy-two persons, men and women. When they left with Musa, they were six hundred thousand, five hundred and some seventy men, apart from the offspring and the aged. The offspring numbered one million and two hundred thousand.

﴿He drew his parents close to him﴾ That is, his father and his maternal aunt. Treating her in the position of a mother is like treating the paternal uncle in the position of a father, in the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿the God of your fathers, Ibrahim and Isma'il and Ishaq﴾. Or because Ya'qub, peace be upon him, married her after his mother. Al-Hasan and Ibn Ishaq said: his mother was still alive, so there is no need for interpretation. The meaning of "drew close to him" is that he embraced them and held them to himself, and it seems that he, peace be upon him, had pitched a tent at the meeting place and settled in it, and they entered upon him, so he drew them close to him. ﴿And he said: Enter Egypt, if God wills, in security﴾ from all hardships and adversities altogether. The will (of God) is connected to the entering, in security.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 100:

﴿And he raised his parents﴾ upon the throne when they came to Egypt, ﴿upon the throne﴾, that is, upon the couch, as an honour to them, above what he had done for his brothers. ﴿And they fell down before him in prostration﴾, that is, his parents and his brothers, ﴿in prostration﴾ as a greeting to him. For prostration among them was practised as a greeting and an honour, like standing up, shaking hands, kissing the hand and the like of the widespread customs of people in showing reverence and veneration. It was said: that was only bowing without placing the foreheads in the dust, and the word "fell down" (kharru) rejects this. It was said: they fell down for his sake in prostration to God in thanks. This is refuted by His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And he said: "O my father, this is the interpretation of my dream"﴾ which I saw and related to you ﴿from before﴾, in the time of childhood, ﴿my Lord has made it true﴾, a truth that has come to pass exactly. The excuse of making Joseph equivalent to the qibla, and making the lam (in "li-qiblatikum") as in His saying:

"Is he not the first who prayed towards your qibla?"

is a far-fetched interpretation that is not hidden. And placing this (the mention of the dream's interpretation) after the raising upon the throne is not a clear text on this matter, since the order of mention need not follow the order of occurrence. Perhaps it was placed after it so that the mention of its being the interpretation of his dream, and what is connected to it, would be joined to His saying: ﴿And He has been good to me﴾. The well-known usage is "ihsan" with "ila" (to), though it may also be used with "bi" (with), as in His, exalted is His name, saying: ﴿(and to parents, good treatment)﴾. It was said: this is by the implicit meaning of "latafa" (to be gracious), which is hidden kindness, as His saying indicates: ﴿Indeed my Lord is Subtle in what He wills﴾, and in this there is a benefit that is not hidden. That is: He was gracious to me, being kind to me beyond this kindness ﴿when He took me out of the prison﴾ after I had been tested with it. He did not state the account of the well, out of caution about reproaching his brothers, because it is apparent that they were present, since the speech followed their falling down in prostration, and being content with what His saying implies: ﴿And He brought you from the desert﴾, that is, the desert, ﴿after Satan had stirred up discord between me and my brothers﴾, that is, he corrupted what was between us by enticement. Its origin is from the goading of a trainer of a beast and urging it to run; it is said "nazaghahu" and "nasaghahu" when he prods it. He, peace be upon him, went to great lengths in kindness by attributing that to Satan. ﴿Indeed my Lord is Subtle in what He wills﴾, that is, subtle in management for its sake, gentle, until it comes in the manner of wisdom and rightness; there is no difficulty that is not easy in relation to His management. ﴿Indeed He is the Knowing﴾ of the aspects of the interests ﴿the Wise﴾ who does everything in accordance with the dictates of wisdom.

It is reported that Joseph took the hand of Jacob, peace be upon them both, and walked him through his treasuries, and he admitted him into the treasuries of silver and gold, the treasuries of ornaments, the treasuries of garments, the treasuries of weapons, and other things. When he admitted him into the treasuries of papers, he said: "O my son, how undutiful you are! You have these papers, and what you wrote to me over eight stages." He said: "Gabriel commanded me." He said: "Will you not ask him?" He said: "You are more open with him than I am." So he asked him, and Gabriel said: "God, exalted is He, commanded me to do that because of your saying: 'I fear that the wolf will eat him.'" He said: "Then why did you not fear Me?"

It is reported that Jacob, peace be upon him, remained with him for twenty-four years, then died, and he bequeathed that he be buried in al-Sham beside his father Isaac. Joseph went himself and buried him there, then returned to Egypt and lived after (p-308) his father for twenty-three years. When his affair was complete and he knew that it would not last for him, his soul longed for the eternal, everlasting King, so he wished for death and said:

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 101:**

﴿My Lord, You have indeed given me some of the kingdom﴾, that is, a great portion of it, namely the kingship of Egypt, ﴿and You have taught me some of the interpretation (ta'wil) of events﴾, that is, some of that as well. This is so if by teaching the interpretation of events is meant making understood the subtle secrets of the divine books and the fine points of the ways (sunan) of the prophets, upon them be peace. Then the order is clear. But if what is meant by it is teaching the interpretation of dreams, as is the apparent meaning, then perhaps the mention of granting kingship before it is because the context is one of enumerating the blessings that God, glory be to Him, bestowed upon him, and kingship is more deeply rooted as a blessing than the teaching mentioned, although that too is a sublime blessing in itself. This explanation cannot be applied to what preceded, because the teaching there comes in the manner of a final cause ('illah ghā'iyyah) of the empowerment. If it is understood in the sense of conferring ownership, it would follow that it comes after it. What occurs here, however, is merely a delay in mention, and conjunction by the particle waw does not require that order in existence.

﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾, its innovator and creator. It is in the accusative, either as an adjective of the vocative, or as another vocative which He described Himself with after describing Himself as Lord, in emphasis on the foundations of what follows from His saying: ﴿You are my guardian﴾, the master of my affairs, ﴿in this world and the Hereafter﴾, or the One who takes charge of me with blessing in both. Since You have completed Your blessing upon me in the world, ﴿cause me to die﴾, take me, ﴿as a Muslim, and join me with the righteous﴾, from among my forefathers, or with the righteous in general in rank and honor, for the blessing is only complete by that.

It is said that when he supplicated, God, mighty and majestic, caused him to die, pure and clean. The people of Egypt disputed over his burial and contended about it until they were on the verge of fighting. They decided to make for him a coffin of marble, placed him in it, and buried him in the Nile so that it would pass over them, then reach Egypt, so that they would all be a single party seeking blessing through him.

And there were born to him Ephraim (Afrayim) and Mishā, and to Ephraim was born Nūn, and to Nūn was born Yūshaʿ (Joshua), the servant (fatā) of Moses, upon him be peace. The Pharaohs after him inherited Egypt from the Amalekites, and the Children of Israel remained under their rule, holding to the remnants of the religion of Joseph and his forefathers, until God, exalted is He, sent Moses, upon him be peace.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 102:

﴿That﴾ is a reference to the account of Yusuf that preceded, and the sense of distance in it (i.e., the demonstrative used for the remote) is due to what has passed repeatedly, indicating the distance of its rank, or because, having already been completed, it is considered in the category of the remote. The address is to the Messenger (ﷺ), and ﴿That﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), whose predicate (khabar) is ﴿of the tidings of the unseen﴾, which no one hovers around.

His saying ﴿We reveal it to you﴾ is a predicate following a predicate, or a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in the predicate. It is also permissible that ﴿that﴾ be a relative pronoun (ism mawsul), with ﴿of the tidings of the unseen﴾ as its relative clause (silah), and the predicate being ﴿(We reveal it to you)﴾.

﴿And you were not with them﴾, meaning the brothers of Yusuf, peace be upon him, ﴿when they resolved upon their affair﴾, which is their placing him in the depths of the well, ﴿while they were scheming﴾ against him and devising plots for him, until you would stand upon the outward aspects of their secrets and their inward dimensions, and be informed of their hidden matters entirely, and comprehend with knowledge what is with them. The meaning is not merely the negation of his presence, peace be upon him, at the scene of their resolving and their scheming only, but at all the scenes as well. Its singling out for mention is because it is the starting point of the story and the most hidden of its circumstances, as His saying "while they were scheming" indicates. Although the address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), the purpose is to impose the proof upon the deniers.

The meaning: That is among the tidings of the unseen which We reveal to you, since there is no way for you to know it except by that, for your not hearing it from others and your not studying books is a matter that the deniers also do not doubt. Nor were you among them at the time the matter occurred, so that you would know it as it is and convey it to them. In this there is a mockery of the disbelievers, as though they doubt this, so it repels their doubt. In it there is also an announcement that what has been mentioned of the account is the truth that corresponds to reality, and that what the People of the Book transmit is not as it really is. That is to say, such verification without revelation is not conceivable except through presence and witnessing, and since that presence did not occur, it is through revelation. A similar statement is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you were not with them when they cast their pens, which of them would take charge of Maryam﴾, and His saying: ﴿And you were not on the western side when We decreed the affair to Musa﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 103:

﴿And most of mankind, even if you were eager, will not be believers﴾. It (the verse) intends by this the generality (of mankind), or the people of Mecca. ﴿Even if you were eager﴾, that is: for their faith, and you exerted yourself in displaying the decisive signs that indicate your truthfulness, ﴿they will not be believers﴾ because of their determination upon disbelief and their persistence in obstinacy.

It is related that the Jews and the Quraysh, when they asked about the story of Yusuf and promised that they would embrace Islam, and he informed them of it in agreement with the Torah, they did not embrace Islam, and the Prophet (ﷺ) grieved, so he was told that.

ÿ﴾And you do not ask them for any wage for it﴿ — i.e., for the news or for the Qur'an — ﴿مِن أجْرٍ﴾ ... 

Let me translate properly.

**Translation:**

﴿And you do not ask them for any wage for it﴾ — that is, for the tidings (al-anba') or for the Qur'an — ﴿any wage﴾ — a recompense (ju'l), as those who transmit reports (hamalat al-akhbar) do. ﴿It is nothing but a reminder﴾ — an admonition from Allah, the Exalted — ﴿to the worlds﴾ — all of them, without restriction; this is not specific to them (i.e., to the people addressed in particular).

And how many a sign there is in the heavens and the earth (﴿وَكَأيِّنْ مِن آيَةٍ﴾), meaning: as many in number as you wish of the signs and indications that point to the existence of the Creator (al-Sani'), His oneness, the perfection of His knowledge, power and wisdom, other than this sign of yours (the Prophet's story) which you have brought. ﴿فِي السَّماواتِ والأرْضِ﴾ means: existing in them, namely the celestial bodies and what is in them of stars and the changes of their states, and the mountains, seas, and all the other wonders in the earth that cannot be counted. ﴿يَمُرُّونَ عَلَيْها﴾ means: they see them and pay them no heed. It has also been read with the earth (al-ard) in the nominative (raf'), as a subject (mubtada'), with ﴿يَمُرُّونَ﴾ as its predicate; and it has been read with it in the accusative (nasb), in the sense of "they tread upon the earth and pass by it." In the codex of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud) it reads: (wa-al-arda yamshuna 'alayha, "and they walk upon the earth"). The intended meaning is what they see in it of the traces of the destroyed nations and other signs and lessons. ﴿وَهم عَنْها مُعْرِضُونَ﴾ means: they are not looking at them, nor reflecting upon them.

The Qur'an: "And most of them do not believe in God without associating others with Him" (Yusuf 12:106), as explained by Abu al-Su'ud in Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim:

﴿And most of them do not believe in God﴾ in their acknowledgment of His existence and of His being the Creator, ﴿except that they associate others with Him﴾ by worshipping other than Him, or by taking the rabbis and monks as lords, or by their saying that God has taken a son, exalted is He above that by a great exaltation, or by (believing in) light and darkness. And this is a circumstantial clause (jumlah haliyyah), meaning: most of them do not believe except while in a state of associating others with Him. It has been said: the verse was revealed concerning the people of Makkah; it has been said: concerning the hypocrites; and it has been said: concerning the People of the Book.

﴿Do they then feel secure that an overwhelming punishment from Allah will not come upon them﴾, meaning a punishment (p-310) that will envelop them and encompass them, ﴿or that the Hour will not come upon them suddenly﴾, unexpectedly, without any prior sign, ﴿while they are unaware﴾ of its coming, not prepared for it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 108:

﴿Say: This is my way﴾ — and it is the call to Tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness), to faith (iman), and to sincerity (ikhlas) in devotion. He explained it with His words: ﴿I call to God with insight﴾ — with clear proof (bayan) and evident argument, not blind (ghayr 'amya'). Or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "my way," the governing element in it being the meaning of indication (al-ishara) — "this." "Ana" (I) is an emphatic for the concealed pronoun in "I call" (ad'u); or "with insight" [is the circumstantial clause], since it is a hal from it; or it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is "with insight." ﴿And whoever follows me﴾ is conjoined to it (the pronoun). ﴿And glory be to God; and I am not of the polytheists﴾ is an affirmation of what preceded regarding the call to God.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 109:

﴿And We did not send before you except men﴾ a refutation of their statement: ﴿"Why has an angel not been sent down to him?" (Had Allah willed, He would have sent down angels)﴾ ﴿to whom We revealed⁠⁠ as We revealed to you⁠⁠﴾, and it is also read with the ya' (نُوحِي, "We reveal"). ﴿from among the people of the towns﴾, because they are more knowledgeable and more forbearing, whereas the people of the desert have ignorance, coarseness and harshness in them. ﴿Have they not travelled through the earth and seen how was the end of those before them?﴾ meaning, of those who denied the messengers and the signs, so that they would take warning from your denial. ﴿And the Abode of the Hereafter﴾, that is, the Hour or the Hereafter life, ﴿is better for those who are mindful of Allah﴾, meaning those who avoid polytheism and sins. ﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾ so that you would employ your intellects to recognise the superiority of the Abode of the Hereafter. It is also read with the ya' (يَعْقِلُونَ), on the basis that it is not included under (قُلْ, "say").

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 110:

﴿Until, when the messengers despaired﴾ is a limit (ghayah) for an omitted element that the context indicates, meaning: let not their persistence in what they are in of ease and comfort deceive them, for those before them were given respite until the messengers despaired of victory over them in this world, or of their faith, because of their immersion in disbelief and their persistence in transgression without any restraint. ﴿And they thought that they had been denied﴾: their own selves denied them when they told them that they would be victorious over them, or their hope denied them, for it (hope) is described as truthful and false. The meaning is: the period of denial and enmity from the disbelievers, and waiting for victory from God, the Exalted, had lengthened and extended, until they sensed despair and imagined that there would be no victory for them in this world. ﴿Our victory came to them﴾ suddenly.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father: "And they thought that they had been failed in what God had promised them of victory." If this is authentically transmitted from him, then perhaps he meant by the (word) "thought" what occurs to the mind of whisperings of doubt and self-talk. It was expressed by "thought" only to magnify the matter. As for the thought that is the inclining of one of the two sides over the other, such a thing cannot be conceived from ordinary members of the community, so what then of the prophets, peace and blessings be upon them, and they being who they are, and their rank in knowing the affairs of God, glory be to Him, is their rank.

It was said: the two pronouns refer to those to whom the messengers were sent. It was said: the first refers to them and the second to the messengers. It is also read with shaddah (tashdid), meaning: the messengers thought that the people had denied them regarding what they had threatened them with. It is read with the light form (takhfif) with the active verb, on the basis that the pronoun refers to the messengers, meaning: they thought that they had been lied to by their people regarding what they had reported, when it was delayed from them and they did not see any sign of it; or on the basis that the first refers to their people.

﴿Then whom We will was saved﴾: they are the messengers and the believers in them. It is read ﴿fa-nunajji﴾ in the future form, with light and with shaddah, and it is read ﴿fa-naja﴾. ﴿And Our might is not turned back from the criminal people﴾ when it descends upon them. In this is an explanation of those to whom the will is attached.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 12, verse 111:

﴿Indeed, in their stories there is a lesson for men of understanding.﴾ That is, the stories of the prophets and their peoples. The reading of those who read it with a kasra on the qaf (qiṣaṣ, "stories") supports this. Or it refers to the story of Yusuf and his brothers. ﴿A lesson for men of understanding﴾: for those of sound intellect, purified from the defects of judgments based on sense perception. ﴿It was not﴾, that is, the Qur'an, which is indicated by what preceded it with clear indication, ﴿a narration that is fabricated, but rather﴾ it was ﴿a confirmation of what lies between its hands﴾ of the heavenly scriptures. It was also read with a raised ending (rafʿ), on the basis that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, that is: "but rather it is a confirmation of what lies between its hands." ﴿And a detailed explanation of all things﴾ of what is needed in religion, since there is no religious matter except that it rests upon the Qur'an, either directly or through an intermediary. ﴿And a guidance﴾ from error, ﴿and a mercy﴾ by which the good of both abodes is attained, ﴿for a people who believe﴾, that is, who affirm it, because they are the ones who benefit from it. As for others, they are not guided by its guidance nor do they benefit from its bounty.

From the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Teach your slaves (ʾriqqāʾ) the surah of Yusuf, for whoever among Muslims recites it and teaches it to his family and to those his right hand possesses, Allah will ease for him the agonies of death and give him the strength not to envy a Muslim."

The Fourth Part is complete, and the Fifth Part follows, beginning with Surat al-Ra'd.
